title: When Life Gives You Lemons
prompt: Hey, let's begin with a quick case. Your client is your nephew. He recently opened a lemonade stall for the summer holidays. However, his sales have been really poor. He has come to his favourite relative for increasing his revenue. How would you help him?

notes.title: Questions
items: What are his working hours?
Location of his stall?
Different products that he offers?
Are there any supply constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: No fixed location makes time and area key levers

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Idea of how his mother and father can also help him push sales through their friends

framework:
Candidate: Oh wow, that's interesting! Anything for family. I'd like to understand a few things about my nephew's business. When did he start? What are his working hours like?
Interviewer: He started last week. He works from 2 PM – 5 PM every day except Sunday.
Candidate: Sure. Does he sell different types of lemonades or any other products? Where is his stall located?
Interviewer: He sells only one type of lemonade. He has a small cart that he pushes around the neighbourhood to make his sales.
Candidate: Sure. Who are his main competitors? Does he have supply-side constraints?
Interviewer: There are no other lemonade vendors around him. However, there are quite a few corner shops and supermarkets that sell juices and other substitutes. No, he does not have supply-side constraints. He, in fact, has a lot of lemonade everyday that goes unsold.
Candidate: Sure, I can begin now.
Total Revenue = Revenue per customer * Number of customers
Starting with number of customers – There are 5 strategies he can use:
1) Time - He can change the time he operates. This would require doing research on when there is maximum potential for tapping customers. Two strategies can be used - increase in hours worked and optimum time brackets chosen
2) Area - His biggest advantage is that he can cover a large area through his cart. He can identify hotspots and be there at particular times. For example, near a school or playground. He can also cover a larger part of his neighbourhood.
3) Quality - He needs to ensure that his lemonade is of good quality. The moment word spreads about its taste, he can be sure to garner more daily attention.
4) Marketing - Distributing pamphlets and putting up small banners across his neighbourhood will definitely garner more attention. His mother and father can, in fact, inform all of their friends to purchase their son's lemonade.
5) Different Channels - Instead of just relying on sales through his cart, he can also set up home delivery for his neighbourhood. He can also invite bookings for birthday parties and other gatherings.
Next, we move on to increasing revenue per customer. There are two ways he can increase this - By increasing the price of his product or by increasing the volume sold. Do we have any information on the price he charges?
Interviewer: He sells his lemonade at Rs. 20/glass of 200ml.
Candidate: That seems like a reasonable price. In fact, keeping in mind that his only competition is established stores that have much higher prices, he can probably increase his price to Rs. 25 without seeing a dip in demand.
To increase his volume sold, he can do two things – First, he can offer discounts on every additional purchase or larger purchases. Second, he can increase the products available - Maybe, selling cookies would incentivise people to buy a combo and help him cross-sell.
Interviewer: Brilliant. Seems like you've covered it all. Your nephew thanks you and offers you a free glass of lemonade.
Candidate: Haha, thank you!

title: When Chai Met Toast
prompt: There's a tea-seller inside your college campus whose business is facing a threat from a new Nescafe stall with more attractive and diverse offerings. How can you help this business survive and grow?

notes.title: Questions
items: What are the current offerings?
What is the time frame in which growth has to be achieved?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Price new products below Nescafe to win customers
Look for non-obvious customer segments to score points
Filter every growth idea through short-term versus long-term

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Looking at moving around college to sell more tea under 'Place'

framework:
Candidate: Okay. I will first start by understanding the tea-seller's business and that of the new Nescafe stall. How long has the tea-seller been in the college? Does he sell anything other than tea? How much does he price these products? What is the new Nescafe stall offering? Are there any other food stalls in the campus?
Interviewer: The tea-seller has been in the college for more than 20 years. He sells 3 items – Tea for Rs. 10, Patty for Rs. 20 and Samosa for Rs. 15. The Nescafe stall offers coffee for Rs. 30, Maggi for Rs. 50 and a variety of Sandwiches for Rs. 40 each. There are no other food stalls.
Candidate: Understood. Do we have a specific objective as to how much we are looking to grow the business by and in what time frame?
Interviewer: The tea-seller has suffered great revenue hits already and is looking at strategies he can employ immediately to face the threat. He would like to grow the business by as much as possible.
Candidate: Got it. My approach is going to be divided into 2:
1) Consolidating the existing business – Here, we will look at improving the way the tea seller operates and how he can increase the sales of his items.
2) Venturing into new business – Here, we will explore new products he can introduce, new areas/colleges he can enter, new customer segments he can look at and finally, inorganic growth methods such as partnering with Nescafe, etc.
In addition, we can also look at ways to eliminate the Nescafe threat in a different way altogether. We can get the Principal to interfere in some way or threaten to close shop if Nescafe continues business. These are not very ethical but are options nevertheless.
Interviewer: Hahaha. Let's concentrate on our stall for the time-being.
Candidate: Sure. Let's first look at ways in which we can improve our revenues in our existing business. There are two components to revenue: Number of items sold and price. Any increase in the prices will further reduce demand. If prices are reduced, it will not matter much as the customers are turning to Nescafe even though it is more expensive. Therefore, changing our prices may not make sense. Let's look at how we can increase the number of items sold.
Here, we can look at supply-side and demand-side constraints. Under supply-side, we can look at 3 things – Availability of ingredients, working hours and capacity. Can the tea-seller arrange enough ingredients, plates, etc. if we increase sales? How long is the stall open for? During peak hours, can the tea-seller cater to all customers or does he have to turn some away?
Interviewer: The tea stall is open on all working days. It opens at 10 AM and closes by 5 PM. The tea seller is always able to cater to all customers, no matter the rush.
Candidate: Maybe the tea seller can consider opening a little earlier as college classes usually start earlier and tea is most demanded in the morning.
Interviewer: Makes sense. Let's move on to demand.
Candidate: Sure. Here, I am interested in 2 things:
1) Experience: Can we improve the taste of the items? Can they be served differently to appeal to more people? Perhaps, a cup that insulates the heat so that it is easy to hold the hot cup of tea.
2) Place: The tea seller can consider changing the location of the stall as well. Somewhere with more seating area, shade, etc. can be explored. Locations that are at some distance from the Nescafe stall would also make sense. Can a person go around to classes and sell the tea inside these rooms as well?
Interviewer: The tea seller likes your idea of going around the campus to sell tea. Is there anything else you want to look at?
Candidate: Yes. We can now look at new products, new areas/campuses, new customer segments and inorganic growth possibilities. Since we are looking for strategies we can implement immediately, it will not make sense to expand to new areas. Under new products, we can look at offering coffee as well. Since our coffee will be cheaper than Nescafe's, price-sensitive customers will return to our stall. In addition, packet food such as chips, snacks, etc. can be introduced as well. During the summer, cool drinks are in demand. Maybe the tea-seller can buy or rent a refrigerator so that he can serve these as well.
Looking at new customer segments, the seller can come up with sugar-free options and classroom delivery for elderly faculty.
Candidate: Should we look at inorganic growth options as well?
Interviewer: That won't be needed. We can end the case here.

When Chai Met Toast Framework & Recommendations
TEA-SELLER VS NESCAFE STALL
Clarifying Questions: What are the current offerings? What is the time frame in which growth has to be achieved?
Brownie Points: Looking at moving around college to sell more tea under 'Place'

title: Netflix & Chill
prompt: You're the CEO of Netflix India and the company has grown by 5x over the previous year and they want to grow by 3x for each of the next 3 years. How will you go about this?

notes.title: Questions
items: How do we define growth?
How is the competition doing?
Are there any constraints we have?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: New verticals split into content and non-content revenue

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Regional language content in India
Government channels for new customers

framework:
Candidate: I have a few preliminary questions; how are we defining growth here? Are there any budgetary or regulatory constraints for us to keep in mind? Also, I wanted to understand the market landscape better in terms of how competitors are performing and the trajectory they're on.
Interviewer: Here, growth refers to the growth in terms of revenue. We can figure the rest out during the discussion, but generally, work without any limiting factors.
Candidate: If we have grown 5x and then we want to go 3x, 3x and 3x, that is a total of 135x of growth over 4 years, which is massive. For this level of growth, we need to work on large-scale ideas and solutions.
Interviewer: Yes. Why don't you jump right into the ideas?
Candidate: Broadly, there are two ways for us to grow - organically and inorganically. Under organic growth, we would look at expanding the scale and scope of our own operations whereas inorganic growth would involve acquiring or partnering with other companies.
Interviewer: Why don't you start off with the organic segment?
Candidate: Sure. There are two primary levers that we can look at - increasing our number of customers or the average revenue per customer. Since this is a market which is quite far from saturation, there are two approaches here. The first would be growing the market as a whole and the second, to increase our own share of the market.
Interviewer: What will you consider under the market?
Candidate: If we look at the market as a whole, we need to understand the customer standpoint and solve the following 3 problems: availability of devices, accessibility of adequate internet and interest/inclination towards the content.
Interviewer: Let's now focus on Netflix specifically and not on the market.
Candidate: At the highest level, we can segment it into 'current business verticals' and 'new verticals', in terms of the content strategy since that also drives which audience we're catering to. There are two different focus areas we can adopt over here: regional language content and individual content. On the former, we can greatly expand content in regional languages, which is where a huge chunk of the Indian market demand lies and OTT still has sufficient scope for penetration. On the other hand, a YouTube-inspired structure where content can be uploaded more freely, similar to that of Amazon Prime, might help us attract fresh content from upcoming creators, with predefined quality controls.
Interviewer: That sounds good for our current channels. What else can we do?
Candidate: We can segment other sources into new content types and non-content revenue sources. In terms of new content types, we can consider podcasts, music and television channels, which can further be split into news & other channels. Offering these might bring Netflix closer to a content super-app if integrated well. On the other hand, we can consider two things: merchandise and new devices. Since Netflix features a lot of shows and movies with a massive fan following, there is an extremely high demand for souvenirs, memorabilia, fan items, gifts and the like, which is fulfilled by other companies altogether. By doing this under the Netflix brand itself, we might be able to attract many fans who look for authentic sources. In the case of new devices, AR goggles or VR handsets might be interesting to consider, especially if we can convert our content into compatible versions and make the customer viewing experience more immersive.
Interviewer: Okay, what else?
Candidate: Having looked at the number of customers, I'd also like to consider the average revenue per user, or more broadly, our payment model. Currently, Netflix offers various plans that all have an unlimited subscription, i.e. access to all of Netflix's content under one scheme. There are two alternate levels of disaggregation possible: thematic and individual. Under thematic, we could club a large number of titles under genres such as Sports, Reality Shows, etc and offer purchase bundles for these. In addition, specific events such as the IPL, Worldwide Wrestling Entertainment and Olympics or even individual movies & shows can be offered on a pay-per-view basis.
Interviewer: Great. Now imagine your Board of Directors comes and tells you that you have a blank cheque. Give me 3 of the craziest ideas that you would like to implement.
Candidate: First, we can launch Netflix T.V. on which only our content runs and we can push them at an extremely low price point. This way, we'll acquire an entirely new type of customer base who was out of the affordability net earlier, as they can't switch over to other competitors easily. Second, we can buy out all the government channels (like Doordarshan, Lok Sabha T.V, Rajya Sabha T.V, etc) as it will help to increase our reach within a demographic group that might not engage with Netflix currently - such as senior citizens, individuals disconnected from other styles of content, etc. Third, we can buy exclusive media rights to events which take place in arenas and stadiums. Then, whatever events happen there automatically work with exclusive streaming rights for Netflix and help us generate a huge repository of content.
Interviewer: Lovely! Thanks for your input, have a great day ahead.

Netflix & Chill Framework & Recommendations
IDEA GENERATION FOR GROWTH
Clarifying Questions: How do we define growth? How is the competition doing? Are there any constraints we have?
Brownie Points: Regional language content in India Government channels for new customers
Keep In Mind: Avoid details unless asked about them. The interviewer wanted to test the range of ideas, and not the depth.

title: The Hunger Games
prompt: Your client is a restaurant owner. He has asked you to identify possible ways of doubling the restaurant's monthly revenue in 1 month. March, 2021 had 'x' revenue. We wish to get to '2x' revenue in April, 2021.

notes.title: Questions
items: Where is it located?
What is the cuisine and customer segment?
What is the current company and industry growth rate?
Is the COVID-19 scenario in scope?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: One month timeframe rules out long payback strategies
COVID lockdown, so prioritise the delivery channel first

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Home-centered celebrations
Introducing safety measures such as health monitoring
Incorporating rural demand

framework:
Candidate: Sure. With the objective of doubling the revenue next month in mind, I would like to begin by understanding the restaurant better. Where are the locations in which the restaurant is present? Are there multiple outlets of the restaurant? If yes, how many? What type of a restaurant is it in terms of the cuisine and the category of customers it caters to? Lastly, as we are looking at April 2021, would it be fair to incorporate the COVID-19 scenario for the purpose of the case?
Interviewer: Yes, let's look at the scenario posed by the pandemic. The restaurant has 10 outlets in Delhi. It is a restaurant popular for its biryani (veg and non-veg). In fact, Biryani is their only dish. The restaurant caters to high-income customers. You can compare it to something like Behrouz.
Candidate: Alright. What is our current growth rate?
Interviewer: Our current growth rate is 14%.
Candidate: Sure. Just to understand it in relative terms, what is the industry's growth rate?
Interviewer: The industry's growth is close to 14% as well.
Candidate: Alright. So, our client is doing fairly well. What are the major sources of revenue? I guess they are orders and advertisements (if any).
Interviewer: Our client doesn't have any revenues from advertisements.
Candidate: Perhaps, as part of our approach, we can look at adding other sources of revenue. I will get to this after laying down my overall approach.
Interviewer: Let's focus on revenue from orders.
Candidate: Thank you, sure! Revenue Growth can be achieved by either: a) Organic means b) Inorganic means - Joint Venture and Acquisitions.
Interviewer: You can limit your analysis to organic means of growth.
Candidate: In terms of organic means,
^ Revenue = Number of restaurants * Revenue per restaurant
As we are looking at a span of just one month, I would like to rule out the possibility of increasing the number of restaurants. Also, considering the lockdown in Delhi, I would like to start off by focusing on the delivery aspect and then move on to dine-in and take-outs.
Interviewer: That sounds good. Let's focus on revenue per restaurant in the delivery segment.
Candidate: Sure.
^ Revenue per restaurant = Average number of orders * Average bill value
1) Under Average number of orders, we can look at:
  a) Supply: If we are not meeting the demand or have the potential to increase supply, we can look at
    i) Increasing our capacity by installing more machinery and improving our kitchens' efficiency
    ii) Hiring more employees and increasing their efficiency
    iii) Exploring the option of cloud kitchens. A cloud kitchen is a delivery-only restaurant that has no physical space for dine-in. This has become exceedingly popular during the pandemic with restaurants exploring innovative ways to cut costs.
  b) Distribution: Existing Channels & New Channels
    i) Adding channels of distribution like Zomato, Swiggy, Dine Out. We can also start our own delivery system like Dominos, etc.
    ii) Optimising the distance for ordering & delivery - if there is a 10 km radius, perhaps we can increase it to gain more customers.
    iii) Increasing the size of our delivery fleet to ensure speedy delivery and increased demand.
  c) Demand: This is the driver which has the maximum potential to increase revenue. Hence, I will look at this in greater detail. Ways in which we can increase demand are:
    i) Need - Creating demand by branding the Biryani as a comfort home food and an attractive alternative to fast food.
    ii) Awareness - Marketing the business and our Biryani by adopting strategies such as paying aggregators like Zomato to be on their homepage and, if possible, be the top choice when someone searches 'Biryani' or 'non-vegetarian dishes'.
    iii) Accessibility - Ensuring last-mile connectivity for delivery would be effective. This is based on a fact that I read about how 1 out of every 5 pre-covid orders placed from urban areas is now being placed from a rural area due to people moving back home.
    iv) Affordability - Adding discounts on large orders, festival season, etc., having coupons and free add-ons or condiments after a certain order value will increase demand.
    v) Experience - We can look at improving individual aspects of our value chain from cooking to packaging and then to delivering. We can focus on marketing the 'luxury' and 'safety' aspects of our Biryani, add a make-your-own biryani box, etc. Additionally, we can look at introducing pleasing aesthetics through packaging, adding a note inside, etc.
2) Moving to the Average Bill Value, we can look at the following aspects:
  a) Average Price: I would like to exclude this component because increasing the price of items just to double revenue for a month can have adverse long-term effects. Also, price is highly-dependent on competitor benchmarking. However, one possible reason we can give for a slight increase in prices can be for additional safety measures we have undertaken such as including sanitizer sachets and regular health monitoring of delivery executives. On the other hand, decreasing the price won't be suitable for this situation as we cater to the premium segment which is not very price-sensitive.
  b) Average Order Size:
    i) Decoy marketing - a strategy adopted to push sales of a dish by asymmetrically presenting product sizes to push sales of larger quantities.
    ii) Add-Ons - free items with higher-priced meals.
    iii) Cross-selling - incorporating combinations like family meals that are economic but induce the customers to spend more.
  c) Product Mix:
    i) Adding complementary products to the menu - raita, papad, salad etc.
    ii) Introducing other North-Indian dishes.
Interviewer: That was very comprehensive, I don't have any follow-up questions for you. The client will be sure to incorporate your suggestions. Do you have anything else to add?
Candidate: Yes indeed. With the lockdown in place, the society has shifted to a world of home-centered celebrations including birthdays, anniversaries, promotions, etc. We could partner with shops selling party props and/or cakes so that a customer gets the convenience to meet all requirements through our outlets.
As mentioned before, this was all about the delivery side of the business; we can incorporate these changes in our dine-in and take-out side of the business too once the lockdown is lifted.
Interviewer: That's perfect! We can end the case now.

The Hunger Games Framework & Recommendations
DOUBLING THE REVENUES OF A BIRYANI CHAIN IN DELHI
Clarifying Questions: Where is it located? What is the cuisine and customer segment of the restaurant?
Brownie Points: Home-centered celebrations Introducing safety measures such as health monitoring Incorporating rural demand Cloud kitchens Decoy marketing
Keep In Mind: There is no strict framework to solve a case, you can always customize frameworks and merge multiple frameworks according to the case.

title: Udta Punjab
prompt: Chandigarh Airport is looking to sell 20% of its airport to Private Equity. I would like your help in figuring out two things: A) At what price should they sell? B) What should they do before selling?

notes.title: Questions
items: Objective for selling?
Potential buyers on the table?
Any regulatory hurdles?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Offer all three valuation methods before picking one
Revenue multiple is fixed, so pull the revenue lever

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Identifying that growing 2x by increasing prices will not be sustainable

visualisations.title: Comparable Company Analysis
rows: A x (1.05)³ at 5% CAGR for 3 yrs
Discount F at 10% for 3 yrs (waived by interviewer)
visualisations.insight: Revenue multiple is industry-driven; with strong buyer interest the high end (7x) is assumed. Discounting to present value was waived by the interviewer, so the synergy-adjusted ₹540 cr is the indicative price for the 20% stake.

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. Can you please tell me a little bit more about this airport?
Interviewer: The airport generates sizeable revenue at par with its peers; it has three runways and caters to both domestic as well as international travellers.
Candidate: Why are they looking to sell? And why only 20%?
Interviewer: Chandigarh Airport has a lot of debt on its balance sheet which it now wants to retire within 3 years. The owners believe that they can get the required capital by selling approximately 20% of ownership and do not want to dilute their stake further.
Candidate: Are there any potential buyers on the table? I am asking because a greater interest in the asset can help our client dominate the negotiations.
Interviewer: There are quite a few boutique funds that have shown interest.
Candidate: Are there any regulatory hurdles that can stop this sale?
Interviewer: We have received a green-light from the regulators to go ahead with the stake sale.
Candidate: Got it. One last question: Is there any specific reason why we are looking to sell only to Private Equity?
Interviewer: No reason as such. Can you think of other strategic investors that we can bring onboard?
Candidate: Sure. They can be airlines (to give themselves preferential treatment like Bangkok airlines), airports (Changi airport in Singapore actively looks out for such investments) as well as certain government entities.
Interviewer: Excellent! Now that we are open to selling it to other players as well, how would you value the 20% stake?
Candidate: We can do this in three ways:
1. Discounted Cash Flow Analysis in which we discount future cash flows the entity is expected to earn and discount them to present value.
2. Comparable Company Analysis in which we can look at the peers and related metrics like P/E Ratio, revenue multiples, etc.
3. Precedent Transactions and how the companies were valued in such transactions if any data is available.
Interviewer: Alright, very comprehensive. Let's assume that the total revenue for the Airport in the last financial year was ₹300 crores. They are projected to grow at a CAGR of 5% in the next three years. Peer valuations have normally varied from 5x to 7x of revenue. What can be an ideal price for us to look at?
Candidate: Going with the comparable companies analysis, revenue after three years comes out to be approximately 350 crores. Since we have enormous interest, we can assume a higher revenue multiple for the purpose of this valuation. That leads to ₹2,450 crores (350 x 7). Since we are looking to sell only a 20% stake, the desired value comes out to be ₹490 crores.
As we have opened up to courting other strategic investors as well, we can include a premium over and above this price to account for the synergies. Assuming this to be 10%, we can look at a price of approximately ₹540 crores. We should now discount this value to get the present value for 3 years at 10% discounting rate.
Interviewer: Nicely done! You can ignore the discounting for now. Since Chandigarh Airport has a maximum of three years to complete this sale, they want to try and double the price that they can currently charge from a potential buyer. How can they make this possible?
Candidate: This can be done in two ways. We can either increase the revenue multiple or increase the revenue. Since we cannot control the revenue multiple as it is an industry-driven metric, we can unlock more monetization opportunities and increase the revenue potential coupled with greater margins.
Interviewer: Why don't you tell me about some ways of increasing our revenues organically?
Candidate:^ Revenue = Price x Quantity
Dynamic pricing can be introduced in several revenue line items based on demand. Along with that, inflation expectations will also increase prices. However, since we are talking about 2x growth and increasing prices by 2x in three years is impossible, I would like to focus on other things.
Interviewer: Sure, go ahead.
Candidate: We can look at this from two aspects: increasing revenue by introducing new offerings/revenue streams or increasing revenue by tweaking/modifying old revenue streams.
Interviewer: Just give me a few broad ideas to explore as soon as they occur to you. You don't have to write things down.
Candidate: For new offerings: We can look at making the airport accessible for non-flying tourists and earn ticketing revenue from them by building attractive parks/entertainment halls like the Singapore airport, leasing out excess land that is not under aviation use to earn rental income, partnering with new-age electrical mobility solutions to ease travel inside the airport and introducing technical tours to demonstrate how an airport is run as well as on-property accommodation in the form of hotels. These are some ideas that I could think of on top of my head. Would you want me to build further on this or move on to older revenue streams?
Interviewer: That won't be necessary. We can close the case here. Thank you for taking out the time.

Udta Punjab Framework & Recommendations
STAKE SALE OF CHANDIGARH AIRPORT
Clarifying Questions: Objective for selling? Potential buyers on the table? Any regulatory hurdles?
Brownie Points: Identifying that growing 2x by increasing prices will not be sustainable
Keep In Mind: Sometimes, the interviewer would want you to give ideas without structuring or writing them down
RECOMMENDATIONS:
Revenue can be increased by:
Increasing new offerings by opening up the airport to non-flying tourists, leasing out excess land, introducing technical tours, etc.
Modifying existing offerings

title: Risk It for the Biscuit
prompt: Hey. Your client is ABC Food Inc, a famous biscuit manufacturer. They have been facing a drop in sales for 3 years and want to grow their market share. They have approached you for the same.

notes.title: Questions
items: Location of client?
Target growth percentage?
Segmenting decline geographically
Single product or multiple types of biscuits?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Diagnose the root cause before proposing growth ideas
Frame a hypothesis early and let the interviewer validate it
Raise M&A proactively when there is only one competitor

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Cultural fit as important consideration before merging or acquiring

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. I'd like to understand the problem a little better. Where is our client located? How many different types of biscuits do they produce? How much is their current market share and by how much do they want to increase their market share?
Interviewer: The client is located Pan-India. For the purpose of this case, assume they sell one kind of biscuit – the Salted Biscuit. Their market share has been steadily dropping. It is currently at 30%. They want to bring it to 40%.
Candidate: Has the decline in market share been Pan-India?
Interviewer: No, in fact, the decline has been only in Gujarat.
Candidate: Interesting. I'd like to divide my approach into 2. First, I'd like to understand the cause for decline in sales and then come up with strategies to increase market share.
Interviewer: You can proceed with your approach.
Candidate: Analysing the declining sales, I would like to break it into the 3 steps of the value chain - Production, Distribution and Demand. Under production, I'd like to understand if there have been any changes causing us to not meet the demand. Either reduction in capacity or reduced efficiency. Under Distribution, I'd like to understand if there has been any change in the number of distributors we have and the amount sold by each distributor. Lastly, I'd like to understand if there has been a decline in the demand for our biscuits.
My hypothesis is that the decline has to be due to a decline in demand since a drop of this magnitude lasting for over 3 years comes mostly from a customer pull issue.
Interviewer: You're right. Analyse demand.
Candidate: Under Demand, there are 4 main segments I'd like to understand. Company, Competitors, Customers and Product.
Under company, factors like firm's goals, its competencies and strategies employed to achieve them. Under competitors, factors like nature of the market, market share and competitor competencies over us become important. Under customers, factors like consumer behaviour, values, demographics shall be analysed. Lastly, under Product, the nature of the product is analysed to see if it meets customer needs and expectations. Is there any one segment you'd like me to analyse?
Interviewer: Why don't you look at competitors?
Candidate: Sure. I'd like to understand how many competitors exist and how they have been performing in the last 3 years. More importantly, have any of their market shares increased in the last 3 years? Has there been a new entrant in the market?
Interviewer: Great. There is one other competitor, Canoli Inc, that exists in the market. As you have identified correctly, their market share has been consistently growing.
Candidate: Ahaa! I'd now like to pin point exactly why Canoli are able to attract customers better than us. Here, I'd like to look at Product, Price, Promotion and Place.
a) Product - Are they offering a superior product?
b) Price - Is their price better?
c) Promotion - Are they marketing their product better? Is their publicity better?
d) Place - Are they available in more accessible and prominent channels/within the outlets?
Interviewer: Yes! Canolli inc offers a superior product because of the superior raw materials they use. Can you think of why the client hasn't done the same?
Candidate: Sure! It might be because:
1) We don't have access to superior raw materials due to certain constraints
2) We have access, but can't maintain price competitiveness if we purchase them
3) We don't have the same supplier relations as our competitors do.
Interviewer: Perfect. Canolli Inc sources its flour from the US and therefore has superior quality. We can't do the same. Why don't we now analyse methods to increase sales?
Candidate: Sure. Since sales is equal to Number of customers x Revenue per customer, we shall try to increase both of them.
Under Revenue per customer, we can try to increase the volume per customer and/or the price charged per serving. Increasing the volume would involve loyalty programmes and incentives for larger purchases. Both volume and price increase are unlikely to happen since we have identified the problem as quality as compared to competitors.
Under Number of customers, we can try and increase customers through 4 methods. Target new customers in the same geographies, target new customers in different geographies, mimicking competitor quality to gain customers, merge or acquire competitors. Targeting customers in different geographies is irrelevant since we are aiming at increasing sales in Gujarat. Replicating competitor quality too is irrelevant since we have understood that they source potatoes from the US.
Candidate: Is there any possibility of merging/acquiring Canolli Inc to increase sales?
Interviewer: There might be. What would you need to know to analyse if that would be the right decision?
Candidate: The following considerations would be important:
1) Willingness of both companies to merge
2) Our ability to acquire
3) Synergies
4) Public perception
5) Government permissions (Competitive laws, licensing requirements, etc.)
6) Compatibility of management styles and cultural fit.
Interviewer: We have learnt that our client is unwilling to merge. All other factors seem to be in our favour. How would you determine if we can and should acquire Canolli Inc?
Candidate: Our ability to acquire would primarily depend on the value of the Gujarat division of Canolli Inc. This value should be compared with the potential increase in sales due to the acquisition since we would then have a stronghold over the market. Thus, if the sales after acquisition justifies the price of acquisition and helps to achieve the 10% increase in market share, we should go ahead with acquisition, provided we can arrange the funds for the same.
Interviewer: Perfect. Thank you for your time. We can close the case here.

Risk It for the Biscuit Framework & Recommendations
TURNAROUND STRATEGIES FOR ABC FOOD INC.
Clarifying Questions: Location of client? Target growth percentage? Segmenting decline geographically?
Brownie Points: Cultural fit as important consideration before merging or acquiring
Keep In Mind: Attempts to increase sales must focus on existing weaknesses in the company to gain maximum growth

title: Make India Great Again
prompt: You're a politician in India and your objective is to increase the number of people who vote in the next municipal election. How would you go about it?

notes.title: Questions
items: When is the next election?
How much power do we have?
Is there a specific objective?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Scope the problem using power and timeline

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Ensuring anonymity to guarantee voter safety
Ruling out eligibility given the timeline

visualisations.title: Votes Cast
visualisations.rhs: Eligible Population × % Who Want To Vote × % Who Are Able To Vote

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. I would like to begin by understanding how far we are from the next election, and whether we have a specific objective in mind.
Interviewer: You can assume the election takes place in a week, and the only objective is to increase the number of people who show up to cast a vote.
Candidate: Got it. We can look at this situation through a simple relation.
^ Number of people who vote = Eligible Population * % Who Want To Vote * % Who Are Able To Vote
Given that we only have a week left, we cannot change the eligibility to vote, because issuing voter ID cards takes time.
Interviewer: Correct. You can look at the percentage who want to vote first, and then move on to the next one.
Candidate: Sure. Is it fair to assume that this politician has substantial power to implement changes, such as policy changes?
Interviewer: Yes, you can assume that.
Candidate: Under willingness, we can look at:
1) Awareness: with the right funding, multiple ad campaigns can be run to draw voters.
2) Number of voting centres: they must be located in convenient areas.
3) Counters per voting centre: increasing the number of booths reduces the time taken per person, and EVMs can be used to reduce turnover time.
4) Amenities: drinking water, a waiting area, washrooms and similar facilities must be available at every booth.
5) Anonymity: the anonymity of every vote must be ensured to guarantee the safety of voters.
Interviewer: Anything else under willingness? Otherwise we can move to the percentage who are able to vote.
Candidate: We can move to the second part. Under ability, we can look at:
1) Timings: the number of hours in which one can vote can be increased, and optimum timings can be chosen.
2) Day chosen: if a weekend is chosen, it is convenient for working professionals to vote.
3) Disability-friendly: wheelchair facilities, ramps and similar arrangements can be ensured so that disabled and elderly people are able to cast their vote.
4) Incentives: companies must be encouraged to give people time off if they can prove they are voting, and monetary incentives can also be implemented.
5) Day care facilities: free day care for one day can be implemented to enable people with children to vote.
Interviewer: Great. We can close the case now.

Make India Great Again Framework
INCREASING THE NUMBER OF VOTES CAST
Clarifying Questions: When is the next election? How much power do we have? Is there a specific objective?
Brownie Points: Ensuring anonymity to guarantee voter safety. Ruling out eligibility given the timeline.
Keep In Mind: Scope the problem using the politician's power and the timeline.

title: Mo Money, Mo Problems
prompt: Your client is the Government of India. They have approached you to help increase the number of digital transactions in the country.

notes.title: Questions
items: What are digital transactions?
What constraints are we under?
What is the target?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Split the metric into users and frequency

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Reducing small-denomination currency in the system
Adding utility via bill splitting and expense management

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. Do they have a target as to how much they want to increase digital transactions by, and in what time frame? Are there any budgetary or other constraints we must keep in mind?
Interviewer: They want to increase it by as much as possible in the next six to twelve months. There are no constraints.
Candidate: I also want to clarify what we mean by digital transactions. Are we referring to NEFT, RTGS, Card, UPI and e-Wallet payments?
Interviewer: Precisely.
Candidate: Okay, there is a lot we can do. I would like to break down the problem using the following relation.
^ Number of digital transactions = Number of people transacting digitally * Number of digital transactions per person
First, we can look at ways in which we can bring more people to try digital payments. Next, we can look at increasing the number of transactions they perform digitally. In order to increase the number of people, we can look at Need, Awareness, Accessibility, Affordability and Experience.
Interviewer: Sure, I am interested to see the suggestions you come up with.
Candidate: First, it is important to establish a need for digital modes of payment. In order to do this, the government can consider passing laws to make digital payments compulsory in certain cases, for example, payments larger than twenty thousand rupees cannot be made in cash. One advantage of digital payments is that there is no problem of loose change. The government can cut the flow of currency notes of low denominations in the system and nudge people towards digital transactions.
Under Awareness, the government can look at two things: Advertisements and a prominent Presence. The advantages of digital transactions can be marketed to people through television ads, hoardings and similar channels. A drive can be conducted to get more shops, including those in rural areas, to introduce digital payment options so that more people know about these platforms. This should first be implemented across all government undertakings, including post offices and ration shops.
Accessibility is of utmost importance when it comes to digital transactions. Most of these payments require a bank account, so the option of creating zero-balance bank accounts must be pushed to citizens. Since smartphones and the internet still have limited penetration, the government must push these simultaneously. However, six to twelve months may not be enough to do this, so we can look at creating an alternative, say a feature on BHIM where payments can be made by purchasers simply by giving their UPI ID and an OTP.
Under Affordability, most digital payment platforms like Google Pay and PayTM are already free for users. However, an attempt can be made to reduce debit and credit card charges across the country. Subsidised smartphones and data plans will also contribute to the cause.
Under Experience, I would like to look at two things: establishing trust and building a seamless experience. It must be reinforced to citizens that digital transactions are safe. This can be done through publicity, public assurances and similar measures. Linking this to other consumer welfare programs, we can ensure adequate compensation in case of any mishandling of money by vendors or payment intermediaries.
Interviewer: This seems very comprehensive. Is there anything else you would like to touch upon?
Candidate: Yes, we are still left with the task of increasing the number of transactions per person. This can be done by increasing the acceptability of digital transactions, incentivising a higher volume of transactions, and increasing utility. Under Acceptability, it should be ensured that digital payments are accepted by more and more vendors. For example, electricity bills and gas bills should allow UPI payment, and laws can be eased for cross-country digital transactions. Under Incentives, platforms can offer cashbacks, loyalty bonuses and similar rewards. Platforms can also offer other services like expense management and bill splitting to increase utility.
Interviewer: Excellent! The government thanks you for your help.

Mo Money, Mo Problems Framework
INCREASE THE NUMBER OF DIGITAL TRANSACTIONS IN THE COUNTRY
Clarifying Questions: What are digital transactions? What constraints are we under? What is the target and timeframe?
Brownie Points: Reducing small-denomination currency in the system. Adding utility via bill splitting and expense management.
Keep In Mind: Split the metric into users and frequency.

title: Gold Digger
prompt: Your client is the Ministry of Sports under the Government of India. It has been concerned with India's performance in the track and field events at the Olympics. It has hired you to come up with a plan of action to improve India's performance and increase the number of gold medals it wins.

notes.title: Questions
items: What does improving performance mean?
How many gold medals are we targeting?
Are there any constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Phase the problem into pre, during, and post.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Catching the trick question on the Olympics year.
Planning ahead for the next Olympics too.

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. I would like to understand the problem a little better. What do we mean by improving performance? How many gold medals does the ministry want to raise its tally to? And what is the time horizon to achieve this?

Interviewer: Sure. Improving performance basically means increasing the gold medal tally. Let us say the number it wants to reach is five gold medals, and it would like to get there by the 2026 Olympics.

Candidate: Forgive me, but isn't the Olympics scheduled for 2024 and then 2028?

Interviewer: Good catch. Let us proceed with the 2028 Olympics.

Candidate: Great. So that gives us about seven years to work with. Lastly, are there any constraints I should keep in mind?

Interviewer: No, there are none. Go ahead with your approach.

Candidate: I see roughly three phases of work here: a preparatory phase, a during the event phase, and a post event phase. The preparatory phase is the most important, so I will start there. I would split it into two parts, resources and implementation.

Under resources, I would look at the quality of the athletes, the infrastructure, the equipment, and the support staff. For the athletes in particular, I would think about by whom they are selected, how many we need, and by when this selection has to be done.

Interviewer: Go ahead. What would you do once those resources are in place?

Candidate: Under implementation, I want to make the best use of these resources, so I would separate it into direct efforts and indirect efforts. Direct efforts act on the athletes themselves: structured training programmes, team coordination, building chemistry within the squad, and familiarity with the playing conditions. One important step here is acclimatising the athletes to the host country by arranging a trip about a year before the event. Indirect efforts happen around the athletes: research and analysis of the other teams, and internal motivational schemes to keep the squad driven.

Interviewer: Got it. What about during and after the event?

Candidate: In the during the event phase, I would look at two things, opponent strategy and motivation. Under opponent strategy, I would analyse the individual teams and athletes we are up against and build a specific game day plan for each of them. This also includes lobbying, where the ministry can request that the schedule and travel for the Indian athletes are not made too strenuous.

Under motivation, I would start with game day readiness, such as proper hydration and rest before each event. I would also use the media and the home crowd. We can subsidise and encourage Indians, both from home and those already living in the host country, to attend the events. A full stadium means constant cheering and a real lift for our athletes.

Interviewer: That covers it. And after the event?

Candidate: The post event phase is about the incentives that exist once athletes bring home medals. I would look at recognition, such as national level sports awards, and monetary incentives, such as cash bonuses. We can also name stadiums and grounds after the athletes as a lasting honour. Finally, I would make sure they get enough rest before we begin preparing them for the next Olympics.

Interviewer: Solid. I like that you also thought about preparing for the Olympics beyond the one in question. We can end the case here.

GOLD DIGGER FRAMEWORK & RECOMMENDATIONS

INCREASE THE GOLD MEDAL TALLY TO 5

Clarifying Questions: What does improving performance mean? How many gold medals are we targeting? What is the time horizon? Are there any constraints?

Brownie Points: Catching the trick question on the Olympics year. Planning ahead for the next Olympics too.

Keep In Mind: Phase the problem into pre, during, and post. Open-ended cases need at least three layers.

title: Rating Neil, Nitin and Mukesh
prompt: We need to develop an online portal to rate actors and actresses in Bollywood. Develop a framework to rate them.

notes.title: Questions
items: Purpose behind the ratings?
Who will use the portal?
An app or a website?
What permissions are required?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Bucket criteria first, then score and weight.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Accounting for the artist's personality
Highlighting the importance of social endeavours

framework:
Candidate: May I know the purpose behind rating these actors and actresses? This will help me come up with the relevant parameters to include in the approach.
Interviewer: The portal will be for the general public who follow the industry. Think of it as an IMDb for actors and actresses.
Candidate: Got it. Should we also look at how the portal will be set up, whether it will be an app or a website, and what permissions we will need to obtain?
Interviewer: That will not be necessary. We are only interested in the rating approach.
Candidate: Okay. My approach would be to first list the relevant parameters that the artists will be judged on. Next, we can assign weights to each of these parameters to complete the structure. If time permits, we can try rating a famous actor or actress using this scale and see if it makes sense. Shall I go ahead with this?
Interviewer: Sure, go ahead.
Candidate: I would like to divide the parameters into three buckets: Movies, Recognition, and Personality.
Under Movies, we should look at the number and quality of movies done by the artist. This shows how much the artist is in demand, which is usually an indicator of skill and popularity. Movies that perform better can be assigned bonus points. Next, we can look at the diversity of roles played by the artist. Actors like Amitabh Bachchan have played diverse roles, which shows their versatility. Third, the number of years the artist has been in the industry is a testament to their experience and continuing relevance in a cut-throat industry. Lastly, we can look at the artist's presence outside Bollywood. For example, Priyanka Chopra has worked alongside names like Zac Efron and enjoys a fan following across the globe.
Moving on to Recognition, we can look at two things: Awards and Popularity. Their performance in award shows like Filmfare and IIFA provides an objective source to judge their performance. This will also lend credibility to our rating. Popularity can be judged by their fan following on social media platforms, the number of times their names appear in Google searches, surveys, and so on.
In today's world, personality is of increasing importance. People look up to artists not just for the work they do but also for their public image. Actors like Sonu Sood have led the way with their social endeavours. While positive activities like charity events can bring points to the artist, negative activities such as hit-and-run cases can lead to a deduction in points. Additionally, many actors and actresses have a well-rounded personality. In addition to acting, some have even ventured into production, singing, and more. We can keep this in mind as well.
Is there anything else we should include in the approach?
Interviewer: It seems very comprehensive. I like your point about including personality. Not many would have thought of that. You can briefly discuss how you will assign weights to the parameters. Then we can end the case.
Candidate: Sure. First, we can make a list of all the parameters in decreasing order of importance. For example, "diversity of roles" will certainly be prioritized over "number of charity events done by the artist". Accordingly, we will assign a higher weight to the parameter higher up in the list. While we make the list, we can also keep in mind the reliability of the parameter. For example, the "number of awards won" can be given a higher weight, as it is a more objective parameter compared to "presence outside Bollywood".
Interviewer: Great.

Rating Neil, Nitin and Mukesh Framework & Recommendations
DEVELOPING AN ONLINE PORTAL FOR RATING ACTORS IN BOLLYWOOD
Clarifying Questions: Purpose behind the ratings? Who will use the portal? An app or a website? What permissions are required?
Brownie Points: Accounting for the artist's personality. Highlighting the importance of social endeavours.
Keep In Mind: Weight parameters by objectivity, not just importance. Bucket criteria first, then score and weight.

title: Left Me High and Dry
prompt: Your client is an online retailer of clothes and has been facing a problem of high churn rate on their payment gateway. You need to analyse why this is happening and give recommendations accordingly.

notes.title: Questions
items: What clothes and target market?
Are competitors facing this?
Do we use a third party?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Map every step of the payment journey.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Isolating the OTP delay as company-specific.

framework:
Candidate: Interesting problem. Before I get into the analysis, I would like to understand our client a little better. What kind of clothes do they sell, and who is the target market?

Interviewer: Our client sells jeans for both men and women, and the target market is everyone in the age bracket of 18 to 50.

Candidate: Got it. A few more clarifiers. Since when have we been facing this problem? Is the churn uniform across modes, and have our competitors reported anything similar? For context, churn rate here is the share of customers who stop using the product over a given period.

Interviewer: This has been the case ever since the website launched. You can consider the churn high enough that we need to act on it, and you do not need to size it. Our competitors have reported no such issues.

Candidate: Sure. What are the modes of payment the website offers, and is the decline uniform across all of them? Also, is it fair to assume we use a third-party payment gateway?

Interviewer: We offer credit and debit cards, PayTM and Google Pay. The decline is fairly uniform across all modes. And yes, we have a partnership with a third party.

Candidate: Understood. I would like to analyse the high churn by breaking the payment journey into two stages, the stage of directing the user to the payment gateway and the stage of actually making the payment.

In the first stage, directing the user to the gateway, I would look at:
1) Obstruction, such as banners appearing on the screen
2) Convenience, mainly the time taken to load the page
3) Security, whether the connection is secure, usually shown by a lock icon in the address bar
4) Success rate, the number of times the redirection itself fails

In the second stage, making the payment, I would look at:
1) Interface, how easy it is to navigate and whether all options are clearly displayed
2) Time, the time taken to send the OTP and to move between pages
3) Additional charges, whether any extra charges show up at this stage

Interviewer: That covers it well. We have found that the time taken to send the OTP is about 3 minutes.

Candidate: From my own experience, 3 minutes feels like a long time for an OTP. To judge whether that is really the issue, do we know how long other websites take?

Interviewer: Yes. Other websites take 5 to 10 seconds.

Candidate: That is a big gap. The time taken to send the OTP can be split into two parts:
1) The information being sent from our payment partner to the wallet or bank
2) The OTP being generated and sent to the payee

Since other websites manage this in seconds, I think it is fair to assume the delay sits on our partner's side, in relaying the information to the wallet or bank. Our competitors are not seeing this, so it points to something specific to our own setup rather than the payment mode itself.

Interviewer: Correct. So what do you think we should do?

Candidate: I see a few ways to improve the situation. We could stick with the same payment gateway and:
1) Push them to improve their efficiency
2) Recover the lost sales from the third party through penalties
3) Introduce a commission-based model that rewards better performance
4) In the interim, add a short note telling customers the OTP may take a little time and asking them to be patient

Alternatively, we could move to a different third party, or build our own payment gateway. Both of those should only be done after a proper cost-benefit analysis.

Interviewer: Great. We can close the case here.

Left Me High and Dry Framework & Recommendations
LOST SALES DUE TO HIGH CHURN RATE OF PAYMENT GATEWAY
Clarifying Questions: What kind of clothes and who is the target market? When did the problem start? Is the decline uniform across payment modes? Are competitors facing the same issue? Do we use a third-party gateway?
Brownie Points: Isolating the OTP delay as a company-specific problem rather than an industry-wide one.
Keep In Mind: Map every step of the payment journey to build an exhaustive list of drop-off points.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
Change the payment gateway
Improve the efficiency of the current gateway

title: Zero Dark Thirty
prompt: You need to advise the government on how to reduce terrorism in India.

notes.title: Questions
items: What counts as terrorism?
What target and timeline?
Any budgetary constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Consider root causes like funding and education

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Noting that a strong response procedure deters future attacks
Segmenting terrorists into domestic and international

framework:
Candidate: Sure. What exactly do we mean by terrorism? Are we talking about cyber terrorism, bomb blasts, and the like?
Interviewer: By terrorism, we mean the number of bomb blasts and shootings that take place in India.
Candidate: Got it. By how much do we have to reduce terrorism, and by when do we need to achieve this goal? Are there any budgetary constraints I should be aware of?
Interviewer: You need to reduce terrorism by as much as possible. There is no fixed timeline, and there are no budgetary constraints.
Candidate: Alright. We can look to reduce terrorism in two stages: preventive measures, and handling the situation, for example defusing bombs based on tips.
Under preventive measures, I would start by segmenting on the basis of geography and following different strategies for Indian and overseas terrorists.
For terrorists within India, we can look at:
1) Banning or regulating guns and ammunition.
2) Better inter-state security by checking at borders.
3) Deploying the military at domestic airports and prominent buildings, in addition to regular security.
For international terrorists, the key is the mode of entry. Airports, land and sea, all the places through which international militants can enter, must be strictly guarded. This requires:
1) Identifying these locations.
2) Deploying the army at them.
Next, we can analyse the pattern of attacks:
1) Festivals: since most attacks happen around festival times, the police must be on high alert during such periods.
2) Places: crowded markets, malls and hotels are prone to attacks and must be well protected.
We can also work on prediction and training:
1) Special force: a dedicated team must exist that works solely on monitoring and anticipating terrorist activities.
2) Training: the military should be well prepared in terms of training and equipment to handle the situation better.
Finally, extremely harsh penalties must be imposed on such activities.
It is important to note that sometimes a single attack comprises multiple bomb blasts, so we must also look at how situations are handled. A good response procedure in place will also discourage future terrorism.
Under handling the situation, we can look at:
1) Identifying the key locations near the epicentre of the attack, issuing a high alert, and evacuating those areas.
2) Reducing regulatory barriers and the permissions required, so that immediate action can be taken.
3) Ensuring that no media coverage is allowed during terrorist attacks.
In the long run, we can also identify ways to reduce the number of terrorists and cut funding to notorious organisations.
Interviewer: Good job.

Zero Dark Thirty Framework
REDUCE TERRORISM IN INDIA
Clarifying Questions: What counts as terrorism? What target and timeline? Any budgetary constraints?
Brownie Points: Noting that a strong response procedure deters future attacks. Segmenting terrorists into domestic and international.
Keep In Mind: Pick one structure and fold others in.

title: Ups and Downs
prompt: Your client owns a theme park. The client is concerned about the increasing wait time for its rides and has hired you to look into it.

notes.title: Questions
items: What are the different attractions?
Are there any budget constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Break wait time into people, turnover, and seats.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Digital queueing
Token system
Making the wait time enjoyable

visualisations.title: Waiting Time
visualisations.rhs: (People in Queue × Turnover Time per Ride) ÷ Number of Seats

framework:
Candidate: Okay. I would like to know a little more about the theme park. Where is it located, and what are the different attractions in the park?

Interviewer: The park is located in Pune. It has water rides as well as land rides, and there are also food stalls placed around the park.

Candidate: Got it. What exactly is the issue? Do we need to bring down the wait time for both the water rides and the land rides?

Interviewer: In fact, the complaints have specifically been about the park's roller coaster. There are long queues for it at all times.

Candidate: That is unfortunate. Do we have a specific target for how much we want to reduce the waiting time, and by when? Also, are there any budget constraints I should keep in mind?

Interviewer: There are no such targets. You can look at both short term and long term solutions, and there are no budget constraints.

Candidate: Let us see what we can do. I will divide my approach into two parts: reducing the actual waiting time for the roller coaster, and making the waiting experience itself better.

Let me start with the waiting time. The waiting time equals the number of people in the queue multiplied by the turnover time per ride, divided by the number of seats on the roller coaster. So I can pull three levers here: the number of people, the time taken per ride, and the number of seats.

To reduce the number of people in the queue, I would first look at managing demand. We could charge an additional fee since this is a top attraction. We could relocate the attraction, though that may not be feasible given the nature of the ride. We could promote and market the other attractions well so that footfall is spread more evenly across rides. We could also raise the height or age requirement. On top of that, we could introduce alternate attractions, such as a 9D cinema, new thrill rides, or even a second roller coaster. Finally, the operating hours of both the park and the roller coaster can be extended so that demand is dispersed across the day.

Interviewer: We can consider building another roller coaster. Move on to the next factor.

Candidate: Sure. Next is the time taken per ride, which I would break into four stages: boarding, the ride itself, de-boarding, and idle time.

For boarding, we can brief the next set of people about the safety measures and how to fasten their seat belts while the coaster is still in use, which saves time. Staff can be properly trained so there are no delays. Some parks have also introduced centralised fastening of seat belts, which removes the need to check each person individually.

For the ride itself, we can increase the speed of the coaster if it is safe to do so, or reduce its length as long as the overall experience is not affected much.

For de-boarding, trained staff should help people get off smoothly, and de-boarding can be done from the opposite side of the coaster to reduce crowding and keep the process efficient.

For idle time, a routine check is usually carried out every hour or so, and staff are given short breaks. Proper rotation of staff would limit this idle time, and the routine check should be organised and automated as much as possible, with a checklist to help the staff move quicker.

Interviewer: Great suggestions. What would you like to look at next?

Candidate: The number of seats on the ride. We can increase the capacity by adding more seats and upgrading the machinery to support them. We can also improve occupancy: if broken seats are reducing the usable count, those should be repaired on priority.

Interviewer: We are done with the first part. You can go ahead with the second part.

Candidate: To make the waiting experience better, I would introduce a few things. A digital queue, where an application lets people book the ride and wait virtually. A token system, so people hold a token instead of physically standing in line. A representative option, where one person can stand in the queue on behalf of their companions, which also reduces crowding. And attractions around the queue, such as parades and people in costumes, so guests can enjoy themselves while they wait.

Interviewer: Not required. Let us close the case here.

UPS AND DOWNS FRAMEWORK & RECOMMENDATIONS

REDUCING WAIT TIME OF RIDES

Clarifying Questions: What are the different attractions? What is the exact issue? Is there a target or timeline? Are there any budget constraints?

Brownie Points: Digital queueing. Token system. Making the wait time enjoyable.

Keep In Mind: Break wait time into people, turnover, and seats.

title: Young Poets Society
prompt: We are working with Teach For India for their flagship programme, under which they hire Fellows for a 2-year time period. They have been facing a problem in recruitment in terms of not getting enough candidates. They want you to draft a Campus Recruitment Strategy for them.

notes.title: Questions
items: What does the role involve?
Which campuses are we targeting?
What are the exit opportunities?
What is the implementation timeframe?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Reflect the social-sector angle at every step.
Target the uncertain fence-sitters, not the decided.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Asking about exit opportunities
Using social clubs as an interest indicator
Proposing internships and volunteering as entry paths

framework:
Candidate: Sure. I'd like to start by understanding the situation better. What exactly does the role involve, and are there any course or college restrictions on eligibility? Is this problem specific to our client, and since when have they been facing it?
Interviewer: The selected fellows go on the ground to teach students in primary and middle classes who go to government schools and live in slums. Teach For India is fine with students coming in from all undergraduate courses and recruits from all colleges across Tier-1 cities. We don't know about other companies, but this has been true for us since our recruiting began, around four years ago.
Candidate: Understood. I'd like to understand the benefits associated with the role, both in terms of the salary and other perks. Additionally, what kind of exit opportunities do fellows usually get? Also, are there other such social fellowship opportunities available?
Interviewer: Being a social organisation, Teach For India offers a stipend of around 20,000 rupees per month, which is competitive for similar fellowships. Although other jobs pay much more, that is acceptable to us because of the inherent type of individuals we wish to attract. Exits are quite prestigious, with graduating fellows joining top global MBA programmes and corporates. About other alternatives, there aren't many with the repute that Teach For India offers.
Candidate: Got it. Should we focus on the recruitment strategy, or should we also consider changes to the programme structure that might make it more attractive? Also, what is the timeframe of implementation that I should keep in mind?
Interviewer: Let's keep the programme structure out of scope and start off with solutions that can be implemented soon, even for the next round.
Candidate: Alright. Ultimately, since we need enough selections, I would like to dive into the recruitment process. First, we would hold a Pre-Placement Talk to inform students about our opportunity, then invite applications and conduct some form of shortlisting through CVs, tests, or essays. Then, we would hold Group Discussions, Personal Interviews, or other forms of rounds to identify the right candidates. Lastly, we would have to retain the students we select, since they might choose another offer. Have I laid the process out correctly, and do we know which step is becoming a hurdle?
Interviewer: The process seems fine. We are not receiving enough applications in the first place.
Candidate: For a student to apply, there are two major requirements: awareness and interest. Can I know how we spread the word about the opportunity?
Interviewer: All students are informed by their Placement Cells of the opportunity, so interest seems to be lacking.
Candidate: This gap can arise from two sources: a mismatch between students and the opportunity, and the system. Students might not be drawn toward such social roles in general. As far as the system is concerned, the time commitment in terms of the number and intensity of the rounds, the lack of corporate structures in the role, or the limited compensation might be issues. The system-related barriers might involve our opportunity coming in late into the placement season, being categorised as a lower grade, or clashing with other firms in terms of when the process is taking place.
Interviewer: Why would students not be drawn toward social roles?
Candidate: There are preference-driven factors and perception-driven factors at play here. In terms of preference, students can have three types of views: disinterested, uncertain about committing full-time, and strongly interested and willing. The first is not part of our relevant target group due to the misalignment of goals, and the last would be applying even in status quo. We should focus on the middle bucket, as they are the fence-sitters who can be tapped if they are convinced about the opportunity. On the other hand, perception also plays a role, as familial or social pressures might make students unwilling to pursue the role.
Interviewer: Fair enough. What can we do about this then?
Candidate: The basic formula I would like to work with is the number of colleges visited multiplied by the recruits per college. While the former might require more resources from our side, the latter might call for a revision in our selection process.
Interviewer: Suppose we want to focus on the former. How will you identify which colleges have the maximum potential for applications?
Candidate: Here, I believe that the number of students in their final year is a base to start off with. To this base, we can apply various other parameters to measure the potential more accurately.
Interviewer: Okay, so what are the other parameters which are relevant here?
Candidate: Naturally, we will have to look for substitutes which might indicate a higher preference, due to a lack of direct indicators. These can include the presence of social wings, societies, and cells; the diversity in courses at the college; the percentage of students who opt for non-corporate paths after their degree; and the past trends of social fellowship applications, along with the presence of alumni in a similar space, if available.
Interviewer: Great. One last question: what do you think we can do to increase such applications in the long term?
Candidate: I believe the experience that this fellowship offers is immensely valuable and enriching for those interested in pursuing a relevant career path, given the grassroot interaction and impact it offers. Thus, if students are exposed to it, a good number will be interested in it full-time. I foresee three ways to facilitate this interaction. The first would be launching a summer internship programme and ultimately looking at potential full-time recruits, similar to how a Pre-Placement Offer works. We can establish Teach For India Chapters in various colleges, where the cell would generate awareness about the organisation and take up local efforts on similar lines. Lastly, we can also look at an annual system of volunteering, where a volunteer is required to fulfil a defined number of hours to complete their tenure. Through these, we should have a larger funnel at the entry point.
Interviewer: Brilliant, thank you for your suggestions.

Young Poets Society Framework & Recommendations
CAMPUS RECRUITMENT STRATEGY FOR A SOCIAL FELLOWSHIP
Clarifying Questions: Details on the role and eligibility. Target campuses. Benefits of the job and exit opportunities. Timeframe of implementation.
Brownie Points: Asking about exit opportunities. Considering social clubs as an indicator of interest. Internships and volunteering as entry paths.
Keep In Mind: Given the client is a social organisation with a unique role, it is critical to reflect this feature in every step of the analysis.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Summer internship program and offering full-time opportunities to appropriate candidates to generate greater interest among students for the fellowship
Teach For India chapters in various colleges to generate greater awareness as well as interest among students organically
Annual volunteering opportunity with a required number of hours to be completed to generate greater interest among students for the fellowship

title: An Apple a Day Keeps the Doctor Away
prompt: Your client is the Ministry of Health. They want you to improve the health of Indian citizens.

notes.title: Questions
items: What is the objective and timeline?
Are there any budgetary constraints?
Any particular region in mind?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Segment by rural, urban, or city tier.
Map the patient journey, not just treatment.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Setting up more medical institutes nationwide.
Tying externalities like pollution and water to disease.

framework:
Candidate: Quite an interesting problem. Before I begin, I would like to understand a few things. What is the objective our client wants to achieve, and by when do we need to meet it? Are there any budgetary constraints?

Interviewer: Good questions. The objective is to improve the general well-being of the citizens. The plan can be both short term and long term, and there are no such constraints.

Candidate: Understood. Do we have any particular region or regions in mind?

Interviewer: You can look at improving well-being across the country.

Candidate: Great, I think I can begin now. I would approach this by focusing on two broad sets of measures. First, preventive measures that stop people from falling ill in the first place. Second, curative measures that help people recover once they fall ill.

Interviewer: Sounds reasonable. Walk me through the preventive side first.

Candidate: Sure. Under preventive measures, I see five government led levers:
1. Awareness. We need to spread knowledge about various diseases. This can be done through television and radio advertisements. A good example is the Amitabh Bachchan advertisements on tuberculosis.
2. Incentives. The government should formulate policies that encourage employers to provide medical insurance to their employees.
3. Investments. The government must invest in building hospitals, setting up labs, funding medicinal research, running vaccination drives, improving the accessibility of medicines and vaccines, and improving the state of cleanliness and hygiene.
4. Encouragement. Individuals should be encouraged to improve their lifestyle, get vaccinated, and get regular health check ups done.
5. Externalities. Bringing pollution under control and ensuring safe drinking water can reduce the incidence and severity of diseases.

Interviewer: That covers prevention well. Now take me through the curative side.

Candidate: On the curative side, I would walk through the patient journey in four stages.

First, diagnostic. Two things matter here:
1. Early diagnosis. We should encourage people to visit clinics or hospitals as soon as they experience any symptoms.
2. Affordability. We can put a cap on consulting fees and subsidise consultations in rural areas so that cost is not a barrier.

Second, admitting. Here I would focus on two points:
1. Reducing the paperwork required for admission.
2. Ensuring the availability of beds and staff.

Third, treatment. I see three priorities:
1. Ensuring an adequate availability of doctors by setting up medical institutes across the country.
2. Ensuring quality treatment by making the best medical devices available and setting performance standards for doctors and nurses.
3. Ensuring that the hospital is sanitised and there is limited spread of diseases within the premises.

Fourth, post treatment. Two measures stand out:
1. Regular follow ups should be scheduled to monitor recovery.
2. Medication. We must ensure the availability of both general and specialised medicines, along with measures to ensure the patient is actually taking the prescribed medicines.

Interviewer: This approach seems great, we can close the case now.

title: Bad Teacher
prompt: Your client is the Education Ministry of Rajasthan and it wants to improve the class 10 and class 12 board exam results.

notes.title: Questions
items: What does improve mean?
Any timeline in mind?
Which board?
Which segment of schools?
Any budgetary constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Structure the fix across each exam stage

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Making exam centres disability-friendly
Offering the exam in more languages

abbreviations: CBSE: Central Board of Secondary Education
ICSE: Indian Certificate of Secondary Education
framework:
Candidate: Alright. I want to begin by understanding the problem in more specific terms. What exactly do we mean by improve? Do we have a timeline in mind?
Interviewer: By improve, we mean increasing the pass percentage. The client would like to implement the solutions as soon as you are ready with them.
Candidate: Thank you. Next, I want to know if we are talking about a specific board, such as the state board, CBSE, or ICSE.
Interviewer: We can restrict this case to the local state board only.
Candidate: Sure. Are we looking at a particular segment of schools in which we need to improve performance?
Interviewer: You need to focus on only public schools.
