Candidate: Thank you. Are there any budgetary constraints that I need to be aware of?
Interviewer: No. You can proceed.
Candidate: I would like to focus on the children who are already enrolled and improve their performance. The total number of students who pass equals the number enrolled multiplied by the percentage who pass, so since we are concerned with improving the result, we need to increase the percentage of children who pass.
We can look at this problem as a process with four stages: eligibility, preparation, examination, and evaluation.
Starting with eligibility, this stage can be divided into two parts. For new admits, new students must meet the required standards, and these standards can also be revised. For already enrolled students, schools should ensure that the pass criteria are rigidly defined for classes 9 and 11, so that only students who are prepared to take the board exams in the subsequent year are promoted.
Next is preparation, which can be divided into infrastructure, teachers, course, and motivation.
Under infrastructure, we can look at the number and quality of computer and science laboratories, libraries, classrooms, extra-curricular opportunities, and cleanliness and hygiene.
Under teachers, we can look at the training of teachers, establishing accountability through regular evaluations, and maintaining an optimum student-teacher ratio so that all students get sufficient attention.
Under course, we can look at ensuring the availability of different subjects and combinations, reducing the marks required for passing, the number of attempts per student, reducing and revising the syllabus, implementing a flexible timetable such as access to recorded lectures, and having multiple mocks like pre-boards and chapter-wise tests.
Under motivation, we can give monetary incentives to students who perform well, such as free uniforms, scholarships, and fee waivers, give examples of alumni who have gone on to do well in life, and confer awards on and ensure recognition of top performers.
The third stage is examination. Here we can increase the number of languages the paper can be attempted in, provide and improve the means of taking the examination for disabled students, and ensure accessible and quality exam centres.
The final stage is evaluation. Here we can offer the option of revaluation of papers, and establish accountability by imposing penalties in case of misconduct by any examiner.
Interviewer: That will be all for this case. All the best.

Bad Teacher Framework
IMPROVING THE CLASS 10 AND 12 BOARD EXAM RESULTS
Clarifying Questions: What does improve mean? Any timeline in mind? Which board? Which segment of schools? Any budgetary constraints?
Brownie Points: Making exam centres disability-friendly. Offering the exam in more languages.
Keep In Mind: Structure the fix across each exam stage.

title: Finding Bambi
prompt: Your client is the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India. They have recently observed that the deer population has significantly declined. You have been hired to figure out why this is happening.

notes.title: Questions
items: What is the magnitude and duration?
Is the decline area-specific?
Which other animals share the biosphere?
What is their lifespan and reproductive age?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Recent, sudden declines usually have man-made causes.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Eliminating genetic causes since the decline is recent
Breaking births into a multiplicative function

visualisations.title: Total Births
visualisations.rhs: Number of Deer × % in Reproductive Age × % Successful × Average Births per Deer

framework:
Candidate: Do we have any information on the magnitude and duration of this decline?

Interviewer: Yes. The rate of decline has been about 10 percent every year, and this has been happening for the past two years.

Candidate: Is the decline uniform across the country, or is it more prevalent in a specific area?

Interviewer: Good question. It has been a bigger phenomenon in one of the biosphere reserves in North East India, which is a closed area that shelters many animals.

Candidate: Could you give me more details about the animals in this biosphere?

Interviewer: Several animals such as cheetahs, tigers and zebras live in this biosphere.

Candidate: Is the decline happening across all types of deer? What is their average lifespan, and when do they start reproducing?

Interviewer: It is, sadly, across all types of deer. They start reproducing one to two years after birth and live for about ten years on average.

Candidate: Alright. Since the overall population is falling, there are broadly three reasons: deaths have increased, births have decreased, or some combination of the two. Would you like me to probe a specific one, or should I walk through all of them?

Interviewer: Let us go over each, and begin with deaths.

Candidate: Sure. A deer can die from either natural or unnatural causes. Natural causes would be a deer growing old and reaching the end of its expected lifespan. Unnatural causes can be split further into deaths caused by humans, deaths caused by other animals, and deaths caused by the surrounding environment, which includes access to resources like water and food. Genetic conditions are also possible, but that seems unlikely, because the decline is recent and is happening all at once.

Interviewer: That is very comprehensive. However, we have reason to believe the number of deaths has not increased. Why don't you explore births instead?

Candidate: I would like to break births down into a clear function. The total number of births equals the number of deer, multiplied by the percentage of deer in the reproductive age, multiplied by the percentage of deer successful in reproduction, multiplied by the average number of births per deer. So a fall in total births could come from fewer deer in the reproductive age, a lower success rate in mating, or each deer bearing fewer fawns.

Interviewer: Good breakdown. We know the deer have not been successful in their mating activities. Can you figure out why?

Candidate: Interesting. This could be due to biological constraints, environmental requirements, or a lack of geographical proximity. Under biological constraints, there may be reasons that make the deer physically incapable of producing offspring, such as an illness or a disease. Under environmental requirements, I would look at external conditions like temperature and weather, as well as internal conditions like proper nutrition and water intake. A lack of geographical proximity could be a third factor keeping them from reproducing.

Interviewer: Very well. Let us drill down on geographical proximity.

Candidate: If the deer are not in close physical proximity, it could come down to either ability or constraint. Are they not willing to be together, or are they constrained from being together?

Interviewer: Let us focus on the latter.

Candidate: Alright. I would divide these constraints into natural constraints and man-made constraints. Natural constraints would be things like rivers, valleys, or any natural blockade that separates the deer. Man-made constraints would be the construction of roads, bridges or dams, or the relocation of deer caused by any of these. Given that this decline is fairly recent, I believe the cause is more likely man-made, because natural constraints usually take a long time to develop.

Interviewer: Spot on. A road was recently constructed in the biosphere reserve to allow easier mobility. Since it is fenced on both sides, much of the population has been scattered and separated. That is what is leading to the decline in mating activity, and in turn the deer population.

FINDING BAMBI FRAMEWORK & RECOMMENDATIONS

SIGNIFICANT DECLINE IN DEER POPULATION

Clarifying Questions: What is the magnitude and duration of the decline? Is the decline area-specific? Which other animals share the biosphere? What is the deer's lifespan and reproductive age?

Brownie Points: Eliminating genetic causes since the decline is recent. Breaking births into a multiplicative function.

Keep In Mind: Recent, sudden declines usually have man-made causes.

title: Houston, We Have a Problem!
prompt: Sylvester, the mayor of Houston, Texas has approached you. There has been an unprecedented rise in criminal activity in the city. Families in Houston are concerned about their safety. With elections approaching, the Mayor would like your advice on how the criminal activity can be brought under control.

notes.title: Questions
items: What defines the rise in crime?
Have other states faced this?
Which crime types have risen?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Building a formula to pinpoint the homicide driver
A protective law can fuel new crime.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Recommending background checks before issuing guns
Asking the new law's rationale before reacting

visualisations.title: Number of Homicides
visualisations.rhs: Population of Houston × % Criminals × % Committing Homicide × Homicides per Criminal

framework:
Candidate: Sounds like an interesting problem. Basically, the mayor wants us to identify the reason behind the increase in criminal activity and come up with suitable suggestions to bring it under control and help him secure the faith of the people again. Is that right?
Interviewer: Correct.
Candidate: Alright. Before we do that, I would like to know what we mean by an increase in criminal activity. Have the number of crimes committed gone up?
Interviewer: Yes, that is right.
Candidate: Okay. Do we know by how much crimes have increased and since when this has been happening? Also, have other states faced a similar problem?
Interviewer: Crime rates have gone up by 20 percent in the last four months. Other states have not faced such an issue.
Candidate: That is a cause for concern. I believe the state will have a segmentation of the different types of crimes: thefts, kidnappings, homicides, sexual harassment, and so on. Have all types of crimes gone up, or is it specific to some? It is also possible that certain ethnicities or groups are being targeted.
Interviewer: Homicides have been increasing of late. We don't have a segmentation of our victims. Other crimes have been steadily decreasing due to the new CCTV cameras installed across the city.
Candidate: That is intriguing. Homicides have seen an increase despite the CCTV cameras. We can get to the number of homicides by constructing the following formula: the number of homicides equals the population of Houston multiplied by the percentage that are criminals, multiplied by the percentage of criminals that commit homicides, multiplied by the number of homicides per criminal. It is unlikely that the population of Houston has seen a significant increase in such a short period. However, it is possible that the percentage of criminals has seen an increase because of factors such as the formation of a new gang. Since other crimes have seen a decline, my hypothesis is that there has been an increase in the percentage of criminals that commit homicides, as well as the number of homicides per criminal. Is this true?
Interviewer: Spot on. What would you like to do next?
Candidate: To further isolate the problem, we can analyse how the homicides are being committed. Some common ways in which a person can be murdered are poisoning, shooting, and stabbing. Do we know if there has been an increase in a specific manner of killing?
Interviewer: Yes. The number of shootings has increased.
Candidate: This could either be because of an increase in motives to commit homicides or a more facilitative environment that makes it easier to carry out these shootings. Motives can be further divided into monetary motives, like stealing jewellery or securing control of new territory, or non-monetary motives, such as hate crimes and revenge. A facilitative environment could mean poor law enforcement, such as inefficient policemen or a reduction in punishments, or easier access to weapons, in this case, guns.
Interviewer: Excellent. Four months ago, Texas passed a law making it easier to procure a gun license. This has resulted in an increasing number of shootings. What should the authorities do now?
Candidate: First, I would like to know the reason behind the new law.
Interviewer: The rationale behind the new law was that families would be better able to defend themselves against intruders if they had a gun at home.
Candidate: Makes sense. This has probably been a factor behind the reduction in other crimes. I would suggest a two-step approach to tackle the problem. First, the law must be reconsidered. Other ways, such as night patrolling by policemen and installing CCTV cameras within houses, can be considered as alternatives to the threats posed by intruders. Second, since there has already been an increase in the number of guns with criminals, there has to be an attempt to seize these guns again and clamp down on the criminals. Conducting psychological tests and checking previous criminal records would be one method. We can explore this further if needed.
Interviewer: That will not be necessary. The mayor thanks you for helping him get a step closer to getting re-elected.

Houston, We Have a Problem! Framework & Recommendations
INCREASING CRIMINAL ACTIVITY IN TEXAS
Clarifying Questions: What do we mean by increase in criminal activity? Have other states faced a similar issue?
Brownie Points: Background checks before handing out guns.
Keep In Mind: Asking the right preliminary questions is important, especially in unconventional cases.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Reconsider the law granting easier access to arms. Night patrolling by policemen. CCTV cameras. Seize existing guns.

title: Crash Course
prompt: There have been an increasing number of deaths by car accidents in Delhi. You need to analyse why this is happening.

notes.title: Questions
items: How much, and since when?
Any time or area segmentation?
Deaths inside or outside the car?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Add exhaustive branches, flag the unlikely ones.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Linking easy licensing to more accidents.

visualisations.title: Total Car Deaths
visualisations.rhs: Total Car Accidents × % Causing Deaths × Deaths per Accident

visualisations.title: Total Car Accidents per Day
visualisations.rhs: Avg Cars on Road × % Meeting an Accident

visualisations.title: Homeless People in Delhi
visualisations.insight: People below the poverty line either live in slums, live in temporary establishments, or are homeless. We assume 1 in 5 are homeless at any given point in time.

framework:
Candidate: Interesting. Before I dig in, I would like to understand the problem better. How much have deaths gone up by, and since when have we been facing this?

Interviewer: We have been facing this for the past one year. Deaths are up by 10 percent.

Candidate: Alright. Do we have any segmentation on when the deaths happen, such as day versus night, or a particular area in Delhi that has been worst affected?

Interviewer: Most accidents take place during the day, and East Delhi has the highest number of deaths.

Candidate: I see. I want to understand the numbers a little better. When we say an increase in deaths, do we mean the people inside the car or outside it?

Interviewer: Good question. The number of deaths of people outside the car has increased.

Candidate: Thank you. Let me lay out how the total deaths break down. The total number of deaths equals the total number of car accidents multiplied by the percentage of accidents that cause deaths multiplied by the number of deaths per accident. Do we know which of these has increased?

Interviewer: Analyse the total number of car accidents.

Candidate: Sure. The total number of car accidents in a day equals the average number of cars on the road in a day multiplied by the percentage that meet with an accident. It is unlikely that the average number of cars on the road would rise significantly in just one year, so do we know what has changed?

Interviewer: That is a good observation. The percentage of cars that meet with an accident has gone up.

Candidate: Thank you. I would understand this by looking at four areas:
1. Car
2. Road
3. Victims
4. Legal

Under Car, I would look at:
1. Whether a particular vehicle is more prone to accidents.
2. Rules such as the number of years for which a car is allowed to run, which is presently 15 years in Delhi.
3. Servicing and maintenance issues, for example brake failures.
4. Rash or careless driving from factors such as phone usage by drivers.

Under Road, I would look at:
1. The number of traffic lights and whether they are functioning.
2. Barricades and traffic that increase road rage due to impatience.
3. The condition of the roads, since the last monsoon may have increased the number of potholes.
4. Parking, if there is excessive parking taking place on the road.
5. Zebra crossings, their number and placement.
6. Signage on the road.

Under Victims, I would look at:
1. The number of beggars and homeless people on the road.
2. The nature of protests taking place.
3. Shops and fairs that may have opened up along the road and caused crowding.

Under Legal, I would look at:
1. Changes in regulations on rash driving, speed limits, and the penalties attached to offences.
2. The ease of securing a driving license.
3. Enforcement, or how well the laws are being enforced by the police.

Interviewer: This looks good, you have identified the reason. The number of homeless people on the road has gone up. I need you to quickly estimate the number of homeless people in Delhi.

Candidate: Sure, that makes sense, since the roads in East Delhi are narrow and that causes more accidents. Let me estimate it. The number of homeless people in Delhi equals the population of Delhi multiplied by the percentage below the poverty line multiplied by the percentage without a house.

The population of Delhi is about 1.4 crore. Around 30 percent are below the poverty line, so 30 percent of 1,40,00,000 = 42,00,000, which is about 40 lakh people below the poverty line.

These people either live in slums, live in temporary establishments, or are homeless. I would assume that 1 in 5 people below the poverty line is homeless at any given point in time. That gives us 40,00,000 / 5 = 8,00,000, or about 8 lakh homeless people in Delhi.

Interviewer: Sure. We can close this case here.

title: Take Me to Mosque
prompt: Your client is the government of Saudi Arabia. You have been hired to increase the number of people coming for Haj and Umrah.

ability-to-attend.label: % That Have the Ability to Attend

notes.title: Questions
items: What are Haj and Umrah?
Current numbers and target?
Any capacity constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Stay sensitive in religious or political cases
It is fine to admit unfamiliarity here

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Using the fear factor to drive attendance
Making the pilgrimage disability-friendly
Improving international relations to ease travel

additionalFrameworkTrees.label: % That Have the Willingness to Attend

willingness-to-attend.label: % That Have the Willingness to Attend

visualisations.title: Total Attendance
visualisations.rhs: World Population × % That Have the Ability to Attend × % That Have the Willingness to Attend

framework:
Candidate: Alright. I would like to understand the problem a little better. I want to begin by understanding the objective that the government has in mind and by when we have to achieve it.
Interviewer: The government wants to increase the number of tourists visiting Saudi Arabia in order to improve the reach of the pilgrimages, and there is no fixed timeline for this project.
Candidate: Next, I would like to understand what Haj and Umrah are. From what I know, these are holy pilgrimages attended by Muslims from across the world.
Interviewer: Yes, that is correct.
Candidate: I would also like to know how they are different from each other.
Interviewer: Haj is a compulsion for Muslims to attend once a year. It happens in Mecca, and a special week is designated for this pilgrimage. Umrah is not a compulsion and happens throughout the year in the city of Medina.
Candidate: That is extremely helpful. I want to now gauge the current situation by understanding how many visitors we have annually for Haj and Umrah, and whether we have a target in mind.
Interviewer: Currently, we have 2 million people coming for Haj and 5 million for Umrah. We want to take this number to 10 million for Haj and 15 million for Umrah.
Candidate: This growth target is quite significant, so I would like to know if there are any capacity constraints to keep in mind while solving this case.
Interviewer: Good observation. Capacity is not a concern.
Candidate: Thank you. I would like to now lay out my overall approach. We can break the problem down using a simple relationship: the total number of attendees equals the population of the world multiplied by the percentage that have the ability to attend multiplied by the percentage that are willing to attend.
Interviewer: Looks fine. We can look at each of these separately.
Candidate: I would like to begin by analysing the ability of people to attend these pilgrimages. The factors affecting ability are affordability, time constraints, demographics, and geo-political and legal constraints.
Under affordability, budget hotels and hostels can be opened in these locations, cheap transport facilities such as public buses and metros can be operated, affordable restaurants and food trucks can be opened, and tie-ups with airline operators can offer discounts on travel to these locations.
Under time constraints, we can explore the possibility of making Haj an all-year-round pilgrimage too, or else make a strategic selection of the week keeping our target groups in mind, for example during popular holiday seasons. We can also introduce compact weekend plans to draw more people.
Under demographics, we can increase the number of people eligible to undertake the pilgrimage by easing restrictions on children, women, and others, and we can also consider opening it up to non-Muslims. For the elderly and disabled populations, we can make the pilgrimage disability-friendly and provide assistance at all stages.
Under geo-political and legal constraints, we can ease visa application and acceptance rules, and make efforts towards better international relations.
Interviewer: Great, this is extremely detailed. We can now move to the second part.
Candidate: Thank you. The second aspect deals with the willingness to attend the pilgrimages. The trip can be divided into three stages: before, during, and after.
Before the trip, we can build awareness through multiple modes of advertising on social and print media, tying up with religious institutes across the globe to nudge more people to undertake the pilgrimage. There are also social reasons we can tap into. One is fear, by spreading the narrative that not undertaking the pilgrimage can lead to consequences. The other is belief, by reinforcing that it is auspicious to undertake the pilgrimage, similar to how attending the Vaishno Devi temple is considered auspicious for a newly-wed couple.
During the trip, we can improve the pilgrimage experience itself through easy transport availability, a good ambience inside the mosque, folk songs, and the like, and we can improve the general infrastructure of Mecca and Medina for other tourist activities.
After the trip, we can encourage word of mouth by getting people to post pictures and entice others to undertake the pilgrimage, and we can offer a token of memory, such as photo booths, so that every time people look at the picture they are reminded of the trip and encouraged to undertake the pilgrimage again.
Interviewer: Quite insightful suggestions. We can close the case now. Have a great day.

Take Me to Mosque Framework
INCREASING ATTENDEES OF HAJ AND UMRAH
Clarifying Questions: What are Haj and Umrah? How do they differ? What objective and timeline? Current numbers and target? Any capacity constraints?
Brownie Points: Using the fear factor to drive attendance. Making the pilgrimage disability-friendly. Improving international relations to ease travel.
Keep In Mind: Stay sensitive in religious or political cases. It is fine to admit unfamiliarity here.

title: Cash Me If You Can
prompt: Your client is a steel manufacturing company. They have excess cash available on their balance sheet. How should they deal with it?

notes.title: Questions
items: What is the specific objective?
How is excess cash defined?
What type of steel is manufactured?
Who are the main competitors?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Split cash uses into business and non-business.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Identifying special steel use-cases like white goods
Looking at multiple macro trends for capacity expansion

framework:
Candidate: Can you tell me a little more about the company? What is its desired objective?

Interviewer: Sure. The client is based in India and supplies steel across the country to other businesses. The objective is to use the cash in a way that benefits the company in the long run.

Candidate: What kind of steel does the client manufacture?

Interviewer: The client manufactures low-carbon steel, which is the most widely used type across multiple sectors. It is a standardised product with no variants.

Candidate: Do we have any information on the competitors?

Interviewer: Yes. The market is dominated by three main players within the closed geography of India. Other players exist but are insignificant.

Candidate: Got it. For clarity, how exactly is excess cash defined here? Do we have a specific figure?

Interviewer: You can think of excess cash as the cash available over and above what is needed to run the company. We do not have a specific figure, but it is more than industry standards.

Candidate: Understood. I would like to split the potential cash spending into two parts: non-business activities and business activities. Non-business activities would mean putting the cash into things outside the main business, while business activities would mean retaining the cash to further our business prospects.

Under non-business activities, I would look at investments in financial asset classes, as well as the option of returning money to investors. Under business activities, I would look at capacity expansion in the current business, both domestic and global, and strategic investments through mergers and acquisitions. I would like to start with non-business activities.

Interviewer: Sure. Go ahead.

Candidate: Are we open to investing in specific asset classes? These could include financial derivatives, real estate, venture capital and the like.

Interviewer: The client is not very keen on making such investments. How else can the cash be used to return money to investors?

Candidate: We can issue dividends to our investors. Depending on the type of company, we can also consider a share buyback, provided we have enough liquidity and are confident it will create the most value over the long term.

Interviewer: Those are interesting ideas, but I would like you to now discuss some ways of using this cash for business purposes.

Candidate: Sure. As I mentioned, capacity expansion and strategic investments can add long-term value from a business perspective. We can either expand or acquire within the existing value chain, or diversify across it.

Interviewer: How would you decide whether capacity expansion is a good idea?

Candidate: I would look at our existing capacity and check whether there is enough demand for it in the market. If we are already operating at a full hundred percent utilisation rate and there is still unmet demand, we can consider scaling up. We should also judge future demand before deciding whether producing more makes sense. Do we have any data on our current production capability?

Interviewer: Yes. The client produces 10 million tonnes of steel, which is currently at par with all three leading competitors. How would you judge future demand?

Candidate: I would analyse the growth rate of the main industries where low-carbon steel is used. That gives a fair idea of how demand will develop.

Interviewer: Good approach. Can you identify a few such industries and suggest how you would ballpark their growth rates?

Candidate: Some of the industries where low-carbon steel is used are construction, white goods such as home appliances and refrigerators, capital goods, and automobiles. I would judge the potential of each using factors like the business cycle, the impact of inflation, and a comparison with GDP growth. If an industry is growing faster than a benchmark, say India's GDP growth rate, that supports investing in capacity expansion.

Interviewer: That makes sense. Can we quickly go over strategic investments as well?

Candidate: Sure. These would be any activity that furthers the business. Strategic investments can be made in two ways: within the same business, such as moving into other qualities of steel, or in adjacent industries, such as cement, which is also used in construction like steel. Under both, we can look at forward linkages, such as building our own distributor and retailer network, as well as backward linkages, such as sourcing key raw material inputs, to build dominance across the value chain.

Interviewer: Those are some really good ideas. We can close the case here.

CASH ME IF YOU CAN FRAMEWORK & RECOMMENDATIONS

DEALING WITH THE EXCESS CASH ON THE BALANCE SHEET

Clarifying Questions: What is the specific objective? How is excess cash defined? What type of steel is manufactured? Who are the main competitors?

Brownie Points: Identifying special steel use-cases like white goods. Looking at multiple macro trends for capacity expansion.

Keep In Mind: Split cash uses into business and non-business.

title: The Godfather
prompt: Hey, let's begin with a quick case. The scene is set in Italy. You have been abducted by Mr. Alessandro, the head of a mafia. He has reported an increase in the number of men being killed in his gang. He wants you to identify the reason behind the same within the next 30 minutes if you wish to walk out alive.

notes.title: Questions
items: How many men, and since when?
What is the gang's line of business?
Which ranks are getting killed?
How are the deaths occurring?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Probe an unexpected node like family.
Locate the single stage where the leak happens.

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Splitting the leak into intentional versus unintentional
Separating an absolute rise from a percentage rise

visualisations.title: Number of People Killed
visualisations.rhs: Number of Men in Gang × % in Higher Ranks × % Being Killed

framework:
Candidate: Oh wow. I'd like to get a better understanding of the problem that Mr. Alessandro is facing. Do we have numbers on how many men have been dying and since when?
Interviewer: Enough men for it to be a concern, and since the last four months.
Candidate: Okay. What exactly is Alessandro's line of activity? Can I assume he is into a majority of illegal activities like drug-dealing, arms, and betting?
Interviewer: Fair enough. He also has certain legal businesses to cover his illegal activities.
Candidate: Great. Do we know if there is a particular segmentation of men, in terms of the work they do, that are getting killed? Maybe more field agents are found dead? Do we have any information on any rival gangs, and whether they have been losing men too?
Interviewer: Good question. You can say more men from the higher ranks are being found dead. Also, there is one more prominent gang operating in Italy, the Mazzerati gang. We don't have conclusive information, but Alessandro's informants have noticed minimal deaths in the rival gang.
Candidate: Do we know how the deaths are occurring? It could be shootings, accidents, hand fights, and so on.
Interviewer: They are being shot dead.
Candidate: Do we have information on where these men are being found dead? Here, I would like to divide it into work-related and non-work-related. Non-work-related would include diseases and other factors that are not directly related to the work the men are doing.
Interviewer: Good question. You can say more men are being found dead in the place of conducting our deals. The clock is ticking, start with your structure.
Candidate: Okay, I believe the number of people getting killed equals the number of men in the gang multiplied by the percentage of them that are in higher ranks, multiplied by the percentage of them that are being killed. Do we know which factor has increased in the last five months?
Interviewer: What is the relevance of the first two buckets?
Candidate: Maybe the number of deaths isn't a sign of worry because we have been hiring more people in the last five months, which would lead to an absolute increase in the number of deaths, but percentage-wise it would remain similar. Also, the second bucket has the same logic, but maybe more people are being promoted to higher ranks, leading to an absolute increase in the number of high-ranking officers being killed.
Interviewer: Fair enough. You can say the percentage of them being killed has gone up.
Candidate: Given that we know the people are getting killed during deals, I would like to identify who the killers are. It could be men from the rival gang, the police, the general public if there is a bounty on our gang members, the party they are conducting the deal with where the deal falls through at the last minute leading to a shootout, or members from our own gang that have gone rogue.
Interviewer: Great. You can say that mainly members from the rival gang and some police officers have been killing our men.
Candidate: Okay. I would like to analyse why these two groups have been able to get the better of us in the last five months and what has changed. It could be because they have an advantage with respect to better information, leading to a tactical advantage; better equipment and guns than us; the number of people being sent for deals, where they might have an advantage with a greater number of hitmen; their skill level, relating to the skills and quality of the men in their gang; or external advantages, such as the location.
Interviewer: Perfect. You can say that they have an advantage with regard to information about our gang and its functioning.
Candidate: Okay. The information about our gang can slip out during the planning stage, the travel to the location, during the deal itself, or at the time of leaving. Do we know at which step information is being leaked?
Interviewer: Look into the planning stage.
Candidate: Sure. Do we have any information on where the planning is done and by whom? Has this process changed in the last five months?
Interviewer: Great. The planning is done at Alessandro's house with the five top-ranking members of his gang. The planning has always been done like this.
Candidate: Here, since the planning is done at Alessandro's house, information could be leaked by Alessandro himself, any of the top five ranking members, the security and staff present at the house, or any mics or cameras present in the house due to bugging.
Interviewer: Are you missing anyone?
Candidate: Oh yes. His family members are present in the house too. Who are the family members that live in his house?
Interviewer: That's right. Analyse his family. He lives with his wife, mother, and two teenage daughters.
Candidate: That is interesting. I'd like to divide the information being leaked into two buckets: intentionally and unintentionally. Under intentionally, I would try to understand the different incentives that his family members would have to betray him and his operations. Under unintentionally, I would like to understand the amount of information they have and the various people they might discuss it with by mistake or without knowing its importance.
Interviewer: Great. We have no reason to believe that anyone in his family would intentionally leak information. Under unintentionally, who do you think might be the prime candidate?
Candidate: The daughters. They might not understand the seriousness of the issue due to their age. They also interact with plenty of people at school, playgrounds, malls, and other places they might visit.
Interviewer: Kudos. You've cracked it. It has been understood that Sophia, his younger daughter, used to talk about matters of these meetings with Pedro, a boy in her grade. The rival gang had gathered that Sophia and Pedro were good friends. Roughly five months back, they inducted Pedro as an informant in their gang. Thank you for your help, you may now leave. Keep in mind, if you reveal these discussions to anyone, you won't see the light of morning.

The Godfather Framework & Recommendations
RISE IN GANG MEMBERS BEING KILLED
Clarifying Questions: How many men, and since when? What is the gang's line of business? Which ranks are getting killed? How are the deaths occurring?
Brownie Points: Splitting the leak into intentional versus unintentional. Mapping the deal's stages to locate the leak. Considering family as an unintentional information source. Separating an absolute rise from a percentage rise.
Keep In Mind: Probe an unexpected node like family. Locate the single stage where the leak happens.

title: Where's Perry?
prompt: Hey. Let's go back 5 years to 2016. Imagine you've just been hired as a Business Analyst and your first task is intriguing. Mr. Perry, a Senior Partner at the firm, used to be disciplined and punctual. However, off-late, he arrives 30 minutes late to the office every day. This is a cause of concern and you have been approached to understand the issue without directly asking him as it may upset him.
framework:
Candidate: Interesting. Before I dive in, I would like to understand a few things. Since when has this been happening? And is it just that he arrives late, or does he also leave early?
Interviewer: Sure. This has been happening for the last 2 weeks. No, he leaves on time.
Candidate: I see. I would like to understand a bit more about his role. Which project has he been working on, which team, and have the office hours changed in the last 2 weeks?
Interviewer: Great question. In fact, he is incredibly satisfied with his work, and none of this has changed in the last 6 months.
Candidate: Sure. Where does he stay? Have there been any notable changes in his personal life, such as a medical issue or anything similar?
Interviewer: Not at all. He has lived in Delhi for the last 10 years. We do not suspect any personal problems either.
Candidate: Understood. Lastly, are there any other partners at the firm who have also been coming in late?
Interviewer: We are not entirely sure of that. In the higher ranks, he is the only one coming late, which makes this an immediate cause of concern.
Candidate: As per the information given, I am willing to rule out any personal or motivational reasons for coming late. Instead, I would like to map Mr. Perry's journey from his house to the office and identify where the delay is arising. His journey would look like this:
^ Wakes Up ~ Morning Routine ~ Gets Ready ~ Travels to Office ~ Arrives at Office ~ Reaches His Desk
I would like to analyse each of these steps. Firstly, has the time he wakes up changed? Under morning routine, I’d like to understand if there is any cause of delay. For example, earlier, he had a meal service, now he cooks on his own. Under getting ready, I’d like to understand if there has been some additional office work that he has to prepare for. There is a good chance that the problem lies in the travel phase. Here, I’d like to analyse the time taken to commute. Once he arrives, I’d like to understand if there is any change in his parking location etc. Finally, I’d like to analyse the manner of reaching his desk and checking in. Maybe he does reach on time but there has been some elevator issue or issue with the attendance procedure causing him to appear late.
Interviewer: Great. You were right. Everything else has been the same. However, his time taken to commute has increased, causing him to reach late.
Candidate: Sure. Since,
^ Commute Time = (Total Distance / Average Speed) + Time Spent in Stoppages
I will analyse each component.
Under Distance, the route might have changed, or the starting or ending points might have shifted.
Under Average Speed, road quality may have deteriorated, traffic may have increased, new speed limits may have been introduced, or more signals and speed bumps may be slowing him down.

title: Dallas Buyers Club
prompt: A pharma company's R&D department created a new drug recently, for which a pilot was held. But, the pilot failed. We're here to understand why that happened and give suggestions for further action on this.

notes.title: Questions
items: What are the drug's specifications?
What is the company's standing?
What did the pilot target?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: In cost-benefit comparisons, it is important to look at all levels in the value chain, from producers and distributors to retailers and customers

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Considering frequency to be a medical parameter
Offering contextual ideas like online delivery of medicines
Highlighting the importance of in-store positioning and the value of shelf space

visualisations.title: Tablets Sold
visualisations.rhs: Number of Pharmacies × Diabetic Patients per Pharmacy × Sales Conversion Rate × Purchase Frequency × Basket Size

visualisations.title: Setting the Target
visualisations.rhs: UP Population × % Diabetic × % Diagnosed × % Can Afford × % Prefer Pills × Market Share × Purchase Frequency × Pilot Duration

framework:
Candidate: Sure. Before diving into the case, I would like to understand the situation better on three fronts: the company, the drug, and the pilot study. On the drug, what use is it meant for, what is the form of intake, and what stage of approval is it at?
Interviewer: Good questions. The new drug is a substitute for insulin taken by diabetic individuals, provided in tablet form. We received clinical approval, so the drug was made available over-the-counter.
Candidate: Understood. On the company, I wanted to know the kind of reputation it enjoys in the market for other products, since that is a key factor especially given the significance of medical consumption. Also, have our client or other competitors carried out similar pilots for similar products? This would help us get some direction about the nature of the problem.
Interviewer: Sure. Our client has a strong reputation and has other successful products. Insulin as medicine is well-established, and our major innovation was the mode of intake. So, there have been successful pilots for the usual mode.
Candidate: Got it. Then, on the pilot study, why did we undertake it, what was the location and duration, and how are we defining failure here?
Interviewer: The pilot was to test the product's performance in the market. We did it across Uttar Pradesh over a 6-month period and were able to sell only one lakh units compared to our target of five lakh.
Candidate: Just to understand it better, when we say Uttar Pradesh, was it full-scale in terms of the pharmacies and stores it was sold in, or a sample proportion? Also, why did we choose this particular state?
Interviewer: We chose UP because of its large population and covered it in its entirety, so full-scale.
Candidate: Alright. I will take a moment and work out a mathematical expression for the tablets sold.
Interviewer: Sure, take your time.
Candidate: I believe we should express the figure as: Number of Pharmacies multiplied by the Average Number of Diabetic Customers per Pharmacy, multiplied by the Sales Conversion Rate, Purchase Frequency, and Basket Size. Here, the sales conversion rate would be the percentage of diabetic customers who visit a typical pharmacy and end up purchasing our product. Using this, we should be able to pinpoint the source of the problem. For instance, if it's purchase frequency, we would try to match the intake requirements with our dosage. Do we have any numbers on these lines?
Interviewer: Yes, we do. Working with 80 clinics, we had 25 customers purchasing our drug regularly, 2 per week.
Candidate: Understood. So we are taking it for roughly 25 weeks. When I look at the key drivers here, since we covered the entire population and frequency is a medical parameter, the 25 customers per clinic would have to be 125, or 5x, for our original target to have been met.
Interviewer: That is right. Why do you think the gap existed?
Candidate: I would like to analyse this across 5 key features: Need, Awareness, Affordability, Accessibility, and Experience.
On Need, since the number of people with diabetes in UP is expected to be much larger than the customer base we got, this should not be a problem. The only caveat is that the drug should satisfy their need appropriately, which seems true given clinical approval.
On Awareness, I would like to understand how we informed the public about our new drug. Also, partnering with doctors to push the product would be important given how their recommendations generally drive consumption.
On Affordability, do we have any information on the price point of our drug and those of competitors?
On Accessibility, since we covered all the clinics in the state, where people would also be buying our competitors' drugs, this does not appear to be the issue. Did we also look at online delivery channels like 1mg?
On Experience, at the drugstore level, we can dive deeper into where the product is placed, how it is stored and packaged, and the convenience of the whole process. Further, on the consumers' side, the preferred method of intake and publicity around the drug could also affect sales.
Interviewer: Brilliant. The client wants to expand to online stores only after we establish a strong physical presence. On the price, one pill from our competitors costs Rs 100 and is taken daily. Our pill costs Rs 250.
Candidate: Right, so on a weekly basis, our pill is actually more cost-effective when we compare Rs 700 and Rs 500. But this might lead to issues on the store owner's front as their quantum of revenue decreases and the margins they can earn are squeezed.
Interviewer: Exactly right. Can you think of other problems they might be facing?
Candidate: I would like to look at production, distribution, and demand to visualise the whole process. Since the problem revolves around the shopkeepers, we can eliminate production. On distribution, there might be concerns about the timings and frequency with which our drug was being delivered to them. Once it reaches, there might be storage-related issues due to the need for refrigerators, limited shelf life, or unusual package dimensions. In terms of selling to customers, the packaging might not be attractive and space on visible shelves might be unavailable.
Interviewer: Great, seems like you have understood the major pain points. What can we do about them?
Candidate: I would like to structure my suggestions into financial and non-financial. On the financial side, we need to improve the economic value our drug offers to store owners, by offering them bulk discounts, easier credit terms, higher margins, or by increasing the price of the drug itself. On the non-financial side, we should engage with store owners to get specific feedback about the customer experience. Some suggestions here would be smaller-sized packaging to save precious shelf and storage space, improved package design for ease in storage and a more attractive name for the drug, and developing a variant that can be stored at room temperature.
Interviewer: Those are some good ideas. But take a step back. Does not matching up to the target necessarily mean the pilot failed?
Candidate: It does not. We implicitly assumed that the target was justified as a base for comparison.
Interviewer: Precisely. So, without going into calculations, quickly tell me how you would set the target here.
Candidate: I would start with UP's population and then narrow it down to the subset that has diabetes, and then those who know they have it. Then, we would segment it based on income distribution and estimate the proportion that can afford our drug. This would bring us to the relevant market size. The last filter would be to zero down on the segment comfortable taking a pill instead of an insulin shot or any other alternate solutions including non-allopathic ones. With this final number, we would multiply it by our market share, the purchase frequency per week, and the number of weeks of the pilot.
Interviewer: Thank you for your insights. Good job.

Dallas Buyers Club Framework & Recommendations
ANALYSING WHY A DRUG PILOT FAILED
Clarifying Questions: What are the drug's specifications? What is the company's standing? What did the pilot target?
Brownie Points: Considering frequency to be a medical parameter. Offering contextual ideas like online delivery of medicines. Highlighting the importance of in-store positioning and the value of shelf space.
Keep In Mind: In cost-benefit comparisons, it is important to look at all levels in the value chain, from producers and distributors to retailers and customers.

RECOMMENDATIONS
Economic benefits by bulk discounts, easy credit terms and higher margins
For non-financial incentives, we should reconsider the package size for space and storage optimization and also, develop a room-temperature friendly variant to eliminate additional costs and hassle of storage
Look at the marketing strategy and drug name to make it more appealing

title: Money Heist
prompt: Your client is the professor from Money Heist. His team has just robbed the Royal Mint of Spain to the tune of €2.4 billion in cash. He needs your help in transporting this to their safe-house located 15 km away. How many mini-trucks will he need to buy?

notes.title: Questions
items: How many trips will the money be transported in?
What denomination are the notes in?
How are the notes packed?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Visualise the problem before calculating
Keep every measurement in one unit
Anchor unknown sizes to familiar objects

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Confirming the truck can bear the load

visualisations.title: Number of Mini-Trucks Formula
visualisations.rhs: (Number of Notes × Volume of 1 Note) ÷ (Volume of 1 Mini-Truck × Number of Trips)
visualisations.content: Number of Mini-Trucks = (Number of Notes × Volume of 1 Note) ÷ (Volume of 1 Mini-Truck × Number of Trips). Where: Volume of 1 Note = Length × Width × Thickness; Number of Notes = Total Cash ÷ Denomination of 1 Note; Volume of 1 Mini-Truck = Length × Breadth × Height.

visualisations.title: Mini-Trucks Calculation
rows: as long as a 15 cm ruler
visualisations.insight: All dimensions are kept in centimetres so the volumes divide cleanly. With a single trip, and assuming the truck runs at full capacity with no wasted space, the loot needs 3 mini-trucks.

framework:
Candidate: Alright. So, our objective is to determine the number of mini-trucks the Professor will require in order to transport €2.4 billion. Am I right?
Interviewer: Yes.
Candidate: I have a couple of questions before I begin. How many trips is the money going to be transported in? What denomination are the notes in? How are they packed?
Interviewer: The money has to be transported in a single trip. You can assume that the currency notes are in €100 denomination. They are to be loosely transported.
Candidate: Got it. I will first estimate the volume of 1 note of €100 and the number of such notes. Next, I estimate the volume of 1 mini truck. The following formula will help us arrive at the number of mini-trucks:
^ Number of mini-trucks required = (Number of notes * Volume of 1 note) / (Volume of 1 mini-truck * Number of trips)
This is based on 2 assumptions:
1) The mini-truck can work at full capacity and will not have a problem carrying the weight of the money.
2) There is no wastage of space when the trucks are loaded.
Interviewer: Sounds good.
Candidate: To calculate the volume of 1 note, we will need its length, width and thickness. A currency note is usually as long as a 15 cm ruler. The ratio of length to width is approximately 2:1. This means we can take the width to be about 7 cm. Calculating the thickness of a single note will be difficult. It will be easier to imagine a bunch of 100 notes. A bunch of 100 notes will be about 1 cm thick. Thus, the thickness of 1 note will be about 0.1 mm or 0.01 cm. We now have enough information to calculate the volume of 1 note.
^ Volume of 1 note = Length * Width * Thickness
^ = 15 cm * 7 cm * 0.01 cm
^ = 1 cm³ (approx.)
Candidate: Let's now calculate the number of notes.
^ Number of notes = Total amount / Denomination of 1 note
^ = €2.4 billion / €100
^ = (2.4 * 10⁹) / 10²
^ = 2.4 * 10⁷
Candidate: We must now estimate the volume of each mini-truck, specifically its cargo body. Can I assume the mini-truck to be similar to a Tata Ace which is commonly used in India?
Interviewer: Sure.
Candidate: Okay. Again, we need to estimate the length, breadth and height of the cargo body of the truck. The breadth of the body is approximately equal to 5 feet or 150 cm and the length is about twice of this, i.e., 300 cm. The height of the cargo body will not be more than 6 feet, i.e., 180 cm (approx.)
^ Volume of 1 truck = Length * Breadth * Height
^ = 300 cm * 150 cm * 180 cm
^ = 8 * 10⁶ cm³ (approx.)
Candidate: We can now substitute the values in the original formula.
^ Number of mini-trucks required = ((2.4 * 10⁷) * 1) / (8 * 10⁶)
^ = 3
Candidate: Therefore, 3 mini-trucks are required.
Interviewer: Great work.

Money Heist Framework
TRANSPORTING THE LOOT
Clarifying Questions: Number of trips the money will be transported in. Denomination of the notes. How the notes are packed.
Brownie Points: Confirming that the mini-truck can bear the weight of the load. Stating the full-capacity and no-wasted-space assumptions before calculating.
Keep In Mind: Visualise the problem before calculating. Keep every measurement in one unit. Anchor unknown sizes to familiar objects.

framework:

Candidate: Got it. A good place to start is India's population. Then, we can keep narrowing the population based on certain eliminating factors. First, it makes sense to divide the population of 1.4 billion into 30% staying in urban areas and 70% staying in rural areas. The demand for jerseys in the rural areas will be negligible due to lower income as well as lower exposure to international football. Even the ones who buy jerseys would probably buy replicas. Therefore, I would like to eliminate this section. That leaves us with about 400 million people.

[VIS:0]

This leaves us with 40 million people. In our country, the people that watch football are young. Therefore, we divide the population into different age groups and look at how many people follow football from each age group. While doing this, we will also keep in mind that boys are more interested than girls when it comes to football.
Interviewer: Sure. Go ahead!
[VIS:1]
Candidate: We have now arrived at the number of people who follow football closely in India and can afford to buy the official jersey. Candidate: We are left with one final step.

visualisations.title: Fleet Size Formula
visualisations.rhs: Number of Lines × Trains per Line
visualisations.content: Number of Trains = Number of Lines × Trains per Line, where Trains per Line = (Journey Time ÷ Train Frequency) × 2 to account for trains running in both directions. Only peak-hour frequency is used, since that captures the maximum number of trains active at once.

visualisations.title: Delhi Metro Fleet Size
rows: first to last station (yellow line ~80 min, adjusted)
visualisations.insight: Peak-hour frequency is used because it captures the maximum number of trains running at once, which equals the active fleet.

framework:
Candidate: Yes, I commute by metro almost everyday. What exactly do we mean by fleet size?
Interviewer: Fleet size means the number of trains in the network at a given point in time.
Candidate: Are we talking about the active fleet of trains in the network or are we also including those which are in the yard and are not in use currently?
Interviewer: Good question. We are only concerned with the active fleet.
Candidate: Understood. The active fleet can be calculated using the following formula:
^ Number of trains = Number of metro lines * Number of trains/line
Candidate: I know that there are 10 metro lines in Delhi. To calculate the number of trains/line, we can look at the frequency of trains and make an estimate of the time it takes the train to complete the trip from the first station to the last station on the line.
Candidate: I travel to college on the yellow line. There is one train which comes every 4 minutes in peak hours. We are only concerned by the frequency in peak hours since our objective is to find the maximum number of trains in use at any point during the day. This will essentially give us the fleet size. The journey from the first stop to the last stop of the yellow line takes about 80 minutes. However, I think the yellow line is one of the longer lines in the metro network. After adjusting for this, we can say that the average metro route can be covered in about 60 minutes.
^ Number of trains/line = Total time taken to complete journey / Frequency of trains
Candidate: Therefore, the number of trains/line is about 15. However, we still have to take one thing into consideration. These 15 trains are going in one direction. There are another 15 which will be going in the opposite direction at the same time. Thus, we are left with 30 trains/line. Finally, we can multiply it with the total number of lines in Delhi, i.e., 10.
Candidate: Hence, the active fleet size of Delhi metro = 10 * 30 = 300.
Interviewer: Good job.

Subway Surfers Framework
FLEET SIZE OF DELHI METRO
Clarifying Questions: What do we mean by fleet size? Are we concerned only with the active fleet?
Brownie Points: Incorporating own travelling experience to make more accurate assumptions.
Keep In Mind: It is easier to solve guesstimates if you can visualise the problem at hand. Account for only peak hours while calculating the fleet size.

title: Don't Do Coke
prompt: Hey, let's begin with a quick case. You are required to estimate the volume of Pepsi sold in a cricket game at the Wankhede stadium, Mumbai.

notes.title: Questions
items: What type of cricket match is it?
Are crowds allowed (pre-covid)?
What is the weather on match day?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Skew uniform splits toward the popular brand
Exact stadium facts are not expected

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Filtering soft-drink buyers on three factors
Asking about the weather

visualisations.title: Pepsi Volume Formula
visualisations.rhs: Total Seats × % Occupancy × % Buying a Soft Drink × % Buying Pepsi × Volume per Person

derivations.rhs: Number of Stands × Seats per Stand
% Affording × % Not Health Conscious × % In the Mood

visualisations.content: Volume of Pepsi Sold = Total Seats × % Occupancy × % Buying a Soft Drink × % Buying Pepsi × Volume per Person. The soft-drink rate is itself filtered by income, health and mood, and each person's volume reflects an average of 1.25 glasses of 300 ml.

visualisations.title: Soft-Drink Purchase Filters
rows: ~4 of 8 stands are budget seats; like a cinema, they skip the costly drink
some avoid soft drinks for health reasons
some who can and do drink are simply not in the mood today

visualisations.title: Pepsi Volume Estimation
rows: 4 popular drinks, skewed up for Pepsi
visualisations.insight: Of 32,000 seats at 90% occupancy, about 30% buy a soft drink and 40% of those pick Pepsi - roughly 3,456 buyers. At 375 ml each, that is about 1,300 litres of Pepsi sold in the match.

framework:
Candidate: Oh wow, that's interesting! Are we talking about an international match, IPL match or Ranji Trophy/domestic tournament match? Also, can I make the assumption that this is pre-covid when crowds were allowed in stadiums? How is the weather during the match?
Interviewer: It is an IPL match between Royal Challengers Bangalore and Mumbai Indians. Yes, assume the year is 2019. It is a pleasant evening - not too cold and not too hot.
Candidate: Okay. I can begin now. My formula would be as follows:
^ Total volume of Pepsi sold = Total number of seats * % occupancy * % that purchase a soft drink * % that purchase Pepsi * Volume purchased by each person
Candidate: I would first estimate the total number of people that can be accommodated by the stadium. Wankhede is an average-sized stadium in India. By my understanding, it has around 8 stands and an average of 4,000 seats in each stand. This would give us a total capacity of 32,000 seats in the stadium.
Candidate: Considering it is a high-profile match with popular players on both sides, it would be reasonable to assume a 90% occupancy rate.
Candidate: ~ To estimate the percentage that would buy a soft drink, I would like to look at 3 filters - Income, Health, Mood. Since around 4 out of the 8 stands have affordable tickets, we can assume that these are people that are budget conscious and considering a glass of Pepsi is expensive inside a stadium, we can rule them out from purchasing the drink. _(The logic is similar to a movie theatre where middle class consumers are reluctant to spend on soft drinks)_. There also exists a percentage of people that avoid soft drinks for health reasons. We can assume this percentage to be around 30%. Lastly, among the people that can afford and do drink soft drinks, we can assume around 20% to not be interested in a soft drink on the given day. This gives us 50% * 70% * 80% = 30% (approx.).
Candidate: Next, there are around 4 popular soft drinks. If the preference was uniform, we would get 25% per drink. However, adjusting for the fact that Pepsi is more popular, we can assume around 40% would purchase Pepsi.
Candidate: Lastly, we can assume an average of 1.25 glasses consumed per person (Around 1 glass per person and accounting for 1 in 4 people buying 2 glasses). Each glass is around 300ml, so this gives us 375 ml on an average.
Candidate: Putting the numbers into the formula we get -
^ Total volume of Pepsi sold = 32,000 * 90% * 30% * 40% * 375ml = 1296 litres
Candidate: Therefore, we can assume approximately 1,300 litres of Pepsi is sold in an IPL match in the Wankhede stadium.

Don't Do Coke Framework
AMOUNT OF PEPSI SOLD
Clarifying Questions: What type of cricket match is it?
Brownie Points: Accounting for different factors while arriving at the % of people that purchase soft drinks at the stadium. Asking about the weather.

framework:

Candidate: Sounds really interesting. There are several categories of people that are present during any race weekend. These include participating teams, organising and support staff, third-party service providers and spectators. I would like to individually account for all of them.
Interviewer: That sounds like a good approach. Please proceed further.
Candidate: I would first like to calculate the total number of people associated with participating teams. I would bifurcate the 10 teams based on their financial status: high budget, medium budget and low budget. The number of people they employ will vary accordingly. As only a specific percentage of staff will be operating on-field, I would like to take that into consideration as well.
^ Total number of people associated with participating teams = Number of teams * Employees per team * Percentage of them on-ground
[VIS:1]
Total number of people associated with the participating teams is equal to ~ 1,700.
Interviewer: Sounds alright! Let's do this for other categories of people as well.
Candidate: Using the same method to determine the number of organizing staff, their presence on the ground will be significantly more as a percentage of total strength during a race weekend. These would include security personnel, support staff, cleaners, race control officials, etc.
^ Total number of people associated with organizing staff = (Number of stands + Number of teams in the paddock) * Average number of people present in each * Percentage of them on-ground

I would then multiply this with average ticket value in order to get the total market size.

Candidate: For determining preference for space travel, we can assume that there are 9 other activities like space travel. The interested individuals are equally likely to choose one of the 10 activities like flying an aircraft and exploring the deep-sea bed alone among others.

Candidate: Sure. I'd like to ask a few preliminary questions first. What is the base metric for market size? For that, are we considering both B2B (eg. Uber) and B2C segments of location data usage?

Interviewer: Yes, consider all possibilities. Anyone who uses the service at least once a month is a customer.
Candidate: Alright. The approach I have in mind is starting with India's population split into rural and urban. Then I would apply various filters such as literacy and availability of devices and the internet to make the use feasible. Lastly, I would segment the populations across age group and estimate the final number using usage patterns. Does this sound fair?

While the service is available in multiple languages, literacy is a key requirement for an individual to use it. So, taking the rural literacy rate at 70%, we get roughly 685 million rural literates and at 85%, we get 360 million urban literates. We can directly exclude the others, who are illiterate. Should I avoid approximating and use the exact figures?
Interviewer: No, that's fine.
Candidate: Another need is that of a device and internet since those without both of these simultaneously would be unable to utilize the service. However, since we have already segmented on literacy lines, which would have a large overlap with the availability of devices and the internet due to the extreme poor being typically excluded from both, we will have to take figures higher than the usual rate. With this logic, I believe 40% of rural literates and 80% of urban literates will be digitally connected, giving us 275 million and 290 million respectively.
Interviewer: Glad you kept that nuance in mind, go on.
Candidate: As a final division, I would like to segment according to age groups as this would greatly determine the usage patterns. Again, since we have narrowed it down to the literate population with digital connectivity, which would tilt towards the younger segment, our population split would have to reflect this. For simplicity, I would like to take the same distribution across rural and urban areas: 30% in 0-18 years, 40% in 18-35 years, 20% in 35-55 years and 10% in 55+ years.
Interviewer: Makes sense. Now, why don't you attach specific use percentages to these groups?
Candidate: Definitely. Due to more personal relevance, I'll start with the urban segment. Within 0-18 years, half the individuals are too young, and the other half would use direction services at a relatively limited rate, as they would often travel with parents. So, I'll take 25% here. The 18-35 years segment should be prime users, as they would travel extensively and have the requisite understanding as well, so I'll take 80% here. Within 35-55 years, there might be technological limitations and they might already know most of their usual routes, so I'll take 50%. I think we should eliminate the 55+ years segment as very few would be equipped to use the service comfortably and those who do use it would rely on younger people for whom the usage is indirect.
Interviewer: Nice analysis, why don't you talk about the rural part first and then you can work on the calculations.

For 0-18 years, with the lower 2/3rd of ages not using the service and 30% of the rest using it, I'll take 10%. Again, as the target age group, a good number of individuals in the 18-35 years bracket might use the service, so we'll take 40%. The factor of technical difficulties would be quite powerful for the rural people of 35-55 years, so we can take 10% here. Lastly, we can safely eliminate the 55+ years segment as non-users.
Interviewer: Great, tell me the final answer now.
Candidate: After multiplying the relevant rural population of 275 million across the population split and usage percentages, we get 58 million. Similarly, for the urban part, we get 145 million. But, this reflects the total usage of direction and location services but we need the specific usage of Google Maps. For this, I will take 80% and 95% for rural and urban respectively. In rural areas, Google Maps does not offer comprehensive coverage, which might help competitors like MapMyIndia. However, in urban areas, Google Maps is widely preferred as alternatives like Apple Maps are greatly limited to a specific niche. So, we get 46 million and 138 million users respectively, which gives us a total of 184 million month-wise active users of Google Maps in India.
Interviewer: Well done, all the best for your next round.
