So, we can now focus on the 50% plots and the 10% constructed land.
Interviewer: Since these plots could have non-agricultural uses as well, say residential or commercial plots which are lying vacant, which of these two categories do they fit in?
Candidate: Ah, that makes sense. While they are plots, in terms of their use of barbed wires, they would fit in more closely with the constructed land. Assuming 80% of the plot area is agricultural, that is 40% of total land - we can consider this to be 40% plots and 20% constructed land.
Interviewer: Great, what next?
Candidate: Now, we need to proceed toward the average landholding size. For simplicity, we can assume square plots. For agricultural purposes, due to repeated fragmentation across generations, landholding sizes have reduced to around 1 hectare on average, which is 100m x 100m, or 0.01 km². Since constructed land is more expensive, the size should be smaller, so we can take it as 0.005 km².
Interviewer: Why don't you calculate the number of landholdings for both categories now?
Candidate: For agricultural plots, we have 3 million km² x 40% x 0.01 km², which gives us 120 million. For constructed plots, we have 3 million km² x 20% / 0.005 km², which is also 120 million. Next, we know that not all plots will have a well-defined boundary of any form, say 40% of agricultural plots and 10% of constructed plots lack boundaries. Of those that have it, the boundary can be a concrete wall, a wall with barbed wire in circles on top or just barbed wire around sticks. The share of concrete walls should be around 20% for agricultural plots and 50% for constructed plots.
Interviewer: Before we proceed further, again, what is the number of plots we are left with?
Candidate: ~ For agricultural plots, we have 120 million x 60% x 80% = 57.6 million plots, or roughly 60 million plots. For other plots, we have 120 million x 90% x 50% = 54 million plots, which we can round down to 50 million plots. Now, we will try and arrive at the total length of barbed wire currently in use. For plots with barbed wire in circles on top of a wall, each unit length would require triple the length of wire because of the circular windings. On the other hand, when there is just barbed wire, many layers are tied, so we can take it as 8x the unit length.
Candidate: Focusing on the 60 million agricultural plots, we can take 30% of plots need 3x and 70% need 8x, while each plot has a perimeter of 4 times 100m, which is 400 metres. Here, we get a total of 156 million km of wire here. Similarly, for the 50 million other plots, we can take 80% of plots with 3x and 20% of plots with 8x, due to a much more formal market that needs security. Since the plot size is 5000 m², each side is roughly 70m and the perimeter is around 300m. This gives us a total of 60 million km of wire, and the grand total is 216 million km.
Interviewer: Impressive analysis. What about common boundaries?
Candidate: Right. It is quite possible that our value would have double-counting involved. Theoretically, every fence could be counted twice, so our maximum discount factor would be 50%. But, a large number of fences are facing the road or are bordered by land which is not fenced, I think a 20% discount would be more appropriate. This brings us to 173 million km of wire.
Interviewer: How do we get to our final answer from here?
Candidate: The 173 million km is the stock value. Assuming a life cycle of 20 years, only 1/20 or 5% of this total will need to be replaced each year. As the total land area of India cannot increase with time, the component of growth would arise from lands that were earlier unfenced being fenced, which we can take at 1%. So, 6% of 173 million km is 10.38 million km of barbed wire sold in India annually.
Interviewer: Great job, all the best!

No Of-Fence Framework
MARKET SIZE OF BARBED WIRES IN INDIA
Clarifying Questions: Way of measuring market size? Use cases of the product?
Brownie Points: Constructed lands would be smaller due to greater cost. Different arrangements of barbed wire. Discounting for common fences with road-facing fences not included.
Keep In Mind: Avoid calculation mistakes by rounding off numbers wherever required.

title: Mile High Club
prompt: Hey! Let's do a quick guesstimate. Can you think about the number of meals prepared by Udaan Airlines in Delhi every morning?

notes.title: Questions
items: Meals on flights only or also on ground?
Domestic and international flights or just domestic?
Are we in a post-pandemic scenario?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Average occupancy varies with context - clarify the pandemic's role
Meals served only in certain time slots
Treat domestic flights as short-haul for crew sizing

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Accounting for wastage and buffer
Knowing not all tier 2 cities have flights from Delhi
Running a runway-throughput sanity check

visualisations.title: Meals Prepared by Udaan in Delhi
visualisations.header: Meals Prepared by Udaan in Delhi

visualisations.title: Number of Meals Formula
visualisations.rhs: Flights Serving Meals x (Passengers per Flight + Flight Crew per Flight) + Wastage

framework:
Candidate: Are we concerned with the meals served on flights alone or other places as well like meals served to the on-ground and corporate staff?
Interviewer: Let's only consider the meals needed in flights for now.
Candidate: Will it be fair to assume that the meals are prepared by Udaan only once during the day which is morning in this case?
Interviewer: Yes, that is a fair assumption.
Candidate: Do I look at both domestic as well as international flights?
Interviewer: No, focus on only domestic flights for now.
Candidate: Are we operating in a post-pandemic world?
Interviewer: Yes, you can assume that.
Candidate: Just to clarify here, can we classify Udaan as a high-frill airline for the purpose of this guesstimate?
Interviewer: Sure!
Candidate: Let me draw out how I want to approach this problem. I will try to estimate the number of meals actually served on flights first and then account for wastage in the end. Given that Udaan is a high-frill airline, the meals are included in the ticket price and would be served to every passenger on board as well as the flight crew. The meals prepared in Delhi in the morning will be served on the flights which depart from Delhi. I have built an expression to estimate the number of meals served.
^ Number of meals = No. of flights where meals are served x (Average number of passengers per flight + Flight crew members per flight) + wastage
Interviewer: This sounds fine, go ahead.
Candidate: Given the scale Udaan operates on, having a sizeable market share, I believe it should have 4 flights a day from Delhi to the tier 1 cities and 2 flights a day from Delhi to the tier 2 cities. Excluding Delhi, there are 7 tier 1 cities and around 100 tier 2 cities but the flights don't go to all tier-2 cities from Delhi. Assuming that the flights go to 40 tier 2 cities, we get 108 flights a day (4x7 + 2x40). However, I assume that the meals would be served only during particular time slots during the day.
Candidate: If we set aside 5 hours each for breakfast, lunch and dinner and assume the flights to be uniformly distributed throughout the day, we get nine hours where we are not serving any meals. The number of flights where meals would be served should be
^ (15/24)*108 = ~ 68 flights
Candidate: The last time I went on a domestic flight, I remember the aircraft having 30 rows with 6 seats per row. That gives us 180 passenger seats when the layout is all economy. Udaan on the other hand has an option for business-class as well. I assume I can replace 6 rows of 3 at the front with 3 rows of 2 to come up with the new estimated number of seats.
^ 180 - 18 + 6 = 168
Candidate: The Pandemic also saw lower than usual occupancy rates, I, therefore, assume that 50% of the seats are occupied on average in flights departing from Delhi.
Candidate: That gives us 84 (168/2) passengers, 4 flight attendants and 2 pilots on board. Flight crew assumptions are made based on the fact that domestic flights out of Delhi can be classified as short-haul, given that the flying time doesn't go far beyond 3 hours.
Candidate: ~ The number of meals served onboard should be around 90*68 = 6120 meals
Candidate: Assuming 5% wastage in the supply chain and another 10% kept as a buffer (for reasons like reordering, grievance redressal, complimentary offerings, etc.) the number of meals prepared goes up to approximately 7000.
Interviewer: How would you check the accuracy of your estimate?
Candidate: The Delhi airport has three runways, two of which are used on a regular basis for commercial passenger flights. Assuming that 50% of the time the runway is used for take-offs and the other 50% for landings, and every flight occupies the runway for 4 minutes while taking off, that gives us 15 flights taking off from the airport every hour. Our assumption of 108 domestic flights a day departing from Delhi gives us around 4.5 flights (108/24) for Udaan taking off every hour.
Candidate: The Indian airline industry is an oligopoly with 5-6 players, Udaan should have a market share of roughly 16-20%. Even the more aggressive end of this range doesn't justify the ~ 33% of take-offs being those of Udaan's out of the Delhi airport. I, therefore, believe that we have slightly overestimated the number of meals prepared.
Interviewer: What do you think might have led to this overestimation?
Candidate: I believe that we have overestimated the number of flights as seen in the sanity check. The most probable reason would be that most cities would not have direct flights from Delhi, but flights with layovers at intermediate cities. This should have a considerable effect on our estimated number of flights and subsequently, meals prepared.
Candidate: We should also be mindful of certain special situations wherein flights departing from elsewhere get meals that are prepared in Delhi when they make a layover during transit. This should also be incorporated in the analysis. Do you want me to dive deeper into it?
Interviewer: No, that will not be required. Thank you for your time.

Mile High Club Framework
NUMBER OF MEALS PREPARED BY UDAAN AIRLINES IN DELHI EVERY MORNING
Clarifying Questions: Only consider meals to be served on flight or also on ground? Incorporate analysis for both domestic and international flights or not?
Brownie Points: Accounting for wastage and buffer in your analysis. Knowing that not all tier 2 cities will have airports or flights landing from Delhi.
Keep In Mind: Average occupancy will vary based on the context so clarify if the pandemic plays a role.

title: Schindler's Fit
prompt:
Schindler, a European giant, has recently merged with Voltas, the previous market leader, which is now left with only 2% market share. Decide on a post-merger branding strategy for the newly incorporated company from the following options:
1) Air India-Vistara model: complete acquisition by Air India, and only its name continues in the market.
2) Vodafone Idea model: both brands merge their names into the new company, Vodafone Idea.
3) Tata-JLR model: Tata, Jaguar, and Land Rover have their own cars, but all operate under the same parent company.

notes.title: Questions
items: Branding objective
Product differences
Regional or segment dominance
Financial or time constraints

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Separate brands only when segments differ
Compare each model on revenue vs cost

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Spotting premium-dilution risk

visualisations.title: Model Comparison: Revenue vs Branding Cost

framework:
Candidate: Thank you for the case. Before I dive in, I'd like to ask a few questions to understand the problem statement better.
Interviewer: Sure, please go ahead.
Candidate: What is our objective with this branding strategy? Are we trying to maximise revenue, expand reach, or maximise profits?
Interviewer: We are looking to maximise both revenue and profitability.
Candidate: Understood. Are there any product differences or core competencies that set the two brands apart?
Interviewer: For this case, assume that the products sold by both brands are identical.
Candidate: Got it. In India, brands usually target specific regions or consumer segments. For example, Blinkit has a stronger presence in northern India, while Zepto has greater penetration in western India. Does the merged company show any regional dominance in terms of its customer base?
Interviewer: Great question. Schindler primarily operates in Tier-1 (T1) cities through outlets such as Vijay Sales, Croma, and Reliance Mart, owing to its premium brand perception. Voltas, on the other hand, operates mainly in Tier-3 (T3) cities.
Candidate: That distinction is helpful. Are there any financial or time constraints I should keep in mind?
Interviewer: None.
Candidate: Perfect. I'll approach this in two parts. First, I'll lay out my initial hypothesis on which of the three models is likely to work best. Then I'll test it by analysing each model on its revenues and branding costs to see which one is most profitable.
Interviewer: Yes, go ahead.
Candidate: Let me start with the qualitative evaluation of the three models. Starting with the Air India-Vistara model: here, Air India had a substantially larger market share and brand recognition in India, so it could fully absorb Vistara and continue under its own name. That logic does not hold for us. Schindler is a new brand that has just entered India, and Voltas is left with only a 2% market share. Neither brand is dominant enough to absorb the other, so I would strike off this first model.
Interviewer: Fair point. Continue.
Candidate: Next, the Vodafone Idea model, where both names are merged into one. In my opinion this is not the best fit either. Schindler carries a premium perception while Voltas carries a non-premium perception, and the two operate in different markets. If we merge them, it creates confusion in the minds of customers. The upper class will no longer see Schindler as a luxurious product once the Voltas name is attached to it, so the premium positioning of Schindler gets diluted. At the same time, we still won't be able to charge a premium from the middle class because that market is price-sensitive.
Interviewer: So why does the third option avoid that problem?
Candidate: Because the third model, the Tata-JLR model, keeps the brands separate under a common parent. The reason Tata and JLR operate separately is that they cater to different market segments. Jaguar and Land Rover serve the rich, while Tata sells cars like the Tiago or Nano that are tailor-made for the lower and middle classes. We have a very similar situation with Schindler and Voltas, where one is premium and T1-focused and the other is mass-market and T3-focused. So operating separately under the same parent company is the best strategy here.
Interviewer: I really appreciate your approach. Now move on to the profitability analysis for these three cases. For simplicity, consider only branding costs.
Candidate: Perfect, let me go case by case. In the first model, where Schindler becomes the sole brand and Voltas is discontinued, the revenue potential is limited. The focus would shift entirely to the T1 cities, letting go of all the revenue that could be earned from the T3 cities. The cost would sit in the middle range, since only one brand needs to be marketed, but it has to be marketed effectively because Schindler has only just entered the Indian market.
In the second model, the merged brand, revenues would likely be the lowest, because the new company is diluted across both T1 and T3 cities. The middle class would find the new product expensive and might switch to other alternatives in the market, while premium consumers may hesitate to pay a higher price for a brand now associated with a mass-market perception. The cost, on the other hand, would be the highest, because the company would need to invest heavily in repositioning and in resolving the brand confusion in the market.
In the third model, where both brands operate separately, revenues would likely be the highest, because both brands play independently in their respective markets. We also avoid keeping all our eggs in one basket. The cost would still be high, since both brands have to be marketed separately, which is the main drawback of this model.
Considering both revenue potential and branding costs together, the third model, the Tata-JLR approach where both brands operate independently under a common parent company, is the one most likely to maximise profitability.
Interviewer: We are thinking on the same lines. Good work on the approach. We can end the case here.

Schindler-Voltas Branding Strategy Framework & Recommendations
POST-MERGER BRANDING STRATEGY FOR A SCHINDLER-VOLTAS MERGER
Clarifying Questions: Objective of the branding strategy (revenue, reach, or profit); Product differences and core competencies of each brand; Regional or segment dominance of the merged customer base; Financial or time constraints
Brownie Points: Splitting the market by city tier (T1 premium vs T3 mass); Applying a diversification lens, not keeping all eggs in one basket; Spotting the premium-dilution risk in the merged-name option
Keep In Mind: Separate brands only when segments differ; Compare each model on revenue vs cost
RECOMMENDATIONS: Adopt the Tata-JLR model & operate Schindler and Voltas as separate brands under one common parent company; this protects Schindler's premium positioning in the T1 cities, retains Voltas's reach in the T3 cities, and across both revenue and branding cost is the most profitable of the three options.

title: Power to the People
prompt: Our client is the Government of India, specifically the Ministry of Commerce. They want us to develop a strategy for the indigenization of electric vehicle (EV) battery manufacturing. Currently, EV batteries are largely imported, and the goal is to set up a domestic, end-to-end value chain so that EV batteries are manufactured within the country.

notes.title: Questions
items: Rationale for indigenization?
Time or budget constraints?
Client landscape and players?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Test domestic cost delta versus imports

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Adding chemical recycling and circularity
Including reverse logistics and compliance

framework:
Candidate: Thanks for the case. Before I dive in, I'd like to note a few clarifying questions across three areas: the problem and its objectives, the client context, and a high-level view of the EV battery industry. Starting with the objective, what is the rationale behind this initiative? My hypothesis is that, with the growing EV ecosystem, the government wants batteries produced domestically rather than imported, to promote the Make in India initiative and to capture greater economic value in the long term.
Interviewer: That's largely the motive, and there's nothing else you need to consider there for now.
Candidate: Understood. Are there any specific time or budget constraints we should keep in mind?
Interviewer: There is a budget aspect that will eventually need discussion, but it is not part of this case. On timelines, the government wants to implement this as soon as possible; for simplicity, assume a timeline of around one year.
Candidate: And on the client context, how does the current landscape look, and how many players exist in this space?
Interviewer: That won't be very relevant here. I'd like you to focus on the strategy itself and how you would approach it.
Candidate: Understood. I'd lay out the strategy as a three-step, sequential approach, where each step builds on the previous one and we proceed only if the previous step is viable. First, financial feasibility: whether domestic manufacturing makes economic sense compared to imports. Second, operational feasibility: whether we can realistically set up a domestic, end-to-end value chain. Third, the policy, compliance, and risk ecosystem: whether there are any regulatory or execution risks that could derail the strategy. Does this approach work, or am I missing anything?
Interviewer: This is a very exhaustive approach and covers everything relevant. Go ahead.
Candidate: I'll start with financial feasibility. The objective is to check whether the delta from domestic production is positive compared to importing EV batteries. I'd break it into three components: revenue per unit, variable cost per unit, and capital expenditure (CAPEX). If domestic production generates higher long-term value than imports across these components, that justifies moving to the next step. Moving to operational feasibility, I'd map the entire EV battery value chain from start to end to identify bottlenecks, breaking it into three stages: raw material procurement; manufacturing, testing, and technology; and distribution and reverse logistics. After evaluating each stage, we can judge whether the ecosystem can be built domestically in a reliable and scalable manner.
Interviewer: This looks quite exhaustive. Walk me through what you would cover within the value chain.
Candidate: Within raw material procurement, I'd look at two sources: domestic mining of the key raw materials required for EV batteries, and recycling, especially chemical recycling, since EV batteries are well suited to circularity and recycled materials can be reused as inputs. Within technology and manufacturing, three parts: research and development, covering in-house research, technology development, and acquisition of the required intellectual property (IP); testing, including both early-stage testing and late-stage quality and safety testing; and production and storage, covering the actual manufacturing of batteries and appropriate storage conditions after production. Within distribution and reverse logistics, last-mile distribution to original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and any reverse logistics for defective units or end-of-life batteries.
Interviewer: Very comprehensive. You mentioned CAPEX under financial feasibility. What would you cover there?
Candidate: I'd look at CAPEX across three categories: human capital costs, physical capital costs, and miscellaneous costs such as insurance, marketing, and other supporting expenditures.
Interviewer: Focus on physical capital costs. What would you include?
Candidate: Within physical capital costs, three key components: land and infrastructure costs; plant and machinery costs; and ecosystem enablers' costs, including licensing, IP-related costs, and environmental compliance costs such as waste management and recycling infrastructure.
Interviewer: This is very comprehensive and covers exactly the strategy I wanted you to focus on. With this, we can close the case.

EV Battery Indigenisation Framework & Recommendations
STRATEGY FOR INDIGENISING EV BATTERY MANUFACTURING FOR THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
Clarifying Questions: Rationale for indigenization (why the government wants to pursue it); any time or budget constraints; current client landscape and number of players
Brownie Points: Sequential, gated approach where each step proceeds only if the previous one is viable; bringing chemical recycling and circularity into raw material procurement; including reverse logistics for defective and end-of-life batteries and environmental compliance under ecosystem enablers
Keep In Mind: Deliverable is a MECE value chain; test the domestic cost delta from local production against imports

title: Parts and Recreation
prompt: Our client is an automotive Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM). They have approached BCG to build a growth strategy. Please go ahead.

notes.title: Questions
items: What is an OEM?
Channels in play?
Can our spare parts fit other companies' cars?
Top line or bottom line growth?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Raise value instead of cutting price

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Defining OEM before proceeding
Bundling service cost into EMI
Building an authorized-partner program

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I structure my approach, I'd like to ask a few clarifying questions. To confirm my understanding, an Original Equipment Manufacturer is a company that produces the actual vehicles along with the parts that go into them. Is that the right way to think about our client?
Interviewer: That's correct.
Candidate: I'd also like to know which part of the business we are focusing on. Is it the vehicle manufacturing business as a whole, or one specific division?
Interviewer: Good question. The client is the spare parts division of an automobile company. That is who has come to us.
Candidate: Understood. For spare parts, I see two broad ways the business can operate. First, a product channel, where we sell spare parts to retailers who then sell them onward. Second, a service channel, where we fit and service the spare parts ourselves for the customer. Do we run both of these?
Interviewer: Yes, that's a good observation. We have both a product channel and a service channel.
Candidate: One more point on the product itself. Can our spare parts be used only in the cars that our own company manufactures, or can they also be fitted in other companies' cars?
Interviewer: They can only be used on our own cars.
Candidate: That's helpful. Finally, I'd like to understand the goal. Are we targeting top line [revenue] or bottom line [profit] growth, and what is the target and the time frame?
Interviewer: We are looking at the top line. The client wants to double its revenue over the next 2 to 3 years.
Candidate: Got it. To structure this, growth can come from two directions: organic growth and inorganic growth. For a spare parts business, I don't think inorganic growth makes much sense. Since our parts can only be used on our own cars, acquiring another company would add limited value and would take a lot of time to merge and fine tune into our operations. So I'd set inorganic growth aside and focus on organic growth. Does that sound fair?
Interviewer: Yes, that sounds fair.
Candidate: For organic growth, I'd break revenue into three levers:
Organic Revenue = Number of Cars × Spare Parts per Car × Price per Spare Part
One quick check before I go deeper: should we also look at increasing the number of cars sold, since more cars on the road directly increases the demand for spare parts?
Interviewer: That's a good observation, but the client is only the spare parts division. So let's focus there.
Candidate: Understood. I'll set the number of cars aside and focus on increasing the number of spare parts sold per car and the price per part. To go deeper, I'd look at our two routes to market separately: the product channel and the service channel.
Interviewer: Let's start with the service channel.
Candidate: Sure. In the service channel, customers come to us directly to get their cars serviced, and we fit our own spare parts during that service. I'd split this channel into two routes: a Direct-to-Consumer route, or D2C, where we deal with the end customer, and a Business-to-Business route, or B2B, where we work with other businesses. Let me start with the Direct-to-Consumer route. I'd think about it in two stages: before the customer buys the car, and after they own it. Before the purchase, there are two opportunities. First, mandatory fitments that are built into the car automatically, for example a spare tyre. At the moment of buying the car, an extra 4,000 to 5,000 rupees for these fitments feels small to the customer, so they rarely object. Second, optional add-ons that the customer can choose to include.
Interviewer: And after the purchase?
Candidate: After the purchase, I'd offer one free service or one free repair along with the car. Customers usually hesitate to visit the official service centre at first. A free first service brings them in, lets them experience the quality of our work, and makes them far more likely to return to us when a real issue comes up later.
Interviewer: You keep mentioning a value proposition. What is the biggest pain point that would push a customer towards a local retailer instead of us?
Candidate: The biggest pain point is price sensitivity. Local retailers are usually cheaper.
Interviewer: So how would you counter that price sensitivity?
Candidate: We can't simply undercut the retailers, because we offer a better service and genuine original parts, so our costs are higher. Instead of cutting the price, I'd raise the value proposition. Many customers, especially price sensitive ones, buy their cars on an Equated Monthly Instalment, or EMI. If we can find a way to fold the cost of their servicing and spare parts into their existing EMI, the value proposition improves a lot. For example, if a local retailer charges 5,000 rupees, our service might cost 10,000 rupees. Paid upfront, that gap feels large. But spread across the monthly EMI, it becomes a small increase of perhaps a hundred rupees a month, which makes our higher quality option feel far more affordable.
Interviewer: Alright. Let's move to the Business-to-Business route within the service channel.
Candidate: In the Business-to-Business route, the key questions are how we sell to our partners and how we get them to prefer us. I'd set up an incentive and milestone program. We define clear milestones, and partners who reach a certain volume of sales or service earn better terms and advantages. The strongest performers can be recognised as our authorized partners. This works as a win-win. Customers get the trust of seeing an official authorized partner badge, so they are comfortable going there. For the retailer, becoming an authorized partner means more business, because customers of our brand will prefer to come to them. And for us, sales rise as more service and parts flow through this partner network.
Interviewer: Good. Can you summarise the case for me?
Candidate: Certainly. Our client is the spare parts division of an automotive OEM that wants to double its revenue in 2 to 3 years. We focused on organic growth and set inorganic growth aside, since our parts only fit our own cars. Within organic growth, we concentrated on selling more spare parts through two channels. In the service channel, on the Direct-to-Consumer side, we capture value before purchase through mandatory fitments and optional add-ons, and after purchase through a free first service that builds trust, supported by EMI bundling to overcome price sensitivity. On the Business-to-Business side, we use a milestone-based incentive and authorized partner program to grow sales through our partner network.
Interviewer: That's a clear summary. We can close the case here.

Parts and Recreation Framework & Recommendations
GROWTH STRATEGY TO DOUBLE REVENUE FOR AN AUTOMOTIVE SPARE PARTS DIVISION
Clarifying Questions: Meaning of OEM Channels in play (product and service) Whether the parts fit other cars Top line or bottom line Target and time frame
Brownie Points: Defining OEM before proceeding Bundling service cost into the EMI Building a milestone-based authorized partner program
Keep In Mind: Grow parts per car, not volume Raise value instead of cutting price

title: Dry Hard
prompt: Your client is a washing machine manufacturer that has witnessed a steady decline in revenues. Diagnose the problem and give your recommendations.

notes.title: Questions
items: Value chain stage
Magnitude & duration of decline
Competitor benchmarking

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Match product features to local utility costs

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Clarifying competitor product differences
Reframing the drought into a marketing message

framework:
Candidate: Sure. Before I lay out my approach, I would like to ask a few preliminary questions.
Interviewer: Certainly, go ahead.
Candidate: To start, which stage of the value chain is the company involved in? And what has been the quantum of this decline, and over what period?
Interviewer: The client is solely involved in the manufacturing of washing machines. The company has witnessed a 20% decline in revenues over the past 1 year.
Candidate: Got it. Should I look only at the revenue side, or has the client also seen any change in costs?
Interviewer: There has been no change in costs. Just focus on revenues.
Candidate: Understood. I would break revenue into two levers:
Revenue = Number of Units Sold * Price per Unit
Have we seen a recent change in either of these?
Interviewer: The number of units sold has gone down. There has been no change in the price.
Candidate: I will further subdivide the factors affecting the number of units sold into three categories: production capacity, distribution, and consumer pull. Have we seen any recent change in the production capacity of the company?
Interviewer: Not really.
Candidate: And has there been any recent change in the distribution of our washing machines?
Interviewer: No.
Candidate: That leaves consumer pull as the likely driver. Should I proceed with that?
Interviewer: Yes, go ahead with consumer pull.
Candidate: For the drop in consumer pull, I see three possible reasons: quality, marketing, and externalities. Am I missing any major factor?
Interviewer: No, you can proceed.
Candidate: Before I examine each one, could you tell me what the market competition looks like?
Interviewer: The market is fragmented, with multiple competitors each holding roughly 15% market share, including our client.
Candidate: Got it. Is our washing machine different in quality from the competitors'?
Interviewer: Yes.
Candidate: I would break quality into four sub-factors: features, after-sale services, maintenance cost, and power requirements. Is any of these different from the competitors'?
Interviewer: Our client's washing machine is smaller in size than the competitors', and is a top-load model, unlike most competitors who have a front-load model. Maintenance cost and after-sale services are the same.
Candidate: My knowledge of washing machine models is limited. Could you elaborate on the difference between top-load and front-load?
Interviewer: A top-load model generally requires more water per cycle than a front-load model.
Candidate: Understood. Moving on, has there been any recent change in the client's marketing strategies?
Interviewer: Nothing as such.
Candidate: Finally, have there been any recent externalities that may have hit consumer pull?
Interviewer: Yes. The nearby region has been struck by drought in the last year.
Candidate: That ties everything together. Our washing machine is smaller in size, so it can wash fewer clothes at once and requires more cycles than the competitors'. On top of that, since the region has been hit by drought, water is scarce and more expensive. So running our machine costs the customer more water and more money than running a front-load competitor's machine, which is why consumer pull has dropped.
Interviewer: You've identified the problem correctly. What corrective action do you recommend?
Candidate: One quick check before I give my recommendations: is it feasible for the client to change the size and type of the washing machine without much expenditure?
Interviewer: That change is likely to be very expensive.
Candidate: Alright. Can I take a couple of minutes to put my recommendations together?
Interviewer: Sure.
Candidate: _(Recommendations on the next page.)_
Interviewer: Sounds great. We can close the case here.

title: Net Worth
prompt: Your client is the Prime Minister's Office (PMO). You are advising the ministry on a vision-setting and economic planning exercise. The brief is to identify sectors where the government should double down on economic policy, with three primary objectives in mind: GDP, private sector investment, and employment. The government has already identified a few sectors and would like your help in confirming whether those choices are prudent.

notes.title: Questions
items: Time horizon for the policy?
Quantitative targets per objective?
Budget or regulatory constraints?
Pre-identified sectors and rationale?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Long horizon makes sustainability a separate lens

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Citing twelve nautical miles for territorial waters
Choosing supply-side because exports matter on an island

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I lay out my approach, I have a few clarifying questions. What is the time period we are looking at for this policy?
Interviewer: Fifteen years.
Candidate: Are there any quantitative targets in mind for the three objectives?
Interviewer: Not really.
Candidate: Are there any budget constraints or regulatory limitations?
Interviewer: No, none. Treat the budget as unrestricted.
Candidate: You also mentioned a few pre-identified sectors. Could you share those along with the rationale?
Interviewer: We will come to that in the latter part of the case. For now, walk me through how you would approach identifying the right sectors.
Candidate: Sure. I will map the economy first, then describe how I would shortlist against the three objectives. I would split the economy into three categories: Primary (agriculture and non-agriculture), Secondary (manufacturing and non-manufacturing), and Tertiary (IT-based and non-IT-based services). I would then assess each sector against three parameters: 1) Current trends, 2) Growth potential over the fifteen-year horizon, and 3) Sustainability, meaning how likely the sector is to remain relevant fifteen years out (kept separate from growth potential because a sector that could be displaced by Artificial Intelligence or automation would score poorly here even if its growth potential looks strong today). I would walk each sector across the three objectives using these parameters, and shortlist the ones that score consistently.
Interviewer: That works. Here are the sectors we have shortlisted so far: Primary: coffee, fruits (oranges and coconuts), fisheries; Secondary: food processing; Tertiary: tourism, Business Process Outsourcing / Knowledge Process Outsourcing (BPO/KPO).
Candidate: Got it.
Interviewer: Based on this list of seven or eight sectors, how would you narrow it down to two or three? What Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) would you use?
Candidate: Let me list the metrics first: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of the sector, employment percentage it accounts for, private sector investment flowing in, startup growth percentage (a leading indicator of investment), a risk or sustainability score, and comparables, sectors in other countries at a similar economic stage in the past and the growth trajectories they followed.
Interviewer: This feels quite cluttered. Remember, you are presenting to a political audience. Simplify it.
Candidate: Fair point. Let me re-organise the metrics directly against the three objectives. GDP: contribution to GDP, GDP growth rate. Private sector investment: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), Foreign Institutional Investment (FII), startup growth percentage. Employment: current employment trends, and the risk of human labour being displaced as technology and capital become more abundant in the sector.
Interviewer: That works. Running these metrics, we have drilled down to fisheries as the sector to focus on. It is currently highly underdeveloped and has substantial scope for further growth. I would now like you to perform a guesstimate: estimate the market size of the fisheries sector in this country. One clarification: the country is not India. It is an island nation in Southeast Asia.
Candidate: Understood. Market size of fisheries can be approximated as number of fishes * average price per fish.
Interviewer: For this exercise, restrict yourself to the number of fishes. Pricing is not what we are testing.
Candidate: Got it. Two broad approaches: demand-side (fishes consumed within the country) or supply-side (fishes harvested or cultivated). The demand-side approach assumes no fish is exported, which is unlikely for an island economy, so I would lean towards supply side.
Interviewer: Agreed. Exports are meaningful here, so demand side is too restrictive. Go with supply side.
Candidate: Before I dive in, how are fishes typically caught in this country? Labour-intensive or capital-intensive? Any advanced technology in use?
Interviewer: No advanced technology. Fishing is largely traditional, through hand and net by local fishermen.
Candidate: That helps. Three possible bottlenecks could constrain the supply side: 1) fishermen, 2) total stock of fishes available, and 3) distributors moving the catch onward.
Interviewer: Focus on the fishes angle. Assume all fishes within the country's territory can be cultivated, so you are estimating the total potential stock irrespective of fishermen, boats, or distributors.
Candidate: Understood. I would first split the country's water bodies into inland and marine.
Interviewer: Assume no fishes in inland water bodies. Focus only on marine.
Candidate: Sure. To estimate the marine area, I would need the country's size and shape.
Interviewer: Land area is 200 km².
Candidate: Two simplifying assumptions: the country is roughly a square island (a 200 km² square gives a side of approximately 14 km), and the ocean surrounds the island on all four sides with fishing possible on all four coasts. One important constraint: a country's fishing rights typically extend only up to its domestic territorial waters, which under international convention is around twelve nautical miles from the coast. Beyond that, fishing requires separate permissions.
Interviewer: Sharp insight. For this case, assume the cultivable marine zone extends 8 km from each coastline.
Candidate: Got it. The outer boundary of the cultivable zone is then a larger square with a side of 14 + 8 + 8 = 30 km. Outer area = 900 km². Subtracting the land area of 200 km², the cultivable marine zone works out to 700 km².
Interviewer: Good. Within this 700 km², fish density is not uniform. How would you think about it?
Candidate: My hypothesis: density is higher closer to the coast (reef and shallow-water habitats) and falls as you move further into the open ocean.
Interviewer: Directionally yes, though the order is slightly different. Moving outward from the coast: Medium-density band covers 25 km² as the first stretch from the coast; High-density band covers 400 km² as the next stretch, holding most of the catch; Low-density band covers 275 km² as the outermost stretch. The three together cover the full 700 km².
Candidate: Got it. I will need a yield assumption for each band.
Interviewer: Take the low-density band as 500 kg of fish per km² per month. Use a 2x multiple for medium and 3x for high.
Candidate: ~ So medium = 1,000 kg per km² per month and high = 1,500 kg per km² per month. Working through each band: Low: 275 * 500 = 1,37,500 kg/month. Medium: 25 * 1,000 = 25,000 kg/month. High: 400 * 1,500 = 6,00,000 kg/month. Total potential fish harvest = 7,62,500 kg per month.
Interviewer: Good. That gives us the size of the prize. One final question: what would you recommend to increase the potential of the fisheries sector in this country?
Candidate: I would split the recommendations into two categories: ways to increase the total number of fishes available, and ways to increase the productivity of catching what we already have access to.
To increase the number of fishes available: 1) Partner with friendly neighbouring countries to cultivate in their waters under a shared arrangement. 2) Pursue international approvals or treaties that allow our fleet to fish in selected international waters. 3) Invest in artificial aquaculture and aquaponics farms on land, which decouple supply from the natural marine boundary entirely.
To increase productivity and efficiency: 1) Introduce better technology, machinery, and modern fishing methods to replace the hand-and-net approach. 2) Group individual fishermen into cooperatives or larger fishing units (analogy: consolidating fragmented agricultural plots, where scale unlocks shared investment in machinery and technology that an individual fisherman or small boat cannot afford alone).
Interviewer: That covers it well. We can close the case here.

Net Worth Framework & Recommendations
SECTOR IDENTIFICATION FOR 15-YEAR POLICY (PMO ADVISORY)
Clarifying Questions: Quantitative targets per objective; Budget or regulatory constraints
Brownie Points: Citing twelve nautical miles for territorial waters; Choosing supply-side because exports matter on an island; Applying agricultural consolidation to fisheries
Keep In Mind: Tie every metric directly to a stated objective; Long horizon elevates sustainability as a separate lens

title: Pound for Pound
prompt: Novo Nordisk has launched a product called Wegovy, which is used to accelerate weight loss. An Indian pharmaceutical company wants to venture into this space and has developed a drug similar to Novo Nordisk's. They want to understand the likely size of the market. The candidate must estimate both the price and the market size, given the drug is launched across urban centres in India, is not recommended for people with cardiac issues or seniors above 60, and has no major side effects.

notes.title: Questions
items: Units vs monetary market sizing?
Eligibility & suitability for drug?
Is the launch in a specific city?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Apply affordability twice: income, then willingness

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Probed relapse cases before sizing revenue
Self-imposed a lower age cap

visualisations.title: Demand Sizing
visualisations.insight: Affordability bites twice on purpose: first as the income screen, then as a 20% willingness-to-pay conversion on the demand pool. The two buyer pools are assumed mutually exclusive.

visualisations.title: Market Size
visualisations.insight: Monthly price is competitor-benchmarked on Novo Nordisk's Wegovy, and each course is one-time (no repeat cycle).

framework:
Candidate: Before I begin, I would like to clarify a few things. Are we estimating the market size in terms of the number of units, or in monetary terms?
Interviewer: We currently do not have information on the price. That is something we would like you to estimate as well, so you will have to estimate both the price and the market size.
Candidate: Understood. Since this is a weight-loss drug, I would like to understand which segments of the population are eligible for the drug and which segments it may not be suited for.
Interviewer: The drug is not recommended for people with cardiac issues.
Candidate: Got it. Are there any age restrictions as well?
Interviewer: Yes. You can assume the drug is not recommended for seniors above the age of 60.
Candidate: Would it also be fair to assume a lower age cap of 20 years, since children and adolescents may not typically opt for such medication?
Interviewer: That sounds reasonable. Let's proceed.
Candidate: One more clarification: are we launching this drug in a specific city, or across urban centres in India?
Interviewer: Across all urban centres.
Candidate: And are there any side effects associated with the drug that may affect adoption?
Interviewer: No, you can assume there are no major side effects.
Candidate: Great. Let me walk you through my approach. When estimating the market size, I would like to focus specifically on the number of people who would realistically purchase the drug, rather than those who may only be interested in it.
Candidate: I will start with the population of India, which I will assume to be 140 crore. Next, I will split this into rural and urban segments, since the drug is only being launched in urban centres. Initially, I would assume the urban population to be roughly 40 crore.
Interviewer: Let's take the urban population as 60 crore instead.
Candidate: Sure, I will proceed with 60 crore.
Candidate: Next, I will apply an income filter, since affordability will be an important factor for a drug like this. Splitting the urban population into four income segments: lower income 20%, lower middle class 30%, upper middle class 30%, rich 20%. Given the likely cost of such treatment, I will focus only on the UMC and rich segments and exclude the rest. That gives us 50% of the urban population, or roughly 30 crore people.
Candidate: Next, I will apply an age filter: less than 20 years 25%, above 60 years 5%, target band 20 to 60 years 70%. Applying 70% to the 30 crore gives approximately 21 crore individuals in the eligible age group.
Candidate: Now I would like to estimate which segments within this population would actually consider purchasing the drug. Broadly, I see two categories of potential buyers:
1) Health-conscious individuals interested in fitness or cosmetic weight loss.
2) People who are obese or suffering from health conditions related to high weight. Does this two-category split sound reasonable, or would you like me to consider any other buyer profile?
Interviewer: That split works well. Go ahead and size each of them.
Candidate: Thank you. For the first category, I will assume around 5% of individuals are highly health-conscious. Applied to the 21 crore eligible base, that gives roughly 1.05 crore people as the cosmetic demand pool. For the second category, I will assume roughly 1 in 5 Indians are obese (20%), giving 4.2 crore people as the medical demand pool. Total demand pool approximately 5.25 crore people.
Candidate: I believe we should move to pricing, because the actual buyers will depend heavily on affordability.
Interviewer: Yes, we can move on to pricing.
Candidate: I would like to determine a price range using three approaches:
1) Competitor-based pricing benchmarked against Novo Nordisk's Wegovy.
2) Cost-based pricing (manufacturing cost plus margin) for the lower bound.
3) Value-based pricing based on willingness to pay for substitutes like gym memberships, supplements, diet programs, for the upper bound.
Interviewer: Focus specifically on competitor-based pricing. How would you approach that?
Candidate: To benchmark, I would like to understand dosage and treatment length.
Interviewer: For fitness or cosmetic weight loss, the treatment lasts about 3 months at roughly Rs 50,000 per month. For obesity cases, the treatment is about one year.
Candidate: I also wanted to clarify whether there are relapse cases.
Interviewer: No, they do not need to repeat the drug cycle, but lifestyle maintenance is required to prevent relapse.
Candidate:~ To close the estimation, I will apply an affordability filter of 20% on the 5.25 crore demand pool, giving 1.05 crore actual buyers: 21 lakh cosmetic buyers (3 months * Rs 50,000 = Rs 1.5 lakh per person) and 84 lakh obesity buyers (12 months * Rs 50,000 = Rs 6 lakh per person). Sizing in rupees: cosmetic segment 21 lakh * Rs 1.5 lakh = Rs 31,500 crore; obesity segment 84 lakh * Rs 6 lakh = Rs 5,04,000 crore. Total addressable market approximately Rs 5,35,500 crore, or about Rs 5.35 lakh crore (roughly $64 billion). The obesity segment dominates because the treatment duration is four times longer.
Interviewer: Makes sense. That was a comprehensive analysis. We can end the case here.

Pound for Pound Framework & Recommendations
Market sizing for Wegovy-style drug (Indian pharma entry)
Clarifying Questions: Units versus monetary market sizing Eligibility exclusions (cardiac and age) Geographic scope (urban versus pan-India) Side effects affecting adoption
Brownie Points: Proposing three pricing approaches with explicit bounds Asking about relapse and lifestyle maintenance Differentiating cosmetic versus medically obese segments
Keep In Mind: Affordability is the binding adoption constraint Cosmetic and medical journeys differ structurally.

framework:
Candidate: Before I dive in I'd like to clarify a few things. First, can I confirm what the business does and where it operates?

Interviewer: Sure. The company runs flying taxis between Chennai's main airport and two or three points across the city. Think of it as a premium service for people who want to skip road traffic.

Candidate: Got it. Next, the specifications of the E-Plane. Fleet size, seating capacity, and the type of vehicle.

Interviewer: We have a fleet of 7 planes. Each one seats 5 passengers, and the vehicle is essentially an electric drone.

Candidate: Understood. And the goal of the pricing strategy. By when does the company want to break even?

Interviewer: In 3 years. That's the horizon we're working with.

Candidate: Last clarification. Is there a predetermined operation plan? Days per week, and number of trips per day?

Interviewer: Yes, the team has locked that in. 7 days a week, 10 trips a day.

Candidate: That gives me what I need. The approach here is straightforward. There are two cost components, fixed and variable, and the minimum price to charge is the one that lets the business recover both within 3 years.

On the fixed side, two heads:
1. Research and Development costs
2. PPE costs, which means Property, Plant, and Equipment, splitting into land and the flight fleet

On the variable side:
1. Operations, mainly energy per trip
2. Repair and maintenance
3. Labour, both skilled and unskilled
4. Any miscellaneous costs

Does this split look reasonable, or should I consider any other cost head?

Interviewer: That covers it. Start with fixed costs. You can take R&D cost as 4 crore rupees.

Candidate: Noted. For PPE, fleet cost dominates. Let me build up the cost of one E-Plane first. I'd think of it as the cost of an average 5-seater car plus the modules needed to make it airborne.

A 5-seater car is around 10 lakh rupees. The airborne modules are frame, rotors, and electrical circuitry, in a ratio of 1:3:2.

1. Frame: 6 lakh rupees
2. Rotors: 18 lakh rupees
3. Electrical circuitry: 12 lakh rupees
4. Module total: 36 lakh rupees

Thus, cost per plane that comes to 10 lakh plus 36 lakh, which is 46 lakh rupees. I'll round to 50 lakh per plane.

^ Fleet Cost = 50 lakh * 7 = 3.5 crore rupees

Adding land into the PPE bucket, total fixed cost lands at around 10 crore rupees.

Interviewer: Take that as the fixed figure. Walk me through variables.

Candidate: For operations, energy cost per trip uses the following formula:

^ Energy Cost per Trip = Distance * Consumption per km * Variability Factor * Cost per Unit Energy

I added a variability factor because for a plane, climatic and landing conditions can move energy consumption significantly trip to trip.

Interviewer: How would you pick the two or three points the plane operates between?

Candidate: Since docking and refuelling happen at the airport, one end of each route is fixed. For the other end, I'd select places that either take a long time to reach from the airport by road, or are inaccessible by road. That's where this service creates the most time-saved value.

Interviewer: Who's actually willing to pay for that?

Candidate: It's a premium service, so the customers will mostly come from the upper strata. Two segments stand out: wealthy residents and tourists.

Interviewer: I'd add government officials to that list. They often need fast point-to-point movement and have budgets that cover it.

Candidate: That's a good addition. So we have three segments: wealthy residents, tourists, and government officials. Combining these with the access-difficulty filter narrows the potential locations to places with a high concentration of premium users. For Chennai, Marina Beach would work on one route, and a cinema district could anchor another. Ideally the two points sit on opposite sides of the city.

Interviewer: Any other filters before you move on?

Candidate: Two more, both turn out to be neutral here:

1. Climatic conditions across Chennai are largely uniform, so they don't change much across points
2. Landing feasibility is also uniform once we pick reasonable open spaces

Back to the energy build. With distance roughly 15 kilometres from the airport to Marina, average consumption around 2.5 kilowatt-hours per kilometre, and energy cost around 20 rupees per kilowatt-hour, per-trip energy lands at about 750 rupees. Spread over 3 years of operation, total energy cost works out to approximately 50 lakh rupees.

Does the per-trip approach look right before I add the rest?

Interviewer: Yes, continue.

Candidate: After energy I'd add:

1. Repair and maintenance, roughly 20 lakh rupees over 3 years
2. Labour, both skilled and unskilled:
  - Skilled: 30 engineers, at 20 lakh rupees per annum each, over 3 years, which is 18 crore rupees
  - Unskilled: effectively negligible, close to zero

Total variable cost is 50 lakh + 20 lakh + 18 crore, which is approximately 18 crore rupees.

Adding fixed costs calculated earlier (10 crore) and variable cost (18 crore), total cost over 3 years is 28 crore rupees.

Interviewer: Now, what about customer side?

Candidate: With 10 trips per day at 5 seats each, full-occupancy capacity is 50 customers a day. Over 3 years that's 50 multiplied by 365 multiplied by 3, which equals 54,750 customer-trips. I'll round to 50,000 for clean math.

Breakeven equation:

^ 50,000 * Price = 28 crore rupees

^ Price = 28,00,00,000 / 50,000 = 5,600 rupees per customer

That's the cost-based price floor.

Interviewer: How do you go from there to an actual pricing strategy?

Candidate: 5,600 is the lower ceiling, the cost-based floor. To set the upper ceiling I'll value-base the price, using the existing cab service as a benchmark.

A cab from the airport to Marina costs 600 rupees for one person over 15 kilometres, and takes roughly 90 minutes in traffic. The e-plane covers the same route in about 10 minutes.

^ Time saved per trip = 90 - 10 = 80 minutes

I'll value that saved time using two methods.
- Method 1: Cab fare scaled by time multiple. The e-plane is 9 times faster than a cab (90 minutes divided by 10 minutes). Scaling the cab fare by the same factor:

^ 600 * 9 = 5,400 rupees per trip

- Method 2: Per-minute value of the customer's time. The idea is to price the trip at what the customer's own time is worth across the 80 minutes saved:

    1) Monthly income: A premium customer earns roughly 5 lakh rupees per month.

    2) Productive minutes per month: Assume the customer is productive for about 8,000 minutes per month, which works out to roughly 133 hours.

    3) Per-minute value of time:

^ Per Minute Value = 5,00,000 / 8,000 = 62.5 rupees per minute

    4) Value of the 80 minutes saved per trip:

^ Trip Value = 80 * 62.5 = 5,000 rupees per trip

So I now have three anchor numbers:

1. 5,000 rupees, low value-based estimate (Method 2)
2. 5,400 rupees, high value-based estimate (Method 1)
3. 5,600 rupees, cost-based breakeven floor

Interviewer: How does that translate into the actual launch strategy?

Candidate: I'd structure it as a 3-year ladder:

1. Year 1: 5,000 rupees, starting at the low value-based estimate to drive early adoption
2. Year 2: 5,400 rupees, stepping up to the high value-based estimate as the customer base matures
3. Year 3: 5,600 rupees, reaching the cost-based floor and breaking even by year 3

This way the business attracts customers at a believable price point in year 1, captures full willingness to pay by year 2, and reaches breakeven by year 3.

Interviewer: Solid. Let's wrap there.


UP IN THE AIR FRAMEWORK & RECOMMENDATIONS
E-PLANE PRICING STRATEGY FOR CHENNAI AIRPORT FLYING TAXI

Clarifying Questions: Business and geography; Specs (fleet, seats, type); Breakeven timeline; Operation plan (days, trips)

Brownie Points: Sense-checking value with two methods off a cab benchmark; Adding a variability factor for climate and landing; Selecting points by road access and premium density

Keep In Mind: Cost sets the price floor, not ceiling; Value time saved via a real alternative

title: Wired Differently

Diagnose why the same policies are not working in Electronics, and estimate the breakeven period for a new set of corrective policies tailored to the Electronics division.

notes.title: Questions
items: Attrition-based or survey-based dissatisfaction?
How long have the new policies been live?
Same location or different geographies?
Workforce demographics per division?
Entire HR bundle replicated or only parts?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Convert revenue uplift to margin before timing breakeven

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Probing the location and gender split early
Flagging raw-versus-net on retention
