framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I lay out my approach, I have a few clarifying questions. First, when you say worker dissatisfaction, do you mean a specific signal like attrition and absenteeism, or a broader survey-based sentiment measure?
Interviewer: It is a survey-based sentiment measure, where workers self-report on morale, fairness, and workplace experience.
Candidate: Understood. How long ago were the Automobiles policies replicated into Electronics, and how recent is the latest survey?
Interviewer: The policies have been in place for about a year, and the latest survey is within the last quarter.
Candidate: Are the two divisions in the same city, or in different geographies?
Interviewer: Different states. The Automobiles factory is in Karnataka; the Electronics factory is in Haryana.
Candidate: That is helpful. Could you describe the workforce in each division by age, gender, and language?
Interviewer: The Karnataka (Automobiles) workforce is predominantly Hindi-speaking, young, and largely female. The Haryana (Electronics) workforce is predominantly local men.
Candidate: That is a meaningful split. One last clarification: was the entire HR bundle replicated, or only specific pieces like compensation and shift structure?
Interviewer: Assume the entire bundle was replicated as-is.
Candidate: Got it. The core question is why an identical policy bundle produces different sentiment across the two divisions. I would group the possible drivers into four pillars:
1. Demographic Factors
2. Union-Related Factors
3. Job-Related Factors
4. Externalities and Work Culture
Candidate: Pillar 1, Demographic Factors. The two workforces differ on gender, language, age, family structure, income, lifestyle, and broader cultural context. A bundle that resonates with a young, Hindi-speaking, largely female workforce in Karnataka will not land the same way on a workforce of local men in Haryana. A one-size-fits-all policy rarely lands equally on both groups.
Interviewer: That makes sense. Move on.
Candidate: Pillar 2, Union-Related Factors. Even with identical policy text, reception depends on the union environment. In Haryana the union may be more entrenched, local demands may differ, and the union may be more effective at translating individual complaints into collective friction. The same policy can read as a minor irritant in one division and an organised grievance in the other.
Interviewer: Fair. Continue.
Candidate: Pillar 3, Job-Related Factors. The work itself differs. Two sub-factors stand out:
1. Labour Intensity: automobile and electronics assembly impose different physical and mental strain, so the same rule on break frequency or shift length may suit one and not the other.
2. Hours and Compensation: differences in shift structure, base pay, and variable perks can make a benefit feel generous in one division and routine in the other.
Candidate: Pillar 4, Externalities and Work Culture. Two sub-factors here:
1. Manager-Worker Relations: how local management treats workers on the floor. A policy is only as good as the manager implementing it.
2. Coworker Relationships: the interpersonal environment among co-workers, heavily shaped by local culture and not directly controlled by HR policy.
Candidate: Across the four pillars, I would expect the demographic and work-culture pillars to carry most of the explanatory weight here, given the location and gender-mix difference. Union and job-related factors are likely amplifiers rather than the root cause, but I would still test them.
Interviewer: That structure works well. Let us switch tracks. Suppose leadership designs a new set of corrective policies tailored to Electronics. Estimate the breakeven period for implementing them. Here are your parameters:
Interviewer: 1. Incremental cost: 50 million dollars one-time fixed, plus 5 million dollars per year variable, on top of existing HR spend.
Interviewer: 2. Total organisation revenue: 200 million dollars.
Interviewer: 3. Productivity uplift modelled as revenue enhancement of 30 percent in Year 1, 20 percent in Year 2, and 10 percent from Year 3 onwards.
Interviewer: 4. Retention: 10,000 workers, attrition falling from 20 percent to 10 percent, at a hiring and training cost of 1,000 dollars per worker.
Candidate: The breakeven question is when cumulative incremental benefit overtakes cumulative incremental cost. I will set up two value drivers against one cost line, then walk year by year.
Candidate: Value driver 1, Revenue Enhancement. The underlying revenue formula is Number of Workers × Hours Worked × Output per Hour. A productivity lift moves the output-per-hour term, so Year 1 incremental revenue is 30 percent of 200 million dollars.
Candidate: Value driver 2, Retention Cost Savings. Every departure must be replaced at 1,000 dollars in hiring and training, so savings equal Attrition Reduction × Total Workers × Hiring Cost per Worker. Attrition falls 10 percentage points, applied to 10,000 workers at 1,000 dollars each.
Candidate: One adjustment to flag on retention. The raw saving captures the avoided hiring and training cost. A stricter view would also subtract the ramp-up inefficiency of new hires we no longer need. For simplicity I will use the raw saving as the base case.
Interviewer: Good. Compute the yearly numbers.
Candidate: Let me first try a compounding view, where each year's gain stacks on the prior year's lifted base.
Interviewer: Hold on. Use a linear baseline: apply each year's productivity percentage to the original 200 million dollar base, not a compounded one.
Candidate: Understood, that is cleaner for a breakeven view and avoids overstating the gain. On the linear baseline the revenue uplift is 60 million dollars in Year 1 (30 percent of 200 million), 40 million dollars in Year 2 (20 percent), and 20 million dollars from Year 3 onwards (10 percent).
Candidate: One important adjustment before I time the breakeven. This revenue uplift is not profit, so to compare like for like against the investment I should convert it to a contribution margin. What margin should I assume on the incremental revenue?
Interviewer: Assume a contribution margin of 50 percent.
Candidate: Then I build the annual position by netting the margin contribution and the retention saving against the incremental cost.
Year 1: Margin contribution 30 million dollars (50 percent of 60 million) plus Retention Savings 1 million dollars, minus incremental cost 55 million dollars (50 upfront plus 5 variable). Net minus 24 million dollars. Cumulative minus 24 million dollars.
Year 2: Margin contribution 20 million dollars plus Retention Savings 1 million dollars, minus incremental cost 5 million dollars variable. Net plus 16 million dollars. Cumulative minus 8 million dollars.
Year 3: Margin contribution 10 million dollars plus Retention Savings 1 million dollars, minus incremental cost 5 million dollars variable. Net plus 6 million dollars. Cumulative minus 2 million dollars.
Year 4 onwards: the same steady-state net of plus 6 million dollars per year, so cumulative turns positive at plus 4 million dollars.
Candidate: On a margin basis the cumulative position climbs from minus 24 million dollars in Year 1 to minus 2 million dollars by the end of Year 3, which essentially recovers the 50 million dollar investment, and turns positive early in Year 4. That puts the breakeven at approximately 3 years.
Interviewer: Roughly 3 years is the right answer. Good work walking through the structure cleanly. Let us close the case here.

Wired Differently Framework & Recommendations
WHY THE SAME HR POLICIES PRODUCE DIFFERENT WORKER SENTIMENT IN TWO DIVISIONS
Clarifying Questions: How dissatisfaction is measured; time in field for the new policies; plant locations; workforce demographics per division; scope of policy replication.
Brownie Points: Probing the demographic and location split before bucketing; splitting drivers into demographic, union, job, and culture pillars; pivoting from a compounding to a linear baseline on the interviewer's cue.
Keep In Mind: Identical policy text is received differently across demographic context; demographic and culture splits often explain policy variance more than the policy text itself.

title: Don't Sweat It
prompt: The client is a corporate-empanelled cab vendor in India. They partner with corporates across the country to provide cab rides to those corporates' employees, where the corporate pays on the employee's behalf, so the ride is free for the employee. Most corporates work with multiple cab vendors at the same time, and employees pick whichever vendor they want for any given ride. For example, BCG has five empanelled cab vendors and our client is one of them. Over the past several months, the share of employees opting for our client's cabs has been dropping. Diagnose what is driving the decline.

notes.title: Questions
items: Time period of the decline?
Charging structure: fixed or variable?
Drop across all corporates or concentrated?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: When the service is free to the user, drop affordability
Run a value chain on the vehicle in the order a rider notices things

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Decomposing revenue into six multiplicative drivers
Forming an early demand-side hypothesis from the breadth of the decline
Raising competitor air-freshener perception, recognising smell can be relative

visualisations.title: Revenue Formula
visualisations.rhs: Partners × Employees/Partner × Opt Rate % ×  Rides/Employee × Distance/Ride × Price/Kilometre
visualisations.content: Revenue = Partners × Employees/Partner × Opt Rate % ×  Rides/Employee × Distance/Ride × Price/Kilometre

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I lay out my approach, I have a few clarifying questions. First, what is the time period over which this drop has been observed?
Interviewer: Roughly the last 7 to 8 months.
Candidate: Understood. Second, how does the client charge the corporate? Is it a fixed fee, a variable fee, or both?
Interviewer: There are two components. A fixed charge per corporate per period, and a variable charge based on usage. For this case, ignore the fixed charge and focus only on the variable side.
Candidate: Got it. Third, is the client operating pan-India or in specific cities?
Interviewer: Assume pan-India.
Candidate: Last clarification. Is the share drop showing up across every corporate partner, or is it concentrated in a subset of them?
Interviewer: Assume it is broadly across the portfolio, not isolated to one corporate.
Candidate: Got it. Let me lay out my approach. I want to start at the profit equation and trace where the decline is coming from.
Profit equals revenue minus cost. Since the symptom is that the share of employees opting for us is dropping, the impact lands on the revenue side, so I will focus there first.
Variable revenue here breaks down into a clean equation:
Variable Revenue = Number of Corporate Partners * Employees per Partner * Opt Rate for our service * Average Rides per Employee * Average Distance per Ride * Price Charged per Kilometre
The fixed charge would sit on top of that as a per-corporate component, but you have asked me to leave that aside.
Interviewer: Good. Of those drivers, which one would you like to focus on?
Candidate: The symptom is specifically about the opt rate, so I will narrow there. The number of corporate partners, the employee base, the ride frequency, and the per-kilometre price are not what you flagged. The opt rate is the term that has moved.
Interviewer: Correct. The opt rate is dropping. Continue.
Candidate: A drop in opt rate can come from one of two broad sources.
1. Supply side: even when an employee wants our cab, the service is not available. For example, not enough cars on the road, long wait times, or limited geographic coverage.
2. Demand side: the cars are available, but employees are choosing one of the other four vendors instead of ours.
My initial hypothesis is that this is a demand-side issue, since the share drop is showing up broadly across corporates and across geographies, which is more consistent with employees actively switching away than with a sudden capacity collapse.
Interviewer: Your hypothesis is right. It is a demand-side issue. Walk me through the demand side.
Candidate: On the demand side, for an employee to choose our cab in any given booking, three conditions have to hold.
1. Need: the employee actually needs a ride at that moment.
2. Awareness: the employee knows our cab is one of the available options.
3. Affordability and acceptability: the cost works for the employee and the experience is acceptable.
The need is constant, because the underlying transport need is unchanged. Awareness should also be stable, since we are already on the booking platform alongside the other four vendors. Affordability is not the constraint here, because the ride is free for the employee in any case. That points the issue toward acceptability, which is really a user experience question.
Interviewer: Yes. The user experience is the issue. Take it forward.
Candidate: I will break the user experience into three phases of the journey.
1. Pre-ride: booking the cab, finding it in the app, downloading or logging in, getting a confirmation, and getting the OTP.
2. During the ride: the actual ride from pickup to drop.
3. Post-ride: drop-off, feedback, ratings, and follow-up.
If awareness is fine and the app is functioning, the pre-ride phase is unlikely to be where the choice is being lost. The post-ride phase mostly shapes future choices through feedback. The during-the-ride phase is where the lived experience happens, and it is the phase most likely to push an employee to switch vendors on the next booking.
Interviewer: The during-ride phase is where the issue sits. Go deeper.
Candidate: Within the during-ride phase, there are three things that shape the experience.
1. The vehicle itself.
2. The driver: behaviour, communication, driving style, professionalism.
3. The route: time taken, traffic, detours.
Interviewer: The issue is with the vehicle.
Candidate: Got it. Let me run a mental value chain on the vehicle, in roughly the order an employee would notice things.
1. Type of vehicle: SUV, sedan, hatchback. Is the form factor appropriate for the rider?
2. Brand of vehicle: is it a recognised brand that signals reliability?
3. Appearance from outside: is the vehicle clean, dent-free, presentable?
4. Quality of interiors: once the employee sits inside, is it well-maintained, are the seats and accessories in good shape?
5. Utilities inside the vehicle: air conditioner working, music system working, charging points functional.
Interviewer: The issue is in the quality bucket. There is a smell coming from the vehicles. What could possibly be causing a smell in a cab?
Candidate: Let me list four reasons a smell could be coming from the inside of the vehicle.
1. The vehicle is physically dirty: dirt, mud, and dust accumulated from the routes it travels, and that is producing the smell.
2. The interiors are not well-maintained: seat covers, mats, and accessories have degraded or are not being cleaned, and the material itself is producing the smell.
3. The driver is not hygienic: the smell is associated with the driver rather than the vehicle itself.
4. Perception driven by competition: our cabs may not actually smell worse, but the other four vendors are using strong air fresheners, so by comparison our cabs are perceived as smelling worse.
Interviewer: The interiors are not well-maintained, and specifically it is the seat covers. About 7 to 8 months ago, the company changed all seat covers to a new sweat-absorbent material. The intent was good, since the new material absorbs sweat from the rider's clothes. The problem is that the material retains sweat instead of letting it evaporate. Over time, the seat covers accumulate retained sweat and start producing a smell, which is what employees are noticing during the ride and what is pushing them toward the other four vendors.

Don't Sweat It Framework
Why are fewer employees opting for our cabs?
Clarifying Questions: Charging structure (fixed versus variable). Drop across all corporates or concentrated.
Brownie Points: Decomposing revenue into six multiplicative drivers.
Keep In Mind: Operational change can produce downstream defects.

title: Critical Condition
prompt: A Delhi hospital that has treated prime ministers and cricketers alike is now the one in need of treatment. Profits are declining and the board has called you in before things get critical.

notes.title: Questions
items: Is this a single branch?
Since when has profit declined?
How large is the decline?
Which services do we offer?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Billed revenue differs from collected revenue

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Segmenting insured payers into public and private
Linking public sector defaults to bad debt

framework:
Candidate: Sure. Before I dive in, I'd like to ask a few clarifying questions to make sure I understand the situation:
- Do we run a single branch, or are there multiple locations?
- Since when has the decline in profits been happening?
- How large is the decline?
- What kinds of services do we offer? The service mix itself could be part of the problem.
Interviewer: Good questions. It is a hospital in Delhi running a single branch. The decline is recent and meaningful, and you can assume a broad set of hospital services for now. Let's focus on why profits are falling.
Candidate: Understood. Profit is revenue minus costs, so I first want to isolate whether this is a revenue problem or a cost problem. Have our costs gone up, or has our revenue come down?
Interviewer: Revenue has declined. Costs have stayed steady.
Candidate: Got it, so I will focus on the revenue side. For a hospital, I would break revenue into three drivers:
1. The number of hospital beds
2. The occupancy rate of those beds
3. The revenue we earn per bed per night
Have any of these three shifted?
Interviewer: Interesting. None of those three has directly changed. The number of beds is the same, occupancy is the same, and our headline rate per bed has not moved either. Yet the revenue we actually realize per bed has come down.
Candidate: That is a useful clue. Let me check the service side first. We offer several service lines, so has any particular service line, a specific department or procedure type, seen a decline?
Interviewer: No, no single service line is the culprit. Keep going.
Candidate: In that case, let me look at our customers rather than our services. Our patients usually pay in one of two ways: either out of their own pocket, or through insurance. My guess is that a large part of our revenue comes from insured patients. Is that right?
Interviewer: That is fair. A large share of our business does depend on insured customers.
Candidate: Then I would like to focus there, since that is where a payment or collection problem would hurt us the most. Have we seen the decline sitting specifically within the insured segment?
Interviewer: Yes, that is exactly where the issue sits.
Candidate: Insured patients are usually covered by either private companies or public sector companies, and the two pay quite differently. Has the mix between them shifted recently?
Interviewer: It has. Business from public sector companies has gone up, while business from private companies has come down.
Candidate: I think that shift explains the drop in realized revenue. Public sector payers tend to default more and pay later than private payers. So even though our beds, occupancy, and rate card look unchanged, a larger share of public sector payers means:
- More delayed payments and defaults
- A higher cost of bad debt
- Lower effective margins on that business
So the revenue we actually collect per bed falls, even while the headline numbers stay the same.
Interviewer: That is exactly the issue. You have found the root cause.

Critical Condition Framework & Recommendations
DECLINING PROFITS OF A DELHI HOSPITAL
Clarifying Questions: Is this a single branch? Since when has profit declined? How large is the decline? Which services do we offer?
Brownie Points: Segmenting insured payers into public and private. Linking public sector defaults to bad debt.
Keep In Mind: Billed revenue differs from collected revenue. Payer mix drives bad debt risk.

title: Variety Is the Spice of Life
prompt: Our client is a vending machine manufacturing company that is struggling to grow its revenues. Suggest possible strategies for revenue growth.

notes.title: Questions
items: Is this client-specific or industry-wide?
Since when, and is it concentrated in a geography?
Who are our competitors?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Think Nescafe stations, not vending machines
Separate USP from price when diagnosing why customers shift

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Proposing shift-based sachet rotation for 12+ varieties
Selling missing flavors as take-home sachets

framework:
Candidate: I'd like to reiterate the problem statement to make sure we are aligned. Our client manufactures vending machines, and the objective is to identify strategies to grow their revenues. This is a new and interesting industry for me, so I'd like to ask a few clarifying questions across three areas: the problem itself, the client, and the industry.
Starting with the problem. Is this a client-specific issue, or an industry-wide trend?
Interviewer: It is not industry-wide. It is specific to our client.
Candidate: Since when have we been facing this, and is there a particular geography where it is concentrated?
Interviewer: There is no specific start date, but it has emerged in the recent past. And there is no specific geography, it is across India.
Candidate: Moving to the client. Could you walk me through the value chain? Who are our customers, and who are our end consumers?
Interviewer: We are an end-to-end manufacturer, and we sell directly to customers, who in turn make the machines available to end consumers. Before you go further, let me ask you: who do you think our customers should be, and who our consumers should be?
Candidate: Our customers could be both residential and commercial buyers, and the end consumers would be the people who actually use the machines for services like juices, coffee, and so on.
Interviewer: Correct. I'd like you to dig deeper on the commercial side. Who do you think a commercial customer would be?
Candidate: I can think of five major segments: schools and colleges, corporates and offices, airports, malls, and metro stations.
Interviewer: Good, that covers it.
Candidate: Lastly, on the industry. What does the competitive landscape look like, and who are our competitors?
Interviewer: There are several emerging players, each holding around 10 to 15 percent market share. We have historically been the market leader with around 50 to 55 percent share, but we are now struggling to grow it as these emerging players have come up.
Candidate: Thank you, I have the context I need. Since the underlying problem is a market share problem, I'd like to take two approaches in sequence. First, a diagnostic approach to understand why we are losing share. Second, once we have identified the root cause, a solution approach to figure out how to grow revenues.
Interviewer: Correct. Go ahead.
Candidate: Starting with the diagnostic. I'd express market share as a function of two components: the number of customers, and the revenue per customer.
The number of customers can be broken down into willingness to buy our machines, and ability to buy them even if willing. Revenue per customer can be broken down into the number of machines bought per customer, and the price per machine.
Interviewer: The issue lies on the number-of-customers side. We have seen a dip in the number of customers buying from us. Walk me through what you would cover under willingness and ability.
Candidate: Understood. With the rise of these emerging players, customers we previously had have been shifting to them. Within willingness, I'd look at three factors in sequence:
- Need: customers may no longer feel the need for our machines
- Affordability: customers may feel competitor machines are cheaper and so are not willing to buy from us
- Customer experience: there may be issues with how customers have experienced our machines historically, which has led to the shift
Within ability, two factors:
- Awareness: customers may not be aware of our offering, though this is unlikely given we have been the market leader
- Accessibility: customers may not be able to access our machines even if they are willing
My hypothesis is that this is a willingness-side issue, most likely customer experience, since customers have gradually shifted away from us.
Interviewer: Customer experience is the right direction. But don't narrow your thinking to just these buckets. Think more broadly. If a customer is shifting from us to a competitor, what are the major factors driving that decision?
Candidate: Two major factors come to mind:
- USP, or unique selling proposition: ours may have been matched or replaced by a stronger one from a competitor
- Price point: a competitor may be offering the same proposition at a better price
Within USP, I'd look at two sub-factors: quantity, meaning how much the machine can serve per customer at a given time, and quality or efficiency, meaning the quality of service the machine offers.
Within price, I'd look at two sub-factors: setup cost, the price of installing the machine for a customer, and operating cost, the price of running the machine on an ongoing basis.
Interviewer: Correct, USP is the major problem. A competitor's machine is offering something we are not. One clarification before you go further: don't think of these as coin-operated vending machines. Think of them more like the Nescafe stations you would find on a college campus, where a person serves customers through the machine. With that in mind, what different USPs could a competitor's machine have that we don't?
Candidate: I can think of three factors along which a machine's USP could vary:
1. Capacity or volume: the number of servings or different taps the machine can offer at once
2. Variety: the number of distinct flavors or products the machine can serve
3. Time or efficiency: how quickly the machine can fill a cup or serve a customer
Interviewer: On the spot. You have identified the problem. The issue lies with variety. Competitors are offering 8 product varieties whereas we offer only 6. That is why customers are shifting from us to them. That is the diagnostic part. Now, knowing the problem, how would you drive revenue growth from here?
Candidate: Before I get into the solution, let me quickly synthesize where we are. Our customer base has been shifting to emerging competitors because they offer 8 varieties while we offer only 6. We now want to grow revenues knowing this is the root cause.
I'd like to look at this from both the demand side and the supply side, and explore growth levers at every step. Starting with demand, I'd split it into catering to more customer segments within the same flavor set, and growing our share within each segment. Within share per segment, I'd look at four levers: product, promotion, price, and customer experience. Within product, I'd look at how we can grow revenues with our current 6 varieties versus expanding to 8 or more to match or exceed competitors.
Interviewer: Stop there. We already know the problem. To grow revenues, we just need to fix this specific issue. Looking at anything else doesn't actually solve the problem, because customers are leaving primarily because of the variety gap.
Candidate: Understood. Since the problem is that we are selling fewer variants, the most direct fix is to start serving 8 variants ourselves, matching what the competitors offer.
Interviewer: But you cannot add new machines to your installed base. How would you still solve this?
Candidate: That is a real constraint. Let me think. I can see three ways to expand variety without adding new machines:
1. Modify the existing machines. We could install additional filling caps or capacity slots on the left or right of the machine, or add a new layer of flavor filling either horizontally below the current layer or vertically alongside it.
2. Move to a shift model. In one shift the machine serves a particular flavor set, and in the next shift we swap out the sachets and serve a different set. With a current capacity of 6, this would let us serve at least 12 distinct varieties across two shifts, and potentially more across additional shifts.
3. Expand each machine through modification, physically increasing its capacity so it can hold sachets for more varieties.
Interviewer: Interesting suggestions. Now let's say you can't modify the machines at all either. What would you do?
Candidate: If we can't touch the machines at all, there are two things we can still do to retain customer traction:
1. Complementary offerings alongside the machine. We could serve confectionery items like cookies or snacks alongside the current drink flavors, so customers can still experience flavors or product extensions the machine itself cannot offer.
2. Take-home sachets of the unavailable flavors. Customers experience the machine on-site for the 6 flavors we have, and we let them take home sachets of the flavors we don't offer in the machine, so the broader 8-variety experience is still ours, just unbundled.
Interviewer: Great suggestions. You did the case very well.

Variety Is the Spice of Life Framework & Recommendations
GROWING REVENUES FOR A VENDING MACHINE MANUFACTURER
Clarifying Questions: Is this client-specific or industry-wide? Since when, and is it concentrated in a geography?
Brownie Points: Pinpointing variety as the specific USP gap, 8 varieties versus our 6. Solving creatively under tightening constraints.
Keep In Mind: Market share splits into number of customers and revenue per customer. Separate USP from price when diagnosing why customers shift.

title: Fields of Gold
prompt: Our client is a mining and metals company that wants to enter different industries. Walk me through how you would evaluate its options.
abbreviations: PESTEL: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, and Legal

notes.title: Questions
items: Where does the client operate?
Any customer segment constraint?
Single product or SKU?
Position on the value chain?
Objective and constraints?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Screen industries by existing strengths first
Cost is moot when funding is unconstrained

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Escalating options from adjacent metals to renewables
Ruling out metals as an oligopoly
Sizing demand bottom-up by consuming industry

visualisations.title: Product x Market Matrix
rows: Grow the current metal SKU in India and the US
Take the current SKU into Asia, Southeast Asia, and Europe
New SKU variation, then adjacent metals like cobalt, nickel, and copper
Renewable energy and biofuel, sold globally
visualisations.insight: The client targets the new product, new market quadrant: entering renewable energy, and biofuel specifically.

framework:
Candidate: Before I begin, a few clarifying questions. Where does the company operate, how large is it, and are there any constraints on customer segment or product scope?
Interviewer: It operates across India and the United States and is a market leader. Assume money is not a constraint, there are no regulatory bans, customer segment is open, and it sells a single product, or SKU.
Candidate: And its competitive position and place in the value chain?
Interviewer: It leads the market in India and is a new, upcoming player in the United States. Why don't you sketch the value chain?
Candidate: For a mining and metals firm, I'd lay it out as research and development, exploration, inbound logistics, refining, outbound logistics, distribution, sales and marketing, and after-sales service, and I'd expect the client to span from research and development through distribution. Does it operate in any other industry, and what is the objective and any constraints?
Interviewer: It is purely a mining and metals firm. The objective is to capture a wide market share, with no constraints. As you structure this, also consider whether to take the current product into new markets or grow in existing ones.
Candidate: I'll use a product-versus-market matrix: existing or new product against existing or new markets. Since the goal is to enter new industries, I'll focus on new products.
Interviewer: Good, focus on new products.
Candidate: A new product could go into our existing markets, India and the United States, or new ones such as Asia, Southeast Asia, and Europe. To evaluate any entry, I'd weigh cost against risk; since money is not a constraint, cost is not binding, so I'd focus on risk: financial, operational, and competitive. This works for any industry, but first I'd screen candidate industries against the firm's strengths.
Interviewer: What are its strengths?
Candidate: Across the value chain: research and development, exploration, mining, logistics including metals handling and heavy transport, and refining, plus market leadership and a strong brand in India. Building on those, I'd escalate through options:
1. A new SKU that varies our current product in the same space.
2. Adjacent metals such as cobalt, nickel, or copper, which reuse the same competencies and infrastructure. But those metal markets offer limited growth, since major players already dominate an oligopoly.
3. So I'd look to renewable energy, an upcoming, high-demand space with government support that fits the wide-share objective. Within renewables, beyond solar, wind, and geothermal, the option that excites me most is biofuel.
Interviewer: Alright. Now, give me a general way to evaluate any industry for market expansion.
Candidate: I'd assess an industry on three dimensions:
- Financial attractiveness: its expected profitability, from market size, market share (roughly price minus variable cost) and costs (especially fixed costs), the competitive intensity read through the four Ps, and a positive growth rate.
- Operational efficiency: how well we could serve it by tweaking our current model, through outsourcing, new facilities, or revamping operations.
- Risk: industry risks such as market segmentation and barriers to entry, and country risks such as PESTEL factors and currency fluctuations.
Interviewer: Looks good. How would you calculate market size, not with that formula, but through the factors you would consider, for a mining and metals company specifically?
Candidate: For a mining and metals company I wouldn't lean on the top-down formula. I'd size the market from the factors that actually drive it:
- Demand: both domestic and global, since the client already spans India and international markets.
- Growth rate: the market is only worth entering if demand is growing at a healthy, positive rate.
- Margins: what we would actually keep, looking at revenue against cost.
To build the demand number bottom-up rather than assume a single figure, I'd:
- Compare underlying demand with actual consumption and study the gap between them, since that gap points to unmet or latent demand.
- Break demand down by the industries that consume metals, such as electronics, automobiles, and construction.
- Estimate each industry's share of total metal demand, then take a weighted average across them to reach a total demand figure.
- Layer in each industry's own growth rate, using an 80/20 lens to focus on the vital few industries that drive most of the consumption.
Interviewer: Good. Let's wrap up.

Fields of Gold Framework & Recommendations
EVALUATING NEW-INDUSTRY ENTRY FOR A MINING AND METALS COMPANY
Clarifying Questions: Where does the client operate? Any customer segment constraint? Single product or SKU? Position on the value chain? Objective and constraints?
Brownie Points: Escalating options from adjacent metals to renewables Ruling out metals as an oligopoly Sizing demand bottom-up by consuming industry
Keep In Mind: Screen industries by existing strengths first Cost is moot when funding is unconstrained

title: Waddle We Eat?
prompt: Our client is a large pet food company, and one of its brands leads a small, specialized segment with a product called Penguin Power. Size the market for penguin food in the United States.

notes.title: Questions
items: Feed made only for penguins?
Which US settings actually buy feed?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Zoos are the only setting that both keeps penguins and pays for feed
Not all penguins eat alike, so split them by role
The female number is a yearly average, since she eats far more post-birth while males fast

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Anchoring feed amounts to a medium-dog benchmark
Skewing the colony female, since zoos run breeding programs

visualisations.title: Feed by Role
rows: Yearly average, eats far more for 2 to 3 months post-birth
visualisations.insight: In the post-birth window females spike well above 300 g a day while males barely eat, so the female number is smoothed to a yearly average.

visualisations.title: Market Size Calculation
rows: C split 1 : 2 : 1 across male, female, offspring
visualisations.insight: Sizing bottom-up from captive penguins to feed to cans lands the US penguin food market at roughly $1M a year.

framework:
Candidate: Happy to. Two quick questions before I start. By penguin food, do we mean feed made specifically for penguins, sold to whoever keeps them? And are we after the current market by annual value?
Interviewer: Yes to both. Feed made for penguins, annual value, in the United States.
Candidate: Here is the equation I will fill in:
Candidate: Market size = captive penguins in the US × annual food per penguin × price per unit of food
Candidate: Before I start plugging in numbers, does that structure look sensible to you?
Interviewer: It does. Go ahead.
Candidate: Penguins in the US live in a few settings: zoos, islands, sanctuaries, and natural coastal stretches. Since the client sells packaged feed, the buyers who matter are the ones that both keep penguins and pay for their food, so I will focus on zoos and set the rest aside as negligible.
Candidate: To get the penguin count, I will start from zoos. Of the 50 states, most have zoos, so call it around 45. Each state has a few big-city zoos and a longer tail of smaller ones, which nets out to something like 30 zoos per state, so roughly 45 times 30, or about 1,350 zoos nationwide.
Interviewer: And how many of those actually keep penguins?
Candidate: Not many, since penguins need cold or aquatic enclosures that most zoos simply do not have. I would say around 15 percent, which brings 1,350 down to roughly 200 zoos with penguins.
Candidate: If each keeps a small colony, say about a dozen birds on average, that is 200 times 12, or around 2,400 captive penguins nationwide. Am I in the right ballpark so far?
Interviewer: That is reasonable. Now think about how much they eat, but keep in mind that not all penguins eat alike.
Candidate: Good point, I will not treat them as identical. Since zoos keep these as breeding colonies, the mix skews female, because a few males can cover many females, and each season the pairs raise roughly one surviving chick. On that logic I will assume about one male to two females to one offspring. Of 2,400 that is about 600 males, 1,200 females, and 600 offspring.
Candidate: For the amounts, I will anchor on a familiar animal rather than guess in a vacuum. A medium dog eats on the order of 300 to 400 grams of prepared food a day, and an adult penguin sits in a similar weight class, so I will scale around that:
- Male: about 500 grams a day, since the males are the largest and most active swimmers
- Female: about 300 grams a day, as a yearly average, in line with the dog benchmark
- Offspring: about 100 grams a day, roughly a growing pup's smaller portion
Interviewer: Before you total that up, are you comfortable using a single female number for the whole year?
Candidate: Good catch, not quite. For the two to three months after giving birth, females eat far more than usual while the males barely eat at all, so the 300 grams is me smoothing that swing into a yearly daily average rather than a steady daily figure.
Interviewer: Fair enough. Carry it through to an annual figure.
Candidate: Taking it role by role, then scaling to a year:
- Males: 600 × 500 grams, so 300,000 grams a day
- Females: 1,200 × 300 grams, so 360,000 grams a day
- Offspring: 600 × 100 grams, so 60,000 grams a day
- Total: about 720,000 grams a day, or roughly 720 kilograms a day
- Across a year: 720 kilograms × about 300 days, rounding 365 down to keep it clean, so about 216,000 kilograms a year
Candidate: So the whole captive population gets through on the order of 216,000 kilograms of feed a year. Shall I turn that into a market value?
Interviewer: Yes. The feed sells in 200 gram cans at about a dollar a can. Take it through to a final number.
Candidate: 216,000 kilograms is 216 million grams. At 200 grams per can, that is about 1.08 million cans a year. At roughly a dollar a can, the penguin food market in the United States comes to about one million dollars a year.
Candidate: As a quick gut check on the price: a can retails at about a dollar to a dollar and a quarter, and after retailer and pet-store margins of roughly 20 to 25 percent the maker keeps something like 65 cents, with the fish and krill ingredients costing less again. So the client's own revenue from this segment is a slice of that one million dollar retail figure, not the whole of it.
Interviewer: Good. That is a sensible number to land on. Let's stop there.

Waddle We Eat? Framework & Recommendations
SIZING THE US PENGUIN FOOD MARKET
Clarifying Questions: Feed made only for penguins? Current annual market by value? Which US settings actually buy feed?
Brownie Points: Anchoring feed amounts to a medium dog benchmark Skewing the colony female because zoos run breeding programs Rounding 365 to 300 days to keep the math clean
Keep In Mind: Only zoos both keep penguins and pay for feed Not all penguins eat alike, so split by role Females eat far more for 2 to 3 months post-birth while males fast, so 300 g is a yearly blended average

title: Tip Tip Barsa Paani
prompt: Our client is the Asian Development Bank (ADB), which wants to raise the income of rural households in India that depend mainly on agriculture. How would you approach this?

notes.title: Questions
items: Fixed income target or a directional lift?
All of rural India or a specific geography?
Is ADB open to any intervention or a particular area?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Water is the biggest swing factor in farm yield
Only medium and large farms can realistically afford drip

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Splitting income into agri versus supplementary streams before diving in
Recommending ADB subsidize early-year costs to drive adoption

visualisations.title: Market Size Calculation
rows: H x Rs 1 lakh per system

visualisations.title: Annual Gains
visualisations.rhs: Increase in Revenue (higher yield) + Decrease in Cost (less borewell and water spend)

visualisations.title: Annualized Cost
visualisations.rhs: (CAPEX ÷ System Life) + Working Capital Costs

visualisations.title: Adoption Decision
visualisations.rhs: Annual Gains > Annualized Cost

framework:
Candidate: A few clarifying questions first. When we say raise income, are we aiming at a specific target, such as lifting incomes by a set percentage or by a fixed amount per household, or are we simply trying to move incomes meaningfully upward without a hard number in mind? Are we looking at all of rural India or a particular geography? And is ADB open to any kind of intervention, or is there a particular area it wants to back?
Interviewer: Good questions. There is no fixed number to hit; the aim is simply to move incomes meaningfully upward across rural India, and ADB is open on the type of intervention for now.
Candidate: Then at the top level I see two ways to raise these households' income: lift what they earn from agriculture itself, or add supplementary income streams outside farming, such as allied activities like dairy or off-season work. Which would you like me to go down?
Interviewer: Let's just focus on agriculture.
Candidate: Within agriculture I will walk the crop value chain and look for where income can improve. I would split it into three stages:
- Pre-sowing: procuring seeds and preparing the land.
- Cultivation: sowing, then crop maintenance, which itself breaks into irrigation and nutrition such as fertilizers and manure.
- Post-harvest: the harvest itself, then storage, processing, and getting produce to market.
Interviewer: Let's zero in on the agriculture-related lever. How would you increase that?
Candidate: Higher farm income really comes from higher and more reliable yield, and water is the biggest swing factor there. On irrigation I see two paths: optimize the traditional sources farmers already use, such as canals and borewells, or bring in newer, more efficient technology such as drip irrigation, which delivers water straight to the roots and cuts waste.
Interviewer: Let's focus on drip irrigation. What do you think the market size for that is in India?
Candidate: Let me build it up. May I lay out my assumptions as I go?
Interviewer: Please do.
Candidate: Starting from the population:
- India has roughly 1.4 billion people. At about 5 people a household, that is around 280 million households.
- Around 60 percent of households depend on agriculture, so about 168 million agricultural households.
Candidate: Not every farm is a realistic buyer, so I will segment by farm size:
- About 10 percent own large farms, so roughly 17 million.
- About 30 percent own medium farms, so roughly 50 million.
- The remaining 60 percent are small or marginal farmers.
Candidate: Drip irrigation needs upfront money and enough land to be worthwhile, so I will assume only medium and large farms are realistic buyers. That is the top 40 percent, or about 67 million farms, as my target market.
Interviewer: Fair. But would all of them actually want it?
Candidate: No, and that is my next cut, by water availability. As a sanity check on the split, close to half of India's farmland is rainfed rather than served by assured irrigation, and even many irrigated belts are turning water-stressed, so leaning the mix toward water-scarce land is fair. I will use roughly one quarter water-rich to three quarters water-scarce:
- About 25 percent sit in arable, water-rich areas, so roughly 17 million.
- About 75 percent sit in arid, water-scarce areas, so roughly 50 million.
Candidate: The logic is that where water is already plentiful the pull toward a new system is weak, but where water is scarce the pull is strong. So I will apply different willingness rates:
- Arable, water-rich: only about 10 percent willing, so roughly 1.7 million farms.
- Arid, water-scarce: about 50 percent willing, so roughly 25 million farms.
Candidate: Adding those gives about 27 million farms, or 2.7 crore, that would realistically adopt drip irrigation. To turn that count into a market value I would need a rough price per system. Do we have a figure to work with?
Interviewer: Assume an average drip system costs about one lakh rupees per farm.
Candidate: Then the market is about 27 million times one lakh rupees, or roughly 2.7 lakh crore rupees. I would treat the count of about 27 million farms as the core number and the rupee figure as an order-of-magnitude read.
Interviewer: Good. Now a different angle. For a farmer, drip irrigation is an investment. If you had to weigh the gains from a drip system against the cost of installing it, so that it makes economic sense to adopt, how would you approach it? I am after the approach, not numbers.
Candidate: I would set it up as annual gains versus annualized cost.
Candidate: On the gains side, gains equal the increase in revenue plus the reduction in cost:
- Higher revenue comes from higher crop yield, since steady water at the roots lifts output and can open up a second cropping cycle.
- Lower cost comes from spending less on water and power, since the farm leans less on borewells and pumping and uses less water and fertilizer overall.
Candidate: On the cost side, rather than charging the whole one-time installation to a single year, I would spread that upfront cost evenly across all the years the system will be in use, so it compares fairly against the yearly gains:
- The capital expenditure, or Capex, spread over the useful life of the equipment, so Capex divided by the life of the system.
- Plus any yearly running and working capital costs, such as maintenance and financing.
Candidate: Adoption makes economic sense once the annual gains clear that annualized cost.
Interviewer: And what would you recommend to ADB?
Candidate: In the early years the gains may not cover the cost. The upfront outlay of about one lakh rupees is large next to what a medium farm clears in a year, while the yield gains and water savings build up only gradually over the first few seasons as farmers learn to run the new system. So a farmer weighing just the first year or two would see the cost loom larger than the benefit and would hesitate. Over the full life of the system, though, the economics turn positive. So my recommendation is that ADB steps in with financial support, subsidizing part of the installation cost or offering low-cost financing, so that farmers are willing to adopt now. Over time the higher yields and lower costs lift farm incomes, which is exactly the rural income increase ADB set out to achieve.
Interviewer: Good. That is a solid place to close.

Tip Tip Barsa Paani Framework & Recommendations
RAISING RURAL INCOMES THROUGH DRIP IRRIGATION
Clarifying Questions: Fixed income target or a directional lift? All of rural India or a specific geography? Is ADB open to any intervention or a particular area?
Brownie Points: Splitting income into agri versus supplementary streams before diving in Walking the crop value chain to locate the lever Recommending ADB subsidize early-year costs to drive adoption
Keep In Mind: Water is the biggest swing factor in farm yield Only medium and large farms can realistically afford drip Willingness is far higher in water-scarce regions

title: Panel Discussion
prompt: Your client is a solar and wind developer. The CEO wants to reduce capital expenditure (CAPEX) by 3 to 4 percent. Advise them on how to approach this.

notes.title: Questions
items: What are the client's core business activities?
What is the current installed capacity?
What is the objective and timeline?
Any data on geography or competitor practices?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Every lever here is judged by its impact on IRR, not just cost
Financing structures like PPP can offload CAPEX, not just reduce it

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Structuring the full solar value chain before diving in
Flagging CAPEX as a capital structure driver, not a financing cost

framework:
Candidate: I'd like to understand the client a bit better before structuring my approach. Firstly, what are their core business activities?
Interviewer: They install solar panels by leasing large plots of land. They supply electricity through power grids and earn revenue on a tariff basis.
Candidate: Understood. Secondly, what is the client's current installed capacity?
Interviewer: 5 gigawatts.
Candidate: Is there any specific objective or timeline behind this CAPEX reduction?
Interviewer: Yes. The client wants to improve its internal rate of return (IRR) by reducing CAPEX. They would like to see results within the next 4 to 5 projects.
Candidate: Do we have information about the geographical spread of projects or competitor practices?
Interviewer: That won't be necessary for this case. Let's move ahead.
Candidate: May I take a moment to structure my thoughts?
Interviewer: Sure.
Candidate: I'll break the problem down by looking at the key stages in the value chain of a solar and wind developer. Broadly, I would divide this into five stages:
- Pre-development
- Design and engineering
- Procurement
- Construction
- Financing
Does this sound comprehensive?
Interviewer: Yes, that works. Let's go through each stage. What factors would you consider under pre-development?
Candidate: Under pre-development, I would focus on two broad areas: site selection, and permits and regulatory approvals. Within site selection specifically, I would examine:
- Land acquisition costs.
- Terrain-related factors, as they influence exploration and construction costs.
- Potential construction delays arising from site constraints.
Interviewer: That makes sense. Let's move to design and engineering.
Candidate: I would divide this into two buckets:
- Technology choices, including the type of modules used, integration costs, and the extent of standardization of components.
- System design, particularly layout optimization and engineering efficiency.
Interviewer: Sounds good. What about procurement?
Candidate: Under procurement, I would focus on how we source raw material components. Specifically:
- Supplier relationships.
- Cost of individual components.
- Availability of government incentives such as production linked incentive (PLI) schemes.
Interviewer: Good. Let's move to construction.
Candidate: Since the objective is CAPEX reduction, I would explore:
- Lean project management techniques to ensure on-time performance.
- Minimizing material waste during construction.
- Optimizing machinery utilization for efficiency.
- Using pre-fabricated mounting structures to reduce construction time and costs.
Interviewer: Good suggestions. Let's now discuss financing. What would you consider there?
Candidate: Given that solar and wind projects are capital intensive, financing structures are critical. I would consider public-private partnership (PPP) models, which are increasingly used. They can help offload the CAPEX burden and improve the cost of capital.
Interviewer: Makes sense. Let's go back to procurement. You mentioned the cost of components. How exactly would you reduce CAPEX there?
Candidate: We could:
- Enter into long-term supplier agreements to lock in prices.
- Leverage bulk sourcing and volume discounts.
- Explore transfer of technology through strategic partnerships.
- Consider backward integration, where we manufacture key components in-house.
Interviewer: That's good. Coming back to financing, you mentioned PPP models. What types of partnership structures would you consider?
Candidate: Two approaches come to mind:
- Build, Own, Operate (BOO).
- Build, Own, Transfer (BOT).
In such models, ownership may initially be retained while planning and investment responsibilities are outsourced. After a defined leasing or concession period, ownership may be transferred depending on the structure.
Interviewer: Fair enough. One final question: is CAPEX part of the financing cost?
Candidate: No, CAPEX itself is not a financing cost. However, it directly influences the capital structure of the firm. A larger CAPEX reduces the free cash flows to the firm and can increase the financial burden, thereby impacting overall financing requirements and IRR.
Interviewer: That makes sense. We can wrap up the case here.
Candidate: Thank you.

Panel Discussion Framework & Recommendations
REDUCING CAPEX ACROSS THE SOLAR VALUE CHAIN
Clarifying Questions: What are the client's core business activities? What is the current installed capacity? What is the objective and timeline behind the CAPEX cut? Any data on geography or competitor practices?
Brownie Points: Structuring the full solar value chain before diving in Deepening component-cost cuts via bulk sourcing, technology transfer, and backward integration Separating CAPEX from financing cost while linking it to IRR
Keep In Mind: The goal is improving IRR, so judge every lever by its cost impact CAPEX is not a financing cost, but it shapes capital structure and IRR Backward integration and PLI schemes can structurally lower component costs

title: Testing the Waters
prompt: Your client is a 5-star hotel considering opening a waterpark within one specific hotel property. Waterpark charges will be automatically included in the room booking, with usage optional. Should they enter this waterpark business?

notes.title: Questions
items: Is this for one hotel or the whole chain?
Any direct competitors offering in-hotel waterparks nearby?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Ground your numbers in a familiar property, like a Gurgaon hotel
Bundling the fee makes perceived value the deciding factor

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Pegging the premium at roughly half the room rate before using it
Offering optional tickets and a pilot instead of an outright no

visualisations.title: Payback Calculation
rows: F is roughly 2x total annual capacity, and only a niche pays

visualisations.title: Contribution per Booking
visualisations.rhs: Premium per Booking - Variable Cost per Booking

visualisations.title: Payback in Room-Nights
visualisations.rhs: Fixed Cost ÷ Contribution per Booking

framework:
Candidate: That's an interesting problem. Before I structure my approach, may I ask a few clarifying questions?
Interviewer: Please go ahead.
Candidate: First, is this being considered for just one hotel, or across the chain?
Interviewer: Just one, for now.
Candidate: Understood. Can I assume a specific location to ground my thinking?
Interviewer: Yes.
Candidate: Then I'll assume a property in Gurgaon, since I'm familiar with that market. And are there any direct competitors already offering a similar in-hotel waterpark nearby?
Interviewer: Assume none for now.
Candidate: Great. Then I'll evaluate this as a market entry decision across four lenses. First, market attractiveness, to see whether there is real demand. Second, financial viability, to check whether the economics work. Third, capabilities and operations, to see whether the hotel can actually run a waterpark. And fourth, the key risks and how we might mitigate them. Does that structure sound reasonable?
Interviewer: Yes, that works. Let's start with market attractiveness.
Candidate: Sure. I'll begin with where the demand comes from. A waterpark appeals mainly to families and leisure travellers. But a 5-star hotel in a market like Gurgaon skews heavily towards business guests and wedding or event groups, who typically won't use a waterpark. So intuitively, the addressable segment is only a slice of the hotel's guests.
Interviewer: That's a fair hypothesis. How would you pressure-test it?
Candidate: I'd anchor on the room economics first. For a property like this, I'd estimate an average room rate of around ₹8,000 to ₹10,000 a night. Is that fair?
Interviewer: That's a fair assumption.
Candidate: And a typical stay of about 2 nights?
Interviewer: Yes.
Candidate: Now I need a sensible waterpark premium to test, since the charge is bundled into the room. If the room itself is ₹8,000 to ₹10,000, an add-on much larger than half the room rate would feel steep to most guests. So I'll assume a premium of about ₹5,000 per room-night, roughly 50% on top of the room.
Interviewer: Yes, ₹5,000 works.
Candidate: At ₹5,000, value perception becomes the deciding factor. A family may see ₹5,000 as fair for a full day of entertainment, but a business traveller is very unlikely to pay it for something they won't use. So demand is confined to a narrow niche rather than the majority of hotel traffic.
Interviewer: Agreed, the demand side looks thin. Let's see whether the financials could still justify it.
Candidate: I'll use a payback lens, comparing the upfront investment against the contribution each booking generates. On the cost side, fixed costs are land, construction, the slides and rides, and safety infrastructure; variable costs are staff, electricity, water, and maintenance.
Interviewer: Let's put numbers to it. What would you assume for the fixed investment?
Candidate: Since the land already exists within the property, I'd estimate the build-out, rides, and safety setup at roughly ₹5 crore. May I proceed with that?
Interviewer: Yes, assume ₹5 crore.
Candidate: For the contribution per booking, a meaningful share of the ₹5,000 premium is consumed by the cost of actually servicing a guest. Waterparks are utility-heavy: water treatment and heating, electricity for pumps and rides, extra staffing, and constant cleaning. So I'd assume variable costs run at about half the premium, roughly ₹2,500 per booking. That leaves a contribution margin of around ₹2,500 per premium room-night.
Interviewer: Reasonable. So what does that imply for payback?
Candidate: To recover the ₹5 crore fixed cost at ₹2,500 contribution per booking, I'd need ₹5,00,00,000 divided by ₹2,500, which is about 2,00,000 premium-paying room-nights.
Interviewer: And how should I read that 2 lakh figure?
Candidate: Let me put it in context. A single hotel might have around 200 to 300 rooms. Even at full occupancy every night, that is under 1,00,000 room-nights a year in total, and only the small leisure niche would actually pay the premium. The payback is simply too long and too uncertain to be attractive.
Interviewer: That's a clear conclusion. Let's move on.
Candidate: The third lens is whether the hotel is operationally equipped to run this, and here I see a real capability gap. The hotel is genuinely strong on hospitality and guest service, which helps, but the overlap largely ends there. Water safety and lifeguarding is a mandatory function the hotel has no existing muscle in. Specialised water treatment and maintenance is critical and again outside its expertise. And managing high-volume recreational usage, queueing, crowd safety, and continuous cleaning, is an entirely new discipline for a hotel. So there is very low operational synergy, which means a steep learning curve and meaningful additional management bandwidth.
Interviewer: Understood. And the risks?
Candidate: I'd flag four. First, low utilisation, since the business-traveller base won't value the park. Second, brand dilution, as a luxury business hotel repositioning around a recreational attraction could confuse its core clientele. Third, focus diversion, pulling management attention away from the core hospitality business. And fourth, the high capital risk we just saw, a large fixed outlay against slow, uncertain payback.
Interviewer: So what's your final recommendation?
_[Recommendations below]_
Interviewer: Thank you, that's a well-structured answer.

Testing the Waters Framework & Recommendations
SHOULD A 5-STAR HOTEL ENTER THE WATERPARK BUSINESS?
Clarifying Questions: Is this for one hotel or the whole chain? Can I assume a specific location? Any direct competitors offering in-hotel waterparks nearby?
Brownie Points: Justifying the ₹5,000 premium as roughly 50% of the room rate before using it Contextualizing 2 lakh room-nights against a 200 to 300 room hotel's capacity Offering optional ticketing and a pilot instead of a flat no
Keep In Mind: Bundling the charge into the room makes value perception the deciding factor A single hotel has too few room-nights to recover a ₹5 crore fixed cost quickly Low operational synergy means a steep learning curve, not just extra cost
RECOMMENDATIONS: Recommend against entering the waterpark segment in this property, at least in the bundled form proposed. If they still want to explore, test the concept with seasonal or temporary mini water features before committing full capital expenditure. Target family-tourism-heavy destinations rather than a business hub like Gurgaon. Offer the waterpark on separate, optional ticketing instead of mandatory bundling.

title: Jab We Met
prompt: Your client is an Indian vaccine manufacturer. Today they sell within India and also export through UN tenders, supplying agencies like UNICEF that distribute to countries across Africa and elsewhere. The client now wants to grow by entering a new, attractive market outside India. How would you approach this?

selection-criteria.label: Screen on Pay, Channel Fit, Regulation, Differentiation

high-willingness.label: Fatal Diseases: High Willingness to Vaccinate

paid-filters.label: x % Aware x % Willing x % Affordable

similar-efficacy.label: Similar Efficacy: Can't Win on Product

notes.title: Questions
items: Is there a target market already in mind, or do I recommend one?
Am I free to choose the vaccine portfolio?
Do you want the sizing approach or a precise number?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: The interviewer bounces the market and portfolio choices back to you, so the reasoning matters more than the answer
This sizing is about the funnel and filters, not a final number
Europe wins on channel fit, since public tenders match the client's model, not on being less regulated

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Screening regions against explicit criteria before naming Europe
Choosing pediatric for recurring booster demand and high willingness to vaccinate
Differentiating on experience like home administration, since vaccines are similar on efficacy

visualisations.title: Serviceable Paid Market
visualisations.rhs: Target-Age Population x % Aware x % Willing x % Affordable

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I structure this, I would like to understand the goal better. Is there a specific target market the client already has in mind, or am I free to recommend one?
Interviewer: Why don't you tell me? What would be an appropriate market for a vaccine manufacturer to venture into, apart from India?
Candidate: Understood, so identifying the right market is part of the problem itself. May I take a moment to reason through it?
Interviewer: Please.
Candidate: Before naming a market, I would define what makes one attractive for us, then screen the options against it. I would use four criteria: the ability and willingness to pay for vaccines, the ease of plugging into a distribution channel we already understand, the regulatory feasibility of entry, and how much the market differs from our existing low-margin tender business.
Interviewer: Alright, walk me through how the options stack up.
Candidate: The client serves two price-sensitive markets today: a large but competitive India, and low-income African tenders via UN agencies. For attractive growth I want a market that adds margin, which rules out similar low-price regions like Southeast Asia or Latin America. That points to the high-income West. North America is mostly private and insurance-driven, sold through commercial payers and pharmacy chains where we have no foothold. Europe is just as regulated, but buys most vaccines through public national immunisation programmes and government tenders, the same institutional, tender-based model we already run. So Europe lets us reuse an existing capability rather than build a commercial engine from scratch, which is why it fits best.
Interviewer: Why Europe specifically?
Candidate: Three reasons, in order of importance:
- Purchasing power: European governments and citizens can afford a broad range of vaccines, both compulsory and optional, which supports far healthier margins than tender-driven markets.
- Distribution and channel fit: European vaccine demand flows largely through public procurement and national immunisation programmes, the same institutional, tender-based channel we already serve through UN agencies, so we can lean on a selling model and partner relationships we already understand rather than build a private commercial network from scratch.
- Structured, reliable demand: Europe has well-funded national immunisation programmes and high public trust in vaccination, so demand is stable rather than dependent on one-off tenders.
Interviewer: Alright, let's go with Europe. What about the product, what would you actually sell there?
Candidate: That is the next question I wanted to raise, the portfolio. May I assume I am choosing the vaccine mix as well?
Interviewer: Yes, you tell me. What kind of vaccines would be best?
Candidate: I would think about it at the category level. Vaccines are broadly either pediatric or adult. I would focus on pediatric vaccines to begin with, for two reasons. They often need repeat and booster doses, which creates recurring demand, and they typically protect against serious or fatal childhood diseases, so willingness to vaccinate is high. That makes pediatric a more reliable base to enter with.
Interviewer: That is reasonable. Go on.
Candidate: From here I would structure the entry along three lenses: financial, operational, and risks. On the financial side, the core question is the size of the opportunity, so I would run a market sizing. I understand this is about the approach rather than a precise number, since neither of us has exact European figures.
Interviewer: Correct, I am interested in how you would size it, not the final number.
Candidate: I would start from the population of the target country and narrow it down through a series of filters:
- Geography: split urban versus rural, since access and delivery differ.
- Age group: split into 0 to 5, 5 to 18, 18 to 40, 40 to 60, and 60 plus, to isolate the pediatric segment that fits our portfolio.
- Compulsory versus paid: set aside compulsory vaccines, which are close to fully penetrated, and focus on paid or optional ones, where the real opportunity lies.
- Paid-segment filters: apply the share of the population aware of the vaccine, the share willing to take it, and the share who can afford it.
Multiplying those filters against the relevant age population gives me the serviceable, paid market.
Interviewer: Good. And on the operational and competitive side?
Candidate: Operationally, I would expect the market to already have three to four big, entrenched players, so we would be entering against established incumbents. Their vaccines would be broadly similar to ours on efficacy, which means we cannot win on the clinical product alone. So the key question becomes how we differentiate.
Interviewer: Exactly what I wanted to get to. What USP would you recommend?
Candidate: I would build our differentiation around the customer experience rather than the vaccine itself, with three ideas:
- Follow-up benefits: children need many vaccines and boosters on a schedule, and parents often struggle to track them all, so we would offer structured follow-up and loyalty-style benefits for families who stay on schedule.
- Home centres and at-home administration: post-COVID, there is a strong shift towards receiving healthcare at home rather than at clinics. Just as at-home blood tests are now common in India, we could offer vaccinations at home, which is convenient and highly differentiated.
- A digital layer: an app that sends reminders and shares clear information with parents, which fits a developed, digitally comfortable market like Europe.
Interviewer: The home administration idea is particularly strong. That is a good place to stop.

Jab We Met Framework & Recommendations
GROWING AN INDIAN VACCINE MAKER INTO A NEW MARKET
Clarifying Questions: Is there a target market already in mind, or do I recommend one? Am I free to choose the vaccine portfolio? Do you want the sizing approach or a precise number?
