title: House of Cards
prompt: Our client is the CEO of a large iron-ore mining company in the state of Wakanda. He has built a successful business, but he now wants to run for Governor of Wakanda. He has no prior political experience, and he would be up against an incumbent who has held the seat for about 15 years. Should he run, and if he does, how does he win?

decision-rule.label: Run Only If Earnings Beat Staying Out

voter-pool.label: Total Voter Pool x % Backing Him

notes.title: Questions
items: What position is he running for, and what powers come with it?
Who is the competitor and what is their background?
What is the client's own company and financial situation?
What is his main motive for contesting?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: The objective is money, so treat this as a financial decision, not a political one
Weight every outcome by its probability rather than assuming he wins
Do not count a benefit to his own company; the interviewer rules that lever out

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Framing the whole case as an expected-value decision
Segmenting voters to target younger and urban groups instead of the rural stronghold
Bounding the most he should pay for a monopoly at the profit from victory

visualisations.title: Should He Run? Expected-Value Maths
visualisations.insight: Win payoff = tender and grant cuts plus salary, net of campaign spend; loss = about 6 Cr campaign spend plus 20 Cr of forgone company profit. Since the expected value is positive, he should contest.

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I structure the problem, I would like to ask a few clarifying questions.
First, what exactly is the position he is running for, and what powers come with being Governor of Wakanda?
Interviewer: The Governor is the chief executive of the state, roughly equivalent to a Chief Minister, with significant control over state contracts, budgets, and administration.
Candidate: Second, who is he up against, and what is their background?
Interviewer: The main competitor is the sitting Governor, who has held the office for around 15 years and has strong support in the rural parts of Wakanda.
Candidate: Third, could you tell me about the client's own company? What business is he in, how is it doing financially, and does he have future business plans that this move is meant to support?
Interviewer: He runs a profitable iron-ore company. Treat it as stable and steadily profitable. He has no specific new business plans; the political move is the focus.
Candidate: And most importantly, what is his main motive for contesting? Public service, influence for his business, personal wealth, or something else?
Interviewer: Let us be blunt. His motive is money. He wants to know whether running for Governor will leave him better off financially than staying out of politics.
Candidate: That settles the objective, so I will treat this as a financial decision rather than a political one. The client should run only if his expected earnings over the term, say the next four years, are greater than what he would earn by staying out. Let me build the two sides of that comparison.
Interviewer: Please do.
Candidate: If he contests, there are two financial components: the cost of running the campaign, and the economic benefit if he wins. Because winning is uncertain, I will weight the outcomes by their probabilities. I will organise the whole thing across three phases: pre-election, during the election, and post-election.
- Pre-election is mostly cost: promotions and campaigning.
- During the election sets the probability of winning.
- Post-election is where the benefit of holding office shows up.
Interviewer: Good. Start with the costs.
Candidate: I would split campaign spending into buckets: online promotion, physical banners and hoardings, travel and processions, public speeches and gatherings, and other activities. Putting rough figures on each, assume the total campaign spend comes to about 6 crore over the run-up to the election.
Interviewer: Fine. Now, how likely is he to win?
Candidate: The probability of winning is the share of the total voter pool that backs him. I would grow that share by segmenting voters rather than fighting everywhere. The incumbent owns the rural vote, roughly half the electorate, so I would not spend there. Instead I would target:
- the younger generation, and
- urban voters,
who are more open to a new face and cheaper to reach through modern campaigning. With sensible assumptions about those segments, I would put his chance of winning at about 50 percent.
Interviewer: Let us use a 50-50 chance. Now the upside. What does he earn if he wins?
Candidate: If he wins, the benefit comes from a few sources. Let me lay them out before sizing them:
- the Governor's salary;
- and the larger levers that come with executive control: a cut on state tenders awarded to private firms, a cut on grants, and bribery.
Interviewer: What about his own business? He runs an iron-ore company. Does being Governor not help there?
Candidate: It could. From a position of power he could steer favourable treatment towards his own company, so there is potentially an indirect benefit to the iron-ore business. I would flag it as a lever but keep it separate, since it is hard to pin a clean number on and it blurs the line with his public role.
Interviewer: Leave that one out, do not count any benefit to his own company. And take the salary as about 25 lakh a year. Focus on the rest.
Candidate: Understood. At 25 lakh a year the salary is small over a four-year term, so the real value sits in the tender and grant cuts and in bribery. The tender cut is the big one, so let me size it explicitly. Assuming about 20 companies each win contracts worth roughly 100 crore, and he takes a 5 percent cut, that is 20 x 100 x 5 percent, which is about 100 crore over the term. Adding the salary and these cuts, then subtracting the campaign spend, the net upside of winning comes to roughly 71 crore.
Interviewer: And if he loses?
Candidate: If he loses, he gets none of that upside and is left only with the downside, which has two parts. First, the campaign money already spent, the roughly 6 crore from earlier. Second, the opportunity cost of the time and focus pulled away from his iron-ore company while he campaigns; if that distraction costs the business about 5 crore a year across the four-year window, that is another 20 crore. Six plus twenty gives a downside of about 26 crore, so that is the figure I will use if he loses.
Interviewer: Put it together.
Candidate: Using expected value:
Expected earnings = probability of winning x benefit if he wins + probability of losing x benefit if he loses.
The 0.5 on each term is just the probability we settled on earlier: a 50 percent chance of winning, and therefore a 50 percent chance of losing, so each outcome is weighted by one half.
= 0.5 x (+71 crore) + 0.5 x (-26 crore)
= 35.5 - 13
= 22.5 crore.
Since the expected value is comfortably positive, my recommendation is that he should contest.
Interviewer: Suppose he wants to push his odds above 50-50. What would you suggest?
Candidate: The cleanest lever is to reduce the competition, the same way a firm tries to move a market towards monopoly. Broadly, he can either collude with the incumbent or buy him out of the contest through an agreement, rather than compete head to head.
Interviewer: And what is the most he should be willing to pay to secure that uncontested position?
Candidate: At most, the profit he would make from winning. Any price up to that still leaves victory worthwhile; paying more than the prize destroys the reason for winning in the first place.
Interviewer: That is a clean way to bound it. Let us stop there.

House of Cards Framework & Recommendations
SHOULD A PROFIT-DRIVEN CEO RUN FOR GOVERNOR OF WAKANDA
Clarifying Questions: What position is he running for and what powers come with it? Who is the competitor and what is their background? What is the client's own company and financial situation? What is his main motive for contesting?
Brownie Points: Framing the whole case as an expected-value decision Segmenting voters to target younger and urban groups instead of the rural stronghold Bounding the most he should pay for a monopoly at the profit from victory
Keep In Mind: The objective is money, so treat this as a financial decision, not a political one Weight every outcome by its probability rather than assuming he wins Do not count a benefit to his own company; the interviewer rules that lever out

title: Padhega India, Badhega India
prompt: You are advising the Ministry of Education in the state of Jharkhand. They want to estimate the annual budget needed to supply science textbooks to every government-school student from grade 1 to grade 10, with the books printed in colour. How would you size it?

notes.title: Questions
items: Are we covering grades 1 to 10 only?
One science book per student per year?
Government schools only, not private?
Are we costing colour printing specifically?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Move top-down through the funnel before calculating
Low-income families rely on government schools the most, so their penetration is the highest
Round numbers at each step to keep the arithmetic clean

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Deriving per-book cost from a per-page colour printing rate
Splitting students into grade bands by book length
Benchmarking the estimate against the existing 4.2 crore allocation

visualisations.title: Government-School Students by Segment
visualisations.insight: Penetration is highest for low-income families, who rely on government schools the most.

visualisations.title: Annual Budget by Grade Band
visualisations.insight: Full coverage costs about 43 crore a year, roughly ten times the ministry's current 4.2 crore allocation.

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I start, let me confirm the scope with a few questions. First, are we covering grades 1 to 10 specifically?
Interviewer: Yes, grades 1 through 10.
Candidate: Second, only the science textbook, one per student per year?
Interviewer: Correct, one science book per student per year.
Candidate: Third, only government schools, not private ones?
Interviewer: Government schools only.
Candidate: And we are costing the printing of those books, in colour, which is more expensive than black and white?
Interviewer: Yes. For context, the ministry currently sets aside about 4.2 crore for this, a 7 crore line item of which roughly 60 percent is meant for these books. They want to know whether that is in the right ballpark.
Candidate: Understood. My plan is to estimate the number of government-school students in grades 1 to 10, group them by the cost of their books, and multiply. I will move step by step: total population, then the school-going share, then urban versus rural, then income segment, then how many of each actually attend government schools, and finally the cost of the book by grade band.
Interviewer: Go ahead.
Candidate: Starting with population, I will assume Jharkhand has about 3.5 crore people. Of these, I need the school-going population, the children roughly aged 6 to 16 who map to grades 1 to 10. That is about eleven single-year age cohorts, and since India skews young, I will take it as roughly 20 percent of the population. That gives about 0.7 crore students in the grade 1 to 10 range.
Interviewer: Fine. Continue.
Candidate: I will now work down from those 0.7 crore students, splitting by geography, then by income, then by how many actually attend government schools. The urban side is about 30 percent of students, so roughly 0.21 crore. Within it I assume high income at 10 percent with about 70 percent in government schools, middle income at 60 percent with about 90 percent in government schools, and low income at 30 percent with nearly all, close to 100 percent, in government schools. Low-income families depend on government schools the most, so their attendance is the highest. Blending these, 0.10 times 0.70 plus 0.60 times 0.90 plus 0.30 times 1.00 is about 0.91, giving roughly 0.19 crore urban government-school students.
Interviewer: And the rural side?
Candidate: The rural side is the other 70 percent of students, about 0.49 crore, and here government schools dominate even more. High income is 10 percent with about 40 percent in government schools, middle income is 40 percent with about 70 percent in government schools, and low income is 50 percent with about 90 percent in government schools. Blending these, 0.10 times 0.40 plus 0.40 times 0.70 plus 0.50 times 0.90 is about 0.77, giving roughly 0.38 crore rural government-school students. Adding urban and rural, I get about 0.57 crore government-school students in grades 1 to 10.
Interviewer: Good. Now bring in the cost.
Candidate: The cost of a book depends on its length, so I will split students into two grade bands and price each book from its page count. Colour printing at government bulk scale, counting paper, ink, and binding, runs roughly 50 paise a page. Grades 1 to 5 use a shorter book of about 100 pages, so about 100 times 0.5, which is 50 rupees a book. Grades 6 to 10 use a longer book of about 200 pages, so about 200 times 0.5, which is 100 rupees a book. Splitting the 0.57 crore students evenly between the two bands gives about 0.285 crore in each band. So the budget is 0.285 crore times 50 rupees for the primary band plus 0.285 crore times 100 rupees for the secondary band, which is about 14 crore plus 28 crore, or roughly 43 crore a year.
Interviewer: How does that compare with the 4.2 crore the ministry has set aside?
Candidate: It is about ten times larger. That gap tells me one of two things. Either the ministry is significantly underfunding colour textbooks and the true requirement is an order of magnitude higher, or the 4.2 crore figure covers only a slice of the need, for example reprints and top-ups rather than a fresh book for every student. My recommendation would be to clarify which of those it is, and if the goal really is a colour science book for every government-school child, to revisit the allocation, since the full-coverage cost is closer to 43 crore than to 4 crore.
Interviewer: That is a sensible place to land. Let us stop there.

Padhega India, Badhega India Framework & Recommendations
ANNUAL COLOUR TEXTBOOK BUDGET FOR JHARKHAND GOVERNMENT SCHOOLS
Clarifying Questions: Grades 1 to 10 only. One science book per student per year. Government schools only. Colour printing costs.
Keep In Mind: Move top-down through the funnel before calculating. Low-income families rely on government schools the most, so their penetration is the highest. Round numbers at each step to keep the arithmetic clean.
Brownie Points: Deriving per-book cost from a per-page colour printing rate. Splitting students into grade bands with different book lengths. Benchmarking the estimate against the existing 4.2 crore allocation.
Recommendation: A full-coverage colour science textbook programme for grades 1 to 10 costs roughly 43 crore a year, about ten times the current 4.2 crore allocation. Either the line item funds only reprints and top-ups, or the programme is significantly underfunded and the allocation should be revisited.

title: Death by Chocolate
prompt: Let's start with a quick case. Your client is a chocolate manufacturer and they are facing a decline in profits. Analyse why.

notes.title: Questions
items: Where does the client lie in the value chain?
Do they sell one product or many, and to which segments?
Is the problem limited to a geography or demographic?
What is the magnitude and time horizon of the decline?
Are competitors facing the same problem?

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Break profit into revenue and costs before diving deeper
Establish whether the issue is company-specific or industry-wide
A stable dollar price can still mean a rising rupee cost when the currency moves

notes.title: Brownie Points
items: Splitting solutions into short term and long term
Spotting the currency mismatch between dollar inputs and rupee operations
Flagging single-supplier and single-currency dependence as a risk

visualisations.title: Rupee Cost of Cocoa
visualisations.rhs: Cocoa Price (USD per kg) x Exchange Rate (INR per USD)

rows.shortTerm:
Hedge the currency exposure with forward or futures contracts to lock in a known rate
Pass part of the increase through to price, using the medium to premium brand's pricing power
Optimise costs elsewhere in the value chain to absorb the higher bean cost
Blend Indian cocoa beans with imported ones to reduce dollar exposure
rows.longTerm:
Diversify sourcing across multiple contractors and cocoa-growing geographies to avoid single-supplier, single-currency dependence
Shift towards Indian cultivation of comparable-quality beans over time, noting current volume and quality limits
Lobby the governments of India and Ghana to enable rupee-settled trade, recognising it is slow and uncertain

framework:
Candidate: Thank you for the case. Before I analyse the problem, may I ask a few questions to understand the client better?
Interviewer: Sure, go ahead.
Candidate: Firstly, where is the client located, and where do they lie in the value chain?
Interviewer: They are present pan-India as a manufacturer and distributor. Assume they are like Cadbury.
Candidate: Do they have multiple chocolate bars, and do they serve all income segments?
Interviewer: For this case, take them to have one chocolate bar, mainly for medium to premium customers.
Candidate: Is the problem limited to a particular geography or demographic?
Interviewer: No, it is uniform across the country.
Candidate: Do we know the magnitude and time horizon of the problem?
Interviewer: The decline is significant and has persisted over the past six months.
Candidate: Are competitors facing the same problem?
Interviewer: We are not certain.
Candidate: To begin, I would break profit into revenue minus costs, so the decline could come from falling revenue, rising costs, or both. Where should I focus?
Interviewer: Look at costs. They are rising.
Candidate: I would split costs into fixed and variable. Fixed costs are capital expenditure like land, building, plant, and machinery, while variable costs are day-to-day expenses. Where does the problem lie?
Interviewer: Look at variable costs.
Candidate: I would break variable costs along the value chain: variable research and development, procurement of raw materials, inbound logistics, processing, packaging, storage and warehousing, outbound logistics, distribution, marketing, and after-sales. Is the problem in one of these?
Interviewer: Yes, it is in raw materials.
Candidate: Are we outsourcing raw materials or producing them in house, and are the main inputs cocoa beans, sugar, and milk solids? Which one is the problem?
Interviewer: They are outsourced, and the problem is in cocoa beans.
Candidate: The cost of cocoa beans is the quantity procured multiplied by the price per kg, adjusted for the quality mix. Have any of these changed?
Interviewer: No, the quoted price and other factors have remained unchanged.
Candidate: Where are we procuring the beans from, and do we use multiple contractors?
Interviewer: We source them from Ghana through a single contractor.
Candidate: Then the rise could be internal or external. Internally I would look at the contractor's cost and the transport from Ghana to the Indian port and from the port to our factory. Externally I would look at economic, governmental, legal, and social factors.
Interviewer: Look at external factors, especially economic.
Candidate: Under economic factors I would consider inflation in Ghana, changes in import duties on cocoa entering India, and foreign exchange movements. Could the exchange rate be at play?
Interviewer: Yes. We buy the beans for USD 6 per kg, and our variable cost of production is around Rs 500 per kg of chocolate.
Candidate: So we pay for the beans in dollars while our costs and revenue are in rupees. The dollar price of the beans has not changed, but the rupee has depreciated against the dollar over the past six months, so each dollar of beans now converts into more rupees, which is raising our costs.
Interviewer: Correct. Can you think of possible solutions?
Candidate: I would split them into short term and long term. In the short term: hedge the currency exposure with forward or futures contracts to lock in a known rate; pass part of the increase through to price, since the brand is medium to premium and has pricing power; optimise costs elsewhere in the value chain; and blend Indian cocoa beans with the imported ones to reduce dollar exposure. In the long term: diversify sourcing across multiple contractors and geographies to avoid single-supplier and single-currency dependence; shift towards Indian cultivation of comparable-quality beans over time, keeping volume and quality limits in mind; and lobby the governments of India and Ghana to enable rupee-settled trade, while recognising this is slow and uncertain.
Interviewer: Sounds good. We can close the case here. Thank you.

Death by Chocolate Framework & Recommendations
RISING COCOA COSTS AT A CHOCOLATE MANUFACTURER
Clarifying Questions: Where the client lies in the value chain Whether they sell one product or many and to which segments Whether the problem is limited to a geography or demographic The magnitude and time horizon of the decline Whether competitors face the same problem
Keep In Mind: Break profit into revenue and costs before going deeper Establish whether the issue is company-specific or industry-wide A stable dollar price can still mean a rising rupee cost when the currency moves
Brownie Points: Splitting solutions into short term and long term Spotting the currency mismatch between dollar inputs and rupee operations Flagging single-supplier and single-currency dependence as a risk
RECOMMENDATIONS: Hedge currency exposure with forwards or futures to lock in rates
Pass part of the cost increase through to price using the brand's premium positioning
Blend Indian cocoa beans with imported ones and optimise other value-chain costs in the short term
Diversify sourcing across contractors and geographies over the long term
Build up Indian cultivation of comparable-quality beans and pursue rupee-settled trade over time
